Title: Release: Final Deployment and Production Validation
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Deploy and validate the final version of the Recipe Suggestion application.

This issue is the final release gate for the project.

At this stage, major application features and infrastructure should already be implemented. The purpose of this issue is to:

- deploy the final approved application version
- verify the production AWS environment
- apply required database migrations
- validate frontend/backend integration
- verify authentication and authorization
- verify security configuration
- verify monitoring
- execute final smoke tests
- confirm documentation matches the deployed system
- record the final release version

Do not use this issue to introduce major new features.

## Where to Work

This task may involve:

```text
backend/
frontend/
.github/workflows/
docs/
```

Relevant documentation includes:

```text
README.md

frontend/README.md

docs/system-design.md
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/database-design.md
docs/api-design.md
```

```bash

python manage.py check
python manage.py test
```

```bash

npm run lint
```

```text
  ▼
```

## Recommendation Validation

```text
AVAILABLE_ONLY
```

## Canonical Ingredient Validation

Verify the final system still follows:

```text
                  Ingredient
                  /        \
                 ▼          ▼
             Inventory    Recipes
                  \        /
                   ▼      ▼

```

## Persistence Test

Perform at least one persistence check.

Example:

```text
User
  ↓
Add Inventory Item
  ↓
RDS
  ↓
Restart/redeploy backend
  ↓
Sign In
  ↓
Inventory Item Still Exists
```

This demonstrates that application state is not tied to an individual EC2 instance.

## Multiple-Instance Validation

If multiple backend instances are deployed, verify:

```text
              ALB
            /     \
           ▼       ▼
        EC2 #1   EC2 #2
```

Both should:

- run the intended application version
- become healthy
- use the same RDS database
- use the same persistent media architecture
- enforce the same authentication/authorization rules
- obtain production configuration securely

Users should not receive inconsistent application state based on which instance serves a request.

## Auto Scaling Validation

Where Auto Scaling is implemented, verify:

```text
Minimum Capacity
Desired Capacity
Maximum Capacity
Scaling Policy
Launch Template
Target Group
Health Checks
```

Do not intentionally generate another large load test if #26 already produced sufficient evidence.

The purpose here is final configuration verification.

```text

   │

EC2
   │
   ▼
```

```text

ALB → EC2            ✓

Internet → RDS       ✗
```

## Secrets Review

Confirm:

```text

✗ production secrets

Docker image
✗ production secrets

React bundle
✗ backend secrets

```

Then verify that the appropriate metrics/logs update.

For example:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
ALB
   │
   ▼
Django
```

Confirm the dashboard remains useful for explaining system behavior during the final presentation.

Do not rerun scalability tests unnecessarily if #26 already produced valid results.

Instead verify that:

```text
docs/performance-testing.md
```

- throughput
- average latency
- p95 latency
- error rate
- infrastructure metrics
- one-vs-multiple-instance comparison where performed

and corresponding graphs/tables.

These statistics should correspond to actual tests.

## Final Security Evidence

Verify:

```text

```

contains the results from #29.

Useful evidence may include:

```text
Authentication tests
Authorization tests
User ownership tests
HTTPS validation
RDS isolation
Security-group validation
Secret-management validation
```

Do not claim tests were performed if they were not.

## Final Integration Evidence

Verify #30's major workflows have been executed against the final application version.

If the final deployment differs substantially from the version previously tested, rerun the affected tests.

## Failure Handling

If a release-blocking problem is discovered:

```text
Final Validation
      │
      ▼
Problem Found
      │
      ▼
Create/Fix Issue
      │
      ▼
PR
      │
      ▼
CI
      │
      ▼
Redeploy
      │
      ▼
Retest
```

Do not silently patch production and leave the repository inconsistent with the deployed application.

## Release-Blocking Problems

Examples include:

```text
Application cannot start
Frontend cannot reach API
Database migrations fail
Authentication is broken
Users can access other users' private data
Admin authorization is broken
Production secrets are exposed
RDS is publicly accessible
Major required workflow does not work
```

These should be resolved before declaring the final release complete.

Minor known limitations may be documented instead where appropriate.

## Evidence Collection

Collect useful final evidence for the report/presentation.

Examples:

```text
Final application
Architecture
AWS deployment
CloudWatch dashboard
Scalability graphs
Security configuration
Successful CI/CD pipeline
```

Review screenshots carefully before including them.

Do not expose:

- passwords
- secret values
- authentication tokens
- private keys
- AWS credentials

## Cost Review

Before considering the project complete, review active AWS resources.

Document which resources are required for the demo/evaluation.

After the course/demo is complete, resources that are no longer needed should be stopped or removed appropriately to avoid unnecessary charges.

Do not destroy required project infrastructure before final evaluation.

## Important

This issue is a **release gate**, not another feature-development sprint.

If a nonessential new feature is proposed at this point, prefer moving it to future work rather than destabilizing the final application.

The priority is:

```text
Correct
   +
Secure
   +
Tested
   +
Documented
   +
Deployable
```

not:

```text
Maximum number of features
```

### Do NOT

- Add major new features during final validation
- Deploy code that failed CI
- Ignore failing tests
- Ignore failed migrations
- Ignore unhealthy ALB targets
- Mark untested workflows as passing
- Fabricate scalability statistics
- Claim unimplemented infrastructure exists
- Expose RDS
- Expose production secrets
- Disable security controls to make the demo work
- Manually patch production without updating source control
- Delete required AWS resources before evaluation
- Present future features as completed
- Push final fixes directly to `main`

Title: Testing: Integration and End-to-End Application Testing
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Perform integration and end-to-end testing of the Recipe Suggestion application.

Verify that the major frontend and backend components work correctly together and that complete user workflows behave as designed.

Unit tests for individual modules are not sufficient for this issue.

This issue should validate interactions between:

- React frontend
- Django REST API
- Authentication
- Ingredients
- Recipes
- Inventory
- Recommendations
- User profiles/preferences
- Saved recipes
- PostgreSQL/RDS
- S3 media where applicable

The goal is to verify that the application works as a complete system before final deployment.

## Where to Work

Testing may involve:

```text
backend/
frontend/
```

Potential additions include:

```text
backend/tests/
frontend/src/
tests/integration/
tests/e2e/
docs/testing.md
```

Use the project's existing testing structure where possible rather than creating unnecessary duplicate test directories.

Relevant documentation:

- `docs/api-design.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `backend/README.md`
- frontend README
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Integration Testing

- [ ] Verify frontend API services communicate with the Django API
- [ ] Verify API responses match frontend expectations
- [ ] Verify related Django modules work together correctly
- [ ] Verify database relationships behave correctly
- [ ] Verify authentication integrates with protected endpoints
- [ ] Verify user preferences affect relevant application behavior
- [ ] Verify inventory uses canonical Ingredient records
- [ ] Verify recipes use canonical Ingredient records
- [ ] Verify recommendations use the expected ingredient/recipe data
- [ ] Verify saved recipes work for authenticated users

### Guest Workflow

- [ ] Open the application without authentication
- [ ] Search/select ingredients
- [ ] Add/remove temporary ingredients
- [ ] Request recipe recommendations
- [ ] Test `AVAILABLE_ONLY`
- [ ] Test `PARTIAL_MATCH`
- [ ] Open a recipe detail page
- [ ] Verify Guest-only restrictions
- [ ] Verify Guest data behaves as temporary state

### Registered User Workflow

- [ ] Sign in as a Registered User
- [ ] Load the user profile
- [ ] Update preferences where supported
- [ ] Update allergies where supported
- [ ] Add inventory ingredients
- [ ] Remove inventory ingredients
- [ ] Request recommendations using stored inventory
- [ ] Open recipe details
- [ ] Save a recipe
- [ ] View saved recipes
- [ ] Remove a saved recipe
- [ ] Sign out
- [ ] Verify protected data is no longer accessible without authentication

### Admin Workflow

- [ ] Sign in with Admin privileges
- [ ] Verify Admin can access intended administrative functionality
- [ ] Verify Admin can still use normal Registered User functionality
- [ ] Verify Admin-only operations are unavailable to normal users

### Recipe / Ingredient Integration

- [ ] Verify Recipe ingredients reference canonical `Ingredient` records
- [ ] Verify Inventory items reference canonical `Ingredient` records
- [ ] Verify the same canonical ingredient can be used by both modules
- [ ] Verify ingredient search returns canonical IDs
- [ ] Verify duplicate parallel ingredient models are not introduced

### Recommendation Integration

- [ ] Verify recommendation input uses canonical ingredients
- [ ] Verify `AVAILABLE_ONLY` behavior
- [ ] Verify `PARTIAL_MATCH` behavior
- [ ] Verify match information is returned correctly
- [ ] Verify frontend renders recommendation results
- [ ] Verify recipe links navigate to the correct Recipe Detail page
- [ ] Verify invalid/empty recommendation inputs are handled appropriately

### Error Handling

- [ ] Test invalid resource IDs
- [ ] Test unavailable recipes
- [ ] Test failed API requests
- [ ] Test unauthenticated protected requests
- [ ] Test unauthorized requests
- [ ] Test empty search results
- [ ] Test empty inventory
- [ ] Verify frontend displays reasonable error/empty states
- [ ] Verify backend does not expose sensitive debug information

### Production Integration

When the AWS environment is available:

- [ ] Test the deployed CloudFront frontend
- [ ] Test API calls through the ALB
- [ ] Verify Django communicates with RDS
- [ ] Verify media loads from S3 where applicable
- [ ] Verify authentication works in the deployed environment
- [ ] Verify HTTPS frontend/backend communication
- [ ] Verify CORS configuration
- [ ] Verify representative workflows through the production architecture

## System Flow

The complete deployed request flow should resemble:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
React
 │
 │ HTTPS API Request
 ▼
ALB
 │
 ▼
Django
 │
 ├────────→ Cognito
 │
 ├────────→ RDS
 │
 └────────→ S3
```

End-to-end testing should verify the application through this architecture rather than testing only isolated components.

## Guest User Flow

A core Guest flow should be tested:

```text
Open Application
      │
      ▼
Search Ingredients
      │
      ▼
Select Ingredients
      │
      ▼
Temporary Ingredient State
      │
      ▼
Request Recommendations
      │
      ├── AVAILABLE_ONLY
      │
      └── PARTIAL_MATCH
      │
      ▼
Recommendation Results
      │
      ▼
Recipe Detail
```

A Guest should not need to create an account for this basic flow.

However, Guest users should not gain access to Registered User-only persistent functionality.

## Registered User Flow

Test the persistent-user workflow:

```text
Sign In
   │
   ▼
Dashboard
   │
   ├── Inventory
   ├── Profile
   ├── Preferences
   └── Saved Recipes
   │
   ▼
Recommendations
   │
   ▼
Recipe Detail
```

Verify persistence.

For example:

```text
User adds Ingredient to Inventory
        │
        ▼
Sign out / new session
        │
        ▼
Sign in
        │
        ▼
Ingredient still exists
```

This distinguishes Registered User behavior from temporary Guest behavior.

## Canonical Ingredient Integration

This is one of the most important cross-module tests.

The architecture should remain:

```text
                  Ingredient
                  /        \
                 /          \
                ▼            ▼
           Inventory       Recipes
                \            /
                 \          /
                  ▼        ▼
                Recommendations
```

Not:

```text
InventoryIngredient

RecipeIngredientName

RecommendationIngredient

GuestIngredientModel
```

as independent definitions of the same real ingredient.

Test that IDs passed between APIs consistently refer to the shared canonical `Ingredient`.

## Recommendation Modes

Both required modes should be tested.

### AVAILABLE_ONLY

Conceptually:

```text
User Ingredients:
chicken
rice
onion

Recipe requires:
chicken
rice

Result:
Eligible
```

A recipe requiring unavailable ingredients should not incorrectly behave as a complete available-only match.

### PARTIAL_MATCH

Conceptually:

```text
User Ingredients:
chicken
rice

Recipe requires:
chicken
rice
onion

Result:
Partial match

Missing:
onion
```

Verify the API and frontend agree on the representation of matching/missing ingredients.

## Preferences and Allergies

Where implemented, verify saved preferences/allergies are correctly integrated with relevant recipe/recommendation behavior.

Conceptually:

```text
User Profile
     │
     ├── Preferences
     └── Allergies
            │
            ▼
      Recommendation
```

Do not assume that a preference filter works simply because it can be saved to the database.

Test the actual resulting behavior.

## API Contract

Integration testing should verify the frontend and backend agree on:

```text
URL
HTTP method
request body
response body
status codes
IDs
pagination
error format
```

For example:

```text
Frontend expects:

recipe.id
recipe.name
recipe.ingredients

Backend returns:

recipe.recipe_id
recipe.title
recipe.items
```

would be an integration failure even if both modules individually pass their own tests.

## Authentication Integration

The deployed flow should be:

```text
User
  │
  ▼
Authentication
  │
  ▼
Frontend obtains authenticated state/token
  │
  ▼
API Request
  │
  ▼
Django verifies authentication
  │
  ▼
Authorization
```

Do not consider React route protection sufficient.

Protected API endpoints must enforce authentication on the backend.

## User Data Isolation

Use at least two test users.

For example:

```text
User A
├── Inventory A
└── Saved Recipes A

User B
├── Inventory B
└── Saved Recipes B
```

Verify:

```text
User A cannot read/write User B private data.

User B cannot read/write User A private data.
```

This overlaps intentionally with #29 because it is both a security and integration requirement.

## Error States

Test expected failures, not only successful workflows.

Examples:

```text
No ingredients selected
No recommendations found
Recipe does not exist
Network/API failure
Unauthorized request
Expired/invalid authentication
Empty inventory
Empty saved recipes
```

The frontend should remain usable and provide an appropriate state rather than crashing.

## Browser Refresh / Routing

Test direct navigation and refresh for routes such as:

```text
/
/recipes/<id>
/dashboard
/profile
```

This is particularly important after CloudFront deployment because React client-side routing must work with the static hosting configuration.

## Database Persistence

Verify persistent data survives application runtime replacement.

For example:

```text
Create Inventory Item
       │
       ▼
RDS
       │
       ▼
Restart Django container
       │
       ▼
Retrieve Inventory
       │
       ▼
Item still exists
```

Persistent application data must not depend on an EC2 instance or container filesystem.

## Media Integration

Where recipe images/media are implemented:

```text
Recipe
   │
   ▼
Media Reference
   │
   ▼
S3
```

Verify media remains available regardless of which backend instance handles the request.

## Multiple Backend Instances

Where Auto Scaling/multiple targets are available, repeat representative workflows with multiple healthy backend instances.

The user should not observe different application state depending on which EC2 instance receives the request.

```text
Request #1 → EC2 #1
Request #2 → EC2 #2

Same persistent application state
```

## Test Data

Create predictable test data where necessary.

Examples:

```text
Test Ingredients
Test Recipes
Test Users
Test Inventory
```

Do not rely on random production data to determine whether tests pass.

Test data should be removable/resettable where practical.

## Automated vs. Manual Testing

Automate repeatable integration tests where practical.

Some full deployment validation may remain manual.

Document both.

Example:

```text
Automated
├── API integration
├── permissions
├── model relationships
└── common error cases

Manual / E2E
├── CloudFront navigation
├── complete browser flow
├── visual error states
└── deployed infrastructure validation
```

The goal is not to automate every click.

The goal is to have repeatable evidence that the important workflows work.

## Test Matrix

Document the major flows.

For example:

```text
Flow                          Guest   User   Admin
-------------------------------------------------
Ingredient Search               ✓      ✓      ✓
Recommendations                 ✓      ✓      ✓
Recipe Detail                   ✓      ✓      ✓
Persistent Inventory            ✗      ✓      ✓
Saved Recipes                   ✗      ✓      ✓
Profile                         ✗      ✓      ✓
Admin Operations                ✗      ✗      ✓
```

Adjust this table to match the final implemented application.

## Security

Integration tests must preserve production security.

Do not:

- disable authentication
- disable authorization
- disable CSRF globally
- expose RDS
- expose secrets
- weaken security groups

simply to make end-to-end testing easier.

If integration testing reveals a security configuration problem, fix the underlying configuration.

## Evidence

Record actual results.

A simple final test record might look like:

```text
Test                          Expected          Result
--------------------------------------------------------
Guest recommendations         Works             PASS
Guest persistent inventory    Denied            PASS
User inventory persistence    Persists          PASS
User A → User B inventory     Denied            PASS
Recipe detail                 Loads             PASS
AVAILABLE_ONLY                Correct matches   PASS
PARTIAL_MATCH                 Correct matches   PASS
CloudFront refresh            Loads app         PASS
```

Do not mark tests as passing before executing them.

## Important

Unit testing asks:

```text
Does this component work?
```

Integration testing asks:

```text
Do these components work together?
```

End-to-end testing asks:

```text
Can the user complete the real workflow?
```

We need all three.

### Do NOT

- Test only individual modules
- Test only successful paths
- Ignore Guest behavior
- Ignore Admin behavior
- Ignore user ownership/isolation
- Create duplicate Ingredient models to simplify integration
- Change API contracts silently
- Disable security controls for testing
- Use the health endpoint as proof the application works
- Depend only on localhost testing for final validation
- Mark unexecuted tests as passing
- Use uncontrolled production data
- Ignore browser refresh/routing behavior
- Modify unrelated functionality
- Push testing changes directly to `main`

Title: Security: Security Testing and Application Hardening
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Perform a structured security review of the application and deployed AWS architecture.

Verify that the security controls implemented throughout the project work as intended and identify configuration or application-level weaknesses before the final release.

The review should cover:

- Authentication
- Authorization
- API access control
- User data isolation
- Input validation
- CORS and CSRF
- HTTPS
- AWS network security
- IAM permissions
- Secret management
- Logging
- Dependency security

This issue should produce documented evidence that the system was reviewed rather than simply claiming that the architecture is secure.

## Where to Work

Security testing may affect both:

```text
backend/
frontend/
```

Potential documentation changes include:

```text
docs/security-design.md
docs/system-design.md
docs/deployment.md
```

If security-specific tests are added, place them alongside the appropriate backend/frontend test suites.

Do not create a completely separate implementation of application functionality just for security testing.

## Tasks

### Authentication

- [ ] Verify protected endpoints reject unauthenticated requests
- [ ] Verify valid authenticated users can access intended functionality
- [ ] Verify invalid/expired authentication credentials are rejected
- [ ] Verify authentication failures do not expose sensitive information
- [ ] Verify authentication is enforced by the backend rather than only React

### Authorization

- [ ] Verify users cannot access another user's private resources
- [ ] Verify users cannot modify another user's inventory
- [ ] Verify users cannot modify another user's profile/preferences
- [ ] Verify users cannot modify another user's saved data
- [ ] Verify normal users cannot access Admin-only operations
- [ ] Verify authorization checks occur on the backend

### Guest Access

- [ ] Verify Guest users can access intended public functionality
- [ ] Verify Guest users cannot access Registered User-only functionality
- [ ] Verify Guest users cannot access Admin functionality
- [ ] Verify temporary Guest data does not accidentally provide access to persistent user data

### API Input Validation

- [ ] Test missing required fields
- [ ] Test malformed input
- [ ] Test invalid IDs
- [ ] Test excessively long values where relevant
- [ ] Test invalid enum/options values
- [ ] Test unsupported request methods
- [ ] Verify invalid requests return appropriate errors
- [ ] Verify invalid input does not cause unhandled server errors

### Ingredient / Recipe Data

- [ ] Verify canonical Ingredient constraints remain enforced
- [ ] Verify duplicate canonical ingredients are rejected appropriately
- [ ] Verify Recipe relationships cannot reference invalid objects
- [ ] Verify API validation prevents malformed relationship data

### CORS

- [ ] Verify the deployed frontend origin is permitted
- [ ] Verify unnecessary origins are not permitted
- [ ] Verify production does not rely on unrestricted CORS without justification

### CSRF

Where applicable:

- [ ] Verify CSRF protection is configured correctly
- [ ] Verify trusted origins match the deployed application
- [ ] Verify CSRF protection was not globally disabled merely to make frontend integration work

### HTTPS

- [ ] Verify production frontend uses HTTPS
- [ ] Verify production API uses HTTPS
- [ ] Verify HTTP redirects appropriately where configured
- [ ] Verify authentication information is not intentionally transmitted over plain HTTP
- [ ] Verify no mixed-content problems exist

### AWS Network Security

- [ ] Review ALB security group
- [ ] Review EC2 security group
- [ ] Review RDS security group
- [ ] Verify backend application ports are not unnecessarily public
- [ ] Verify RDS is not publicly accessible
- [ ] Verify PostgreSQL is not open to `0.0.0.0/0`
- [ ] Verify administrative access is restricted

### IAM

- [ ] Review backend EC2 IAM role
- [ ] Review CI/CD deployment permissions
- [ ] Review S3 permissions
- [ ] Review ECR permissions
- [ ] Review Secrets Manager permissions
- [ ] Verify roles follow least privilege where practical
- [ ] Verify application components do not use `AdministratorAccess`

### Secrets

- [ ] Verify production secrets are not committed to Git
- [ ] Verify production secrets are not embedded in Docker images
- [ ] Verify backend secrets are not present in the React bundle
- [ ] Verify secrets are not exposed through API responses
- [ ] Verify secrets are not intentionally written to logs
- [ ] Verify AWS credentials are not hardcoded

### Logging

- [ ] Review CloudWatch logs for sensitive information
- [ ] Verify passwords are not logged
- [ ] Verify authentication tokens are not logged
- [ ] Verify secret values are not logged
- [ ] Verify application errors provide useful operational information without exposing sensitive configuration

### Dependency Review

- [ ] Review Python dependencies for known security issues
- [ ] Review npm dependencies for known security issues
- [ ] Investigate relevant high-severity findings
- [ ] Update vulnerable dependencies where appropriate and compatible
- [ ] Document accepted/unresolved findings

### Django Deployment Review

- [ ] Run Django deployment security checks
- [ ] Review all relevant warnings
- [ ] Verify `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Verify production `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
- [ ] Verify secure-cookie settings where applicable
- [ ] Verify HTTPS/proxy settings
- [ ] Verify production CORS/CSRF configuration

## Security Model

The application uses multiple security layers.

```text
                       User
                        │
                      HTTPS
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
          CloudFront             ALB
              │                   │
              ▼                   ▼
          Frontend              Django
                                  │
                      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
                      ▼           ▼           ▼
                  Cognito        RDS          S3
```

Additional controls include:

```text
IAM
    → AWS service authorization

Security Groups
    → Network isolation

Secrets Manager
    → Sensitive configuration

Django
    → API authorization + validation

CloudWatch
    → Monitoring and audit evidence
```

Security testing should verify these layers rather than evaluating only the React interface.

## Authentication vs. Authorization

These must be tested separately.

Authentication asks:

```text
Who are you?
```

Authorization asks:

```text
Are you allowed to do this?
```

For example:

```text
User A logs in successfully.

User A requests:
User B's private inventory.

Authentication:
✓ User A is valid

Authorization:
✗ User A must not receive User B's inventory
```

A system is not secure merely because login works.

## Object Ownership

User-owned resources must enforce ownership on the backend.

Examples include:

```text
Inventory
Profile
Preferences
Saved Recipes
Shopping Lists (if implemented later)
```

Test scenarios such as:

```text
User A owns resource 123.

User B sends:

GET /api/.../123/
PUT /api/.../123/
DELETE /api/.../123/
```

The backend should reject operations User B is not authorized to perform.

Do not rely on React hiding buttons.

## Admin Security

Admin privileges must be enforced server-side.

Incorrect:

```text
React:
if admin:
    show admin button
```

This is useful for UI behavior but is not authorization.

Required:

```text
Request
   ↓
Django
   ↓
Check authenticated role/permission
   ↓
Allow / Deny
```

Attempt Admin requests using a normal Registered User account during testing.

## Input Validation

Test APIs with invalid data intentionally.

Examples:

```text
Missing fields
Invalid IDs
Incorrect data types
Unknown values
Very long strings
Malformed request bodies
```

Expected behavior should be controlled errors such as appropriate `4xx` responses.

Avoid:

```text
Invalid request
      ↓
Unhandled exception
      ↓
500 + sensitive error details
```

## Injection Protection

Use Django ORM and serializers appropriately.

Avoid manually constructing SQL using user-provided values.

Where search/filter inputs are supported, test unusual input and verify it does not alter query structure or cause unsafe behavior.

Do not implement custom SQL escaping as a replacement for safe database APIs.

## Error Handling

Production errors should not reveal:

```text
Database credentials
File paths unnecessarily
Environment variables
Secret values
Internal configuration
Debug tracebacks
```

Useful errors should still be returned to clients where appropriate.

Example:

```json
{
  "detail": "Recipe not found."
}
```

rather than exposing internal server information.

## Frontend Security

Remember:

```text
React = client-controlled environment
```

Users can inspect and modify frontend JavaScript and manually call APIs.

Therefore:

```text
Frontend validation
        +
Backend validation
```

is required.

Frontend validation improves usability.

Backend validation enforces security.

## Secret Scan

Review the repository for accidentally committed secrets.

Check for patterns related to:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
DB_PASSWORD
private keys
tokens
```

If a real credential has ever been committed, removing it from the current file does not make that credential safe again.

Rotate exposed credentials.

## Docker Image Review

Verify the production Docker image does not contain:

```text
.env
AWS credentials
database passwords
private keys
development secrets
```

The Docker image should contain application code and dependencies, not production secrets.

## Dependency Security

Use the appropriate ecosystem tools to inspect dependencies.

For Python, use an appropriate dependency vulnerability scanner.

For frontend dependencies, review the project's npm security results where applicable.

Do not blindly apply major dependency upgrades without testing compatibility.

Prioritize meaningful/high-severity findings.

## Security Testing Evidence

Document the tests performed.

Example:

```text
Test                         Expected          Result
------------------------------------------------------
Guest → private inventory    Denied            PASS
User A → User B inventory    Denied            PASS
User → admin endpoint        Denied            PASS
Public → RDS                 Blocked           PASS
HTTP → frontend              Redirect HTTPS    PASS
Invalid recipe ID            4xx               PASS
```

Use actual results.

Do not mark tests PASS without performing them.

## Severity

If issues are discovered, classify them approximately:

```text
Critical
High
Medium
Low
Informational
```

Prioritize security problems that could expose:

- credentials
- private user data
- administrative functionality
- database access
- AWS infrastructure

## Security Findings

For each meaningful issue, document:

```text
Finding
Severity
Affected component
Expected behavior
Actual behavior
Resolution
Retest result
```

Example:

```text
Finding:
Users could retrieve another user's inventory.

Severity:
High

Resolution:
Added ownership filtering.

Retest:
PASS
```

This can provide strong evidence for the final report.

## Scalability Security

Security must continue working with multiple backend instances.

Test/verify that:

```text
ALB
 ├── EC2 #1
 └── EC2 #2
```

does not change:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Ownership validation
Secret access
Network boundaries
```

New Auto Scaling instances should automatically receive the intended:

```text
IAM role
Security group
Production configuration
```

without manual security configuration.

## Important

The goal is not to claim:

```text
"The system is 100% secure."
```

No meaningful review can prove that.

The goal is to demonstrate:

```text
Threats considered
       +
Controls implemented
       +
Tests performed
       +
Findings corrected
       =
Evidence of secure system design
```

This is much stronger for the professor's security criterion.

### Do NOT

- Disable authentication to make tests easier
- Disable authorization to make tests easier
- Disable CSRF globally to fix integration
- Enable unrestricted CORS unnecessarily
- Make RDS public for testing
- Open PostgreSQL to `0.0.0.0/0`
- Open backend ports publicly unnecessarily
- Commit test credentials
- Put real credentials in documentation
- Print authentication tokens
- Test infrastructure you do not own or have authorization to test
- Perform destructive security testing against unrelated systems
- Claim the application is completely secure
- Mark tests as passing without executing them
- Ignore high-severity dependency findings without review
- Modify unrelated functionality
- Push security fixes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Authentication

- [ ] Protected endpoints reject unauthenticated access
- [ ] Invalid credentials are rejected
- [ ] Authentication is enforced server-side

### Authorization

- [ ] User-owned resources enforce ownership
- [ ] Users cannot modify another user's private resources
- [ ] Guest restrictions are enforced
- [ ] Admin permissions are enforced by the backend

### Application Security

- [ ] Invalid API input is handled safely
- [ ] Production errors do not expose sensitive configuration
- [ ] Backend performs authoritative validation
- [ ] Relevant dependency vulnerabilities have been reviewed

### Infrastructure

- [ ] Public traffic uses HTTPS
- [ ] Backend application port is appropriately restricted
- [ ] RDS is not publicly accessible
- [ ] Database access is restricted to the backend tier
- [ ] Administrative access is restricted

### Secrets / IAM

- [ ] Production secrets are not committed
- [ ] Production secrets are not embedded in Docker images
- [ ] Frontend contains no backend secrets
- [ ] CloudWatch logs do not intentionally expose secrets
- [ ] IAM permissions have been reviewed for least privilege

### Evidence

- [ ] Security test checklist is documented
- [ ] Actual test results are recorded
- [ ] Meaningful findings are documented
- [ ] High-priority findings are resolved
- [ ] Resolved findings are retested
- [ ] Remaining known limitations are documented

## Before Submitting

Run backend tests:

```bash
cd backend

python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy
python manage.py test
```

Run applicable frontend checks:

```bash
cd frontend

npm run lint
npm run build
```

Perform the security test checklist against the deployed environment.

Review:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Ownership
Input Validation
HTTPS
Security Groups
IAM
Secrets
Logs
Dependencies
```

Record actual results in the security documentation.

Fix discovered security problems and retest them.

Update:

```text
docs/security-design.md
```

and other relevant documentation.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push security fixes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`security/testing-hardening`

Title: Security: Configure HTTPS and Production Network Security
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Secure the deployed application's production network architecture.

All public application traffic should use HTTPS, backend resources should expose only the network access they require, and communication between AWS components should follow clearly defined security boundaries.

This issue focuses on:

- HTTPS
- TLS certificates
- ALB security
- EC2 network exposure
- RDS isolation
- security-group relationships
- production Django HTTPS settings

The intended architecture is:

```text
                         Internet
                            │
                          HTTPS
                            │
             ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
             ▼                             ▼
        CloudFront                        ALB
             │                             │
             ▼                             ▼
      S3 Frontend                     EC2 / Django
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                          RDS
```

Public traffic must not require direct access to EC2 or RDS.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and Django production configuration.

Potential repository changes include:

- `backend/config/settings.py`
- deployment configuration
- `.env.example`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `docs/security-design.md` if created

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### HTTPS / TLS

- [ ] Determine the production frontend and backend endpoint strategy
- [ ] Configure an AWS Certificate Manager certificate where required
- [ ] Configure HTTPS for the public backend endpoint
- [ ] Configure the ALB HTTPS listener
- [ ] Forward HTTPS requests to the backend target group
- [ ] Redirect HTTP to HTTPS where appropriate
- [ ] Verify HTTPS works without certificate errors
- [ ] Verify the frontend uses HTTPS
- [ ] Verify frontend API requests use HTTPS
- [ ] Document certificate and HTTPS configuration

### ALB Security

- [ ] Review ALB security-group rules
- [ ] Allow only required public application ports
- [ ] Ensure backend traffic is routed through the ALB
- [ ] Verify health checks continue working
- [ ] Verify unnecessary ports are not exposed

### EC2 Security

- [ ] Review backend EC2 security-group rules
- [ ] Restrict the Django/Gunicorn application port to the ALB security group
- [ ] Remove unnecessary direct public backend access
- [ ] Review administrative access
- [ ] Restrict SSH if SSH remains enabled
- [ ] Prefer non-public administrative access where practical

### RDS Security

- [ ] Verify RDS is not publicly accessible
- [ ] Restrict PostgreSQL access to the backend security group
- [ ] Verify port `5432` is not open to the Internet
- [ ] Verify frontend infrastructure cannot directly access RDS

### Django Production Security

- [ ] Verify `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Configure secure proxy/HTTPS behavior correctly
- [ ] Configure secure cookies where applicable
- [ ] Configure trusted origins where required
- [ ] Verify production `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
- [ ] Run Django deployment security checks
- [ ] Review remaining deployment warnings

## Public Traffic

The intended public paths are:

```text
User
 │
 │ HTTPS
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
React Frontend
```

and:

```text
React / Client
      │
      │ HTTPS
      ▼
     ALB
      │
      ▼
    Django
```

Avoid:

```text
Internet
   │
   ├────────→ EC2:8000
   │
   └────────→ RDS:5432
```

EC2 and RDS should not act as arbitrary public application entry points.

## HTTPS Architecture

The backend public entry point should terminate TLS through the intended AWS edge/load-balancing layer.

Conceptually:

```text
Browser
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
  ALB
   │
   ▼
Django
```

The frontend should also be served securely:

```text
Browser
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Frontend S3
```

This avoids mixed-content problems such as:

```text
HTTPS Frontend
      │
      X
      ▼
HTTP API
```

## HTTP Redirect

Where HTTP is exposed for convenience, configure it to redirect to HTTPS.

Conceptually:

```text
HTTP :80
   │
   ▼
301 Redirect
   │
   ▼
HTTPS :443
```

Do not maintain HTTP as the normal production communication path.

## AWS Certificate Manager

Use AWS Certificate Manager where appropriate for TLS certificates.

Conceptually:

```text
ACM Certificate
      │
      ▼
ALB HTTPS Listener
      │
      ▼
Target Group
```

If a custom domain is not yet available, document what is achievable with the AWS-provided endpoints and what remains dependent on domain configuration.

Do not commit private TLS keys to Git.

## Security Group Architecture

Security groups should establish clear network boundaries.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
ALB Security Group
   │
   ▼
Backend Security Group
   │
   ▼
Database Security Group
```

### ALB Security Group

Expected public access:

```text
HTTPS / TCP 443
Source: Internet
```

If HTTP is used only for redirect:

```text
HTTP / TCP 80
Source: Internet
```

### Backend Security Group

Application traffic should come from:

```text
Source:
ALB Security Group
```

rather than:

```text
Source:
0.0.0.0/0
```

### Database Security Group

PostgreSQL traffic should come from:

```text
Source:
Backend Security Group
```

rather than:

```text
Source:
0.0.0.0/0
```

## Security Group Chaining

The intended model is:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
[ ALB SG ]
   │
   ▼
[ EC2 SG ]
   │
   ▼
[ RDS SG ]
```

Each layer trusts only the previous layer for the required traffic.

This provides a clear security boundary that can be explained in the final system-design report.

## EC2 Administrative Access

Do not expose SSH broadly.

Avoid:

```text
TCP 22
0.0.0.0/0
```

If SSH is required, restrict the source appropriately.

Where practical, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager can be used for administrative access without exposing SSH publicly.

Administrative access and application traffic should be treated as separate concerns.

## RDS Isolation

RDS must remain isolated from public users.

Correct:

```text
User
  │
  X
  ▼
 RDS
```

Application access:

```text
Django
  │
  ✓
  ▼
 RDS
```

The database should never need to accept direct connections from React or CloudFront.

## Django HTTPS Configuration

Because Django runs behind a proxy/load balancer, production configuration must correctly recognize secure requests.

Review settings such as those related to:

```text
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS
```

Configure only what is appropriate for the final architecture.

Do not blindly copy security settings without understanding how the ALB forwards requests.

## Authentication Tokens

Authentication credentials/tokens must be transmitted only over secure connections in production.

Avoid:

```text
Authentication Token
        │
        ▼
Plain HTTP
```

Use:

```text
Authentication Token
        │
        ▼
HTTPS
```

HTTPS protects data in transit but does not replace application authentication or authorization.

## CORS

Production CORS should permit the intended frontend origin rather than arbitrary websites.

Conceptually:

```text
CloudFront Frontend
        │
        ✓
        ▼
     Django API
```

Do not use unrestricted CORS as the final solution unless the API is intentionally designed for arbitrary origins.

## CSRF

Where Django CSRF protection applies, trusted origins should correspond to the actual deployed application.

Do not globally disable CSRF merely because the frontend and backend are deployed separately.

## Security Headers

Review Django's applicable production security settings and headers.

Use:

```bash
python manage.py check --deploy
```

as one part of the review.

Do not treat this command as proof that the entire AWS architecture is secure.

Network configuration, IAM, authentication, authorization, and application behavior must also be reviewed.

## Scalability

Security controls must continue working when backend capacity changes.

Incorrect:

```text
ALB
 ↓
EC2 #1 ✓

New EC2 #2
 ↓
Manual firewall setup required
```

Prefer:

```text
Auto Scaling
     │
     ▼
New EC2
     │
     ▼
Backend Security Group
     │
     ▼
Automatically accepts ALB traffic
```

Security groups should therefore be associated with backend roles/tiers rather than individual hardcoded IP addresses.

This allows secure horizontal scaling.

## Security Verification

The final architecture should demonstrate:

```text
Publicly reachable:
✓ CloudFront
✓ ALB HTTPS

Not generally publicly reachable:
✗ Django application port
✗ PostgreSQL
```

Administrative interfaces should also be restricted appropriately.

## Security Evidence

For the final report, capture evidence such as:

```text
HTTPS frontend
HTTPS API
ALB listener configuration
Security-group relationships
RDS public-access setting
Django deployment security check
```

Do not include:

- passwords
- secret values
- private keys
- authentication tokens
- sensitive AWS account information

in screenshots or documentation.

## Cost Awareness

HTTPS and network security should use the infrastructure already required by the application where practical.

Do not create unnecessary load balancers or duplicate resources simply to demonstrate security.

## Important

Different security mechanisms solve different problems:

```text
HTTPS
└── Protects data in transit

Security Groups
└── Restrict network access

Cognito
└── Authentication

Django Permissions
└── Authorization

Secrets Manager
└── Protects sensitive configuration

IAM
└── Controls AWS resource access
```

A secure design uses these layers together.

### Do NOT

- Leave the Django application port publicly open unnecessarily
- Expose RDS publicly
- Allow PostgreSQL from `0.0.0.0/0`
- Leave SSH open to `0.0.0.0/0`
- Use HTTP as the intended production API transport
- Send authentication tokens over plain HTTP
- Disable CSRF simply to fix frontend integration
- Allow unrestricted production CORS unnecessarily
- Commit TLS private keys
- Commit certificates containing sensitive private material
- Hardcode individual Auto Scaling instance IP addresses
- Give the frontend direct database access
- Treat HTTPS as a replacement for authentication
- Treat security groups as a replacement for authorization
- Ignore `check --deploy` warnings without reviewing them
- Modify unrelated application features
- Push security configuration directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### HTTPS

- [ ] Public frontend is served using HTTPS
- [ ] Public backend API is accessed using HTTPS
- [ ] HTTP redirects to HTTPS where appropriate
- [ ] Certificate configuration is valid
- [ ] Frontend does not generate mixed-content API requests

### ALB

- [ ] HTTPS listener is configured
- [ ] Requests route correctly to the backend target group
- [ ] ALB security group exposes only required public ports
- [ ] Health checks continue working

### EC2

- [ ] Backend application port is restricted to the intended ALB security group
- [ ] Direct public backend access is removed where unnecessary
- [ ] Administrative access is restricted
- [ ] Auto-scaled instances inherit the intended network security configuration

### RDS

- [ ] RDS is not publicly accessible
- [ ] PostgreSQL access is restricted to the backend tier
- [ ] Port 5432 is not open to `0.0.0.0/0`
- [ ] Frontend infrastructure has no direct database access

### Django

- [ ] `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is configured appropriately
- [ ] HTTPS/proxy settings are configured appropriately
- [ ] Secure cookie settings are enabled where applicable
- [ ] CSRF trusted origins are configured where applicable
- [ ] Production CORS is appropriately restricted
- [ ] `python manage.py check --deploy` has been reviewed

### Documentation

- [ ] HTTPS architecture is documented
- [ ] Security-group relationships are documented
- [ ] Public/private resource boundaries are documented
- [ ] Administrative access strategy is documented
- [ ] Updated architecture diagram reflects production network security

## Before Submitting

Verify:

```text
Browser
  ↓
HTTPS
  ↓
CloudFront
```

and:

```text
Frontend
  ↓
HTTPS
  ↓
ALB
  ↓
EC2
```

Verify direct Internet access is not available to:

```text
EC2 application port
RDS PostgreSQL port
```

Review security groups.

Run:

```bash
cd backend
python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy
```

Review the output rather than simply suppressing warnings.

Verify normal application functionality still works through the secure public endpoints.

Update:

```text
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/deployment.md
docs/security-design.md
```

where appropriate.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push security changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`security/https-network`

## Related Work

This issue should remain compatible with:

- #19 Infrastructure: Configure Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
- #21 Infrastructure: Configure EC2 Auto Scaling
- #24 Infrastructure: Configure AWS Secrets Management and Production Configuration

Title: DevOps: Configure CI/CD Pipeline
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Create a CI/CD pipeline for the project using GitHub Actions.

The pipeline should automatically validate changes before they are merged and automate production builds/deployment where appropriate.

The pipeline should support both:

- Django backend
- React frontend

The intended workflow is:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Feature Branch
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
GitHub Actions
    │
    ├── Backend Tests
    ├── Frontend Checks
    └── Build Validation
    │
    ▼
Code Review
    │
    ▼
main
    │
    ├── Backend Deployment
    │
    └── Frontend Deployment
```

CI failures should prevent broken code from being treated as deployment-ready.

## Where to Work

GitHub Actions workflows should be stored in:

```text
.github/workflows/
```

Potential files include:

```text
.github/workflows/ci.yml
.github/workflows/backend-deploy.yml
.github/workflows/frontend-deploy.yml
```

The exact workflow organization may be adjusted if a simpler structure is preferred.

Other affected files may include:

- `backend/requirements.txt`
- `frontend/package.json`
- Docker configuration
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Continuous Integration

- [ ] Create GitHub Actions CI workflow
- [ ] Trigger CI for Pull Requests
- [ ] Trigger CI for relevant pushes
- [ ] Install backend dependencies
- [ ] Run Django system checks
- [ ] Run backend tests
- [ ] Install frontend dependencies
- [ ] Run frontend linting
- [ ] Run frontend tests if available
- [ ] Verify frontend production build succeeds
- [ ] Verify backend Docker image can build
- [ ] Fail the workflow when required checks fail

### Backend Deployment

- [ ] Trigger production backend deployment only from the intended branch/workflow
- [ ] Build the backend Docker image
- [ ] Tag the image with a traceable version
- [ ] Authenticate securely with AWS
- [ ] Push the backend image to Amazon ECR
- [ ] Deploy/update the backend infrastructure using the new image
- [ ] Verify backend health after deployment
- [ ] Document rollback/redeployment procedure

### Frontend Deployment

- [ ] Build the React production application
- [ ] Use the production API configuration
- [ ] Upload production assets to the frontend S3 bucket
- [ ] Update/invalidate CloudFront where required
- [ ] Verify the deployed frontend is reachable
- [ ] Document frontend deployment behavior

### Security

- [ ] Configure AWS authentication securely
- [ ] Do not commit AWS credentials
- [ ] Do not expose production secrets in workflow logs
- [ ] Restrict deployment permissions to required resources
- [ ] Separate CI validation from production deployment permissions

## Pull Request Workflow

For Pull Requests:

```text
Feature Branch
      │
      ▼
Pull Request
      │
      ▼
GitHub Actions
      │
      ├── Backend Check
      ├── Backend Tests
      ├── Docker Build Check
      ├── Frontend Lint
      └── Frontend Build
      │
      ▼
Pass / Fail
```

A Pull Request should **not automatically deploy to production**.

PR workflows exist to validate proposed changes.

## Backend CI

Backend validation should include at minimum:

```bash
cd backend

python manage.py check
python manage.py test
```

The CI environment should use appropriate test configuration.

Do not require access to the production RDS database simply to execute normal backend tests.

## Frontend CI

Frontend validation should include the project's established commands.

Conceptually:

```bash
cd frontend

npm ci
npm run lint
npm run build
```

If automated frontend tests are added:

```bash
npm test
```

or the project's equivalent command should also be included.

Use the commands actually defined in `package.json`.

## Docker Validation

CI should verify that the backend Docker image still builds.

Conceptually:

```text
Backend Source
      │
      ▼
Docker Build
      │
      ├── Success → continue
      │
      └── Failure → CI fails
```

This prevents application changes from reaching `main` while breaking the deployment image.

## Production Backend Deployment

After approved changes reach `main`:

```text
main
 │
 ▼
GitHub Actions
 │
 ▼
Build Docker Image
 │
 ▼
Amazon ECR
 │
 ▼
EC2 / Auto Scaling
 │
 ▼
Django
```

The exact deployment mechanism should match the final EC2/Auto Scaling architecture.

## Image Versioning

Do not rely exclusively on:

```text
latest
```

for identifying production versions.

Prefer a traceable image tag.

For example:

```text
recipe-backend:<git-commit>
```

Conceptually:

```text
Git Commit
   abc123
      │
      ▼
Docker Image
recipe-backend:abc123
      │
      ▼
Production
```

This makes it possible to determine which application version is deployed.

## Frontend Deployment

Frontend deployment should follow:

```text
main
 │
 ▼
GitHub Actions
 │
 ▼
npm build
 │
 ▼
S3
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
```

The workflow should use the production backend API configuration.

Do not hardcode an individual EC2 address during the build.

## AWS Authentication

CI/CD must not require committed AWS access keys.

Prefer secure short-lived AWS authentication where supported, such as GitHub Actions using AWS IAM federation/OIDC.

Conceptually:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      ▼
AWS Identity / IAM Role
      │
      ▼
Authorized AWS Resources
```

Avoid:

```text
GitHub Repository
      │
      ▼
Permanent AWS Access Key
      │
      ▼
AWS
```

## Least Privilege

The deployment identity should receive only the permissions required by the pipeline.

For example:

```text
Backend Deployment
├── Push image to required ECR repository
└── Perform required deployment operation

Frontend Deployment
├── Update required frontend S3 bucket
└── Perform required CloudFront invalidation
```

Do not grant:

```text
AdministratorAccess
```

simply because it makes the workflow easier to configure.

## GitHub Secrets

If a sensitive value must be supplied to GitHub Actions, use the appropriate GitHub secret mechanism.

However, application runtime secrets should remain in the AWS production secret-management architecture whenever possible.

Conceptually:

```text
GitHub Actions
     │
     └── Deployment authorization

AWS Secrets Manager
     │
     └── Application runtime secrets
```

Do not copy all production application secrets into GitHub unnecessarily.

## Workflow Logs

CI/CD logs must not expose:

- AWS credentials
- database passwords
- Django secret keys
- authentication tokens
- Secrets Manager values

Do not intentionally print environment variables containing sensitive information.

## Deployment Safety

Production deployment should occur only after CI succeeds.

Preferred:

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
CI passes
     │
     ▼
Review
     │
     ▼
Merge into main
     │
     ▼
Deployment
```

Avoid:

```text
Feature branch push
       │
       ▼
Production deployment
```

## Failed Deployment

A failed deployment must be visible.

The workflow should clearly report:

```text
Success
```

or:

```text
Failure
```

where possible.

Do not report deployment success simply because the Docker image was pushed successfully.

The application should also pass an appropriate post-deployment health verification.

## Backend Health Verification

After backend deployment:

```text
New Backend Version
        │
        ▼
Deployment
        │
        ▼
ALB Health Check
        │
        ▼
Healthy
```

Where practical, perform a simple application health request after deployment.

If the new backend does not become healthy, the deployment should be treated as unsuccessful.

## Rollback

Document how the team can return to a previously working backend version.

Because Docker images are versioned:

```text
Current:
recipe-backend:def456

Problem detected
       ↓

Redeploy:
recipe-backend:abc123
```

Do not delete previous working image versions immediately after every deployment.

The project does not need a complex enterprise rollback system, but the recovery procedure should be documented.

## Branch Protection

Where repository permissions allow, configure `main` so changes normally arrive through Pull Requests.

Recommended checks include:

```text
Backend Tests
Frontend Checks
Build Validation
```

Required checks should pass before merge.

This complements the project's existing rule:

```text
Do not push feature implementation directly to main.
```

## Security Requirements

CI/CD must preserve the security architecture established elsewhere in the project.

Do not:

- weaken security groups during deployment
- expose RDS
- expose secrets
- bypass authentication
- place production secrets in Docker images
- grant broad AWS permissions unnecessarily

Automation should make the existing secure deployment reproducible, not bypass it.

## Scalability Requirements

CI/CD must support the horizontally scalable backend architecture.

The deployment process should not require manually updating individual EC2 instances.

Avoid:

```text
SSH EC2 #1
update code

SSH EC2 #2
update code
```

Prefer:

```text
Build New Image
      │
      ▼
     ECR
      │
      ▼
Update Backend Deployment
      │
      ▼
Equivalent EC2 Instances
```

This ensures scaled instances run consistent application versions.

## Reproducibility

A deployment should be traceable to:

```text
Git Commit
    ↓
CI Result
    ↓
Docker Image
    ↓
Deployment
```

This improves both maintainability and the quality of the final system-design explanation.

## Cost Awareness

CI/CD should not create unnecessary AWS resources for every Pull Request.

PR validation can generally perform:

```text
tests
lint
build
Docker build validation
```

without deploying a new production environment.

Production AWS deployment should happen only when intended.

## Important

CI and CD are related but serve different purposes.

```text
CI
────────────
Check
Test
Lint
Build
Validate


CD
────────────
Package
Publish
Deploy
Verify
```

A Pull Request should primarily execute CI.

Deployment should occur only through the intended production workflow.

### Do NOT

- Deploy every feature branch to production
- Deploy failed CI builds
- Commit AWS credentials
- Commit GitHub secrets
- Print secrets in workflow logs
- Put runtime secrets in Docker images
- Give GitHub Actions `AdministratorAccess`
- Depend on manual SSH deployment to every EC2 instance
- Use only `latest` with no traceable image version
- Hardcode EC2 IP addresses
- Bypass Pull Request review
- Treat successful ECR push as proof of successful deployment
- Delete all previous deployable image versions immediately
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push CI/CD implementation directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### CI

- [ ] Pull Requests automatically trigger CI
- [ ] Django checks run
- [ ] Backend tests run
- [ ] Frontend linting runs
- [ ] Frontend production build is validated
- [ ] Backend Docker build is validated
- [ ] Required failures cause CI to fail

### Backend CD

- [ ] Approved production workflow can build the backend image
- [ ] Backend image receives a traceable version
- [ ] Image can be pushed to ECR
- [ ] Production backend can be updated using the new image
- [ ] Backend health is verified after deployment

### Documentation

- [ ] Backend deployment workflow is documented
