Title: Testing: Load Testing and Scalability Evaluation
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Evaluate the scalability and performance of the deployed application using controlled load testing and measurable statistics.

The project must demonstrate scalability using actual measurements rather than architecture claims alone.

Testing should evaluate how the backend behaves as request load increases and compare different backend capacities where possible.

The results will be used as evidence in the final system design report and presentation.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves testing, AWS monitoring, and documentation.

Potential repository additions include:

- `tests/load/` — load-testing scripts
- `docs/performance-testing.md` — test methodology and results
- `docs/system-design.md` — scalability conclusions
- `docs/aws-architecture.md` — tested infrastructure configuration

Create these files/directories if needed.

This task builds on the deployed and monitored AWS architecture.

## Tasks

### Load Testing Setup

- [ ] Select a load-testing tool
- [ ] Create reproducible load-test scripts
- [ ] Define representative API test scenarios
- [ ] Define concurrency/load levels
- [ ] Define test duration
- [ ] Define warm-up behavior if required
- [ ] Record infrastructure configuration used for every test
- [ ] Verify tests target the ALB/stable API endpoint rather than individual EC2 instances

### Baseline Testing

- [ ] Establish a low-load baseline
- [ ] Test the application with one backend instance
- [ ] Record throughput
- [ ] Record average response time
- [ ] Record p95 response time
- [ ] Record error rate
- [ ] Record EC2 CPU utilization
- [ ] Record relevant RDS metrics
- [ ] Record ALB metrics

### Scaling Testing

- [ ] Increase request concurrency in controlled steps
- [ ] Determine how performance changes as load increases
- [ ] Identify when response latency begins degrading
- [ ] Identify when errors begin increasing, if applicable
- [ ] Record infrastructure utilization at each load level

### Horizontal Scaling Comparison

- [ ] Run a controlled test with one backend instance
- [ ] Run the equivalent test with multiple backend instances
- [ ] Keep other test conditions as consistent as practical
- [ ] Compare throughput
- [ ] Compare average latency
- [ ] Compare p95 latency
- [ ] Compare error rate
- [ ] Compare EC2 utilization
- [ ] Compare database utilization

### Auto Scaling Test

Where practical:

- [ ] Begin with minimum backend capacity
- [ ] Generate sustained application load
- [ ] Observe the scaling metric
- [ ] Verify Auto Scaling launches additional capacity
- [ ] Verify the new instance becomes healthy
- [ ] Verify the ALB begins routing traffic to it
- [ ] Record scaling-event timing
- [ ] Record application performance before and after scaling

### Results

- [ ] Store raw test results where practical
- [ ] Create comparison tables
- [ ] Create performance graphs
- [ ] Document test methodology
- [ ] Document limitations
- [ ] Identify observed bottlenecks
- [ ] Write evidence-based scalability conclusions

## Load-Testing Tool

Use an appropriate reproducible load-testing tool.

Examples include:

```text
Locust
k6
```

For this project, a scriptable tool is preferred because the same workload should be repeatable.

Do not rely on manually refreshing pages in a browser as scalability testing.

## Test Through the Real Architecture

Tests should target:

```text
Load Generator
      │
      ▼
     ALB
      │
      ▼
EC2 Backend(s)
      │
      ▼
     RDS
```

Do not benchmark:

```text
localhost
```

and use those results as proof of AWS scalability.

Local testing may be useful during development, but final scalability evidence should come from the deployed architecture.

## Representative Workloads

Do not test only the health endpoint.

The health endpoint performs almost no application work and would produce misleading results.

Select representative application endpoints.

Examples may include:

```text
Ingredient Search
Recipe Search
Recipe Detail
Recommendations
```

If authentication is available, additional scenarios may include:

```text
Inventory Retrieval
Saved Recipes
Profile Retrieval
```

Choose endpoints that represent realistic application usage.

## Read vs. Write Workloads

Where practical, distinguish between read-heavy and write operations.

Example:

```text
Read-heavy:
GET ingredient search
GET recipe search
GET recipe detail

More computational:
POST recommendation request

Write:
POST/PUT inventory
Save recipe
Update profile
```

Do not perform destructive or uncontrolled writes against important production data.

Use dedicated test data where necessary.

## Test Levels

Use several controlled load levels.

For example:

```text
25 concurrent users
50 concurrent users
100 concurrent users
250 concurrent users
```

These are starting examples, not required final values.

Adjust the levels based on:

- EC2 size
- RDS size
- application behavior
- AWS cost
- observed performance

Do not generate unnecessarily extreme traffic simply to make the system fail.

## Metrics

At minimum, collect:

```text
Concurrent Users
Requests per Second
Average Response Time
p95 Response Time
Error Rate
```

Infrastructure metrics should include:

```text
EC2 CPU Utilization
Backend Instance Count
ALB Target Response Time
ALB Healthy Host Count
RDS CPU Utilization
RDS Database Connections
```

Additional metrics may be collected where useful.

## Why p95 Matters

Average latency alone can hide slow requests.

For example:

```text
Average:
180 ms

p95:
850 ms
```

This means most requests may be reasonably fast while a significant tail of requests is much slower.

Therefore, report both:

```text
Average latency
p95 latency
```

rather than only the average.

## One-Instance Test

Establish a controlled configuration:

```text
ALB
 │
 ▼
EC2 #1
 │
 ▼
RDS
```

Record the exact infrastructure configuration.

Example:

```text
Backend instances: 1
EC2 type: <actual type>
RDS type: <actual type>
Backend image: <version>
Test duration: <actual duration>
```

Then execute each defined load level.

## Multi-Instance Test

Repeat equivalent tests with:

```text
              ALB
            /     \
           ▼       ▼
        EC2 #1   EC2 #2
            \     /
              RDS
```

Keep the following as consistent as practical:

```text
API endpoints
Test duration
Test data
Load level
EC2 instance type
RDS configuration
Backend version
```

This gives us a meaningful comparison.

## Results Table

Create a table similar to:

```text
Users | EC2 | Req/s | Avg ms | p95 ms | Error % | Avg CPU
-----------------------------------------------------------
25    |  1  |       |        |        |         |
50    |  1  |       |        |        |         |
100   |  1  |       |        |        |         |
250   |  1  |       |        |        |         |

25    |  2  |       |        |        |         |
50    |  2  |       |        |        |         |
100   |  2  |       |        |        |         |
250   |  2  |       |        |        |         |
```

Populate this table only with actual measurements.

## Graphs

Create useful graphs from the measured results.

Recommended graphs:

```text
Concurrent Users
       vs.
p95 Response Time
```

```text
Concurrent Users
       vs.
Requests / Second
```

```text
Concurrent Users
       vs.
Error Rate
```

For the horizontal scaling comparison, show:

```text
1 EC2
vs.
2 EC2
```

on the same comparison where appropriate.

## Auto Scaling Evaluation

If Auto Scaling is implemented, perform a separate dynamic test.

Conceptually:

```text
1 Instance
    │
    ▼
Load increases
    │
    ▼
Scaling threshold reached
    │
    ▼
ASG launches EC2 #2
    │
    ▼
Health check passes
    │
    ▼
ALB distributes traffic
```

Record a timeline such as:

```text
Time | Load | CPU | Instances | p95 | Event
----------------------------------------------
0m   |      |     |     1     |     |
2m   |      |     |     1     |     |
4m   |      |     |     1     |     | Scale triggered
6m   |      |     |     2     |     | Instance starting
8m   |      |     |     2     |     | Target healthy
```

Use actual measurements.

## Bottleneck Analysis

Do not simply report that the application became slower.

Try to determine why.

Example:

```text
Latency increases
      │
      ├── EC2 CPU = 95%
      └── RDS CPU = 30%

Likely bottleneck:
Backend compute
```

Another example:

```text
Latency increases
      │
      ├── EC2 CPU = 40%
      ├── RDS CPU = 95%
      └── DB latency increases

Likely bottleneck:
Database
```

These conclusions should be based on observed metrics.

## Scalability Interpretation

A scalable architecture does not mean:

```text
Response time never increases.
```

Instead, evaluate whether adding resources allows the application to support additional load while maintaining acceptable performance.

For example:

```text
1 EC2:
Performance degrades significantly at X load

2 EC2:
Comparable degradation occurs at a higher load
```

That is useful scalability evidence.

Do not force the results to show that scaling improved performance.

If it does not improve performance, investigate why.

Possible reasons may include:

```text
Database bottleneck
Inefficient queries
Application-level bottleneck
Insufficient test duration
Scaling delay
External dependency
```

Unexpected results are still valid engineering results.

## Recommendation Endpoint

The Recommendation API should receive particular attention because it may be one of the more computational/database-intensive endpoints.

Test it independently where practical.

Compare it with simpler endpoints such as Ingredient Search or Recipe Detail.

This can help identify whether recommendation logic becomes a bottleneck.

## Query Performance

If load testing identifies database-heavy endpoints, investigate Django query behavior.

Look for:

```text
N+1 queries
Missing indexes
Repeated queries
Loading unnecessary objects
Unbounded result sets
```

Optimization should be evidence-driven.

Do not prematurely add caching or architectural complexity without identifying the bottleneck first.

## Security Requirements

Load testing must not weaken production security.

Do not:

- disable authentication simply to make tests easier
- expose RDS publicly
- expose backend ports publicly
- commit test credentials
- put authentication tokens into Git
- bypass authorization checks

Where authenticated tests are required, use dedicated test accounts and secure test configuration.

## Test Data

Use controlled test data.

Do not generate thousands of permanent user accounts, inventory records, or saved recipes in the real application without a cleanup strategy.

Where write testing is necessary:

```text
Create Test Data
      ↓
Run Test
      ↓
Collect Results
      ↓
Clean Up Test Data
```

## Reproducibility

Another team member should be able to repeat the test.

Document:

```text
Test tool
Test script
Backend version
Infrastructure configuration
Test data
Load levels
Test duration
Relevant environment assumptions
```

This is important because otherwise the performance statistics cannot be meaningfully verified.

## Cost / Safety

Load tests intentionally generate traffic and may trigger Auto Scaling.

Before testing:

- verify Auto Scaling maximum capacity
- verify AWS budget/cost expectations
- verify test duration
- verify target environment

Do not accidentally run uncontrolled load tests for hours.

Do not target systems that the team does not own or have permission to test.

## Final Scalability Evidence

The final report should be able to show:

```text
Architecture
     +
Controlled Experiment
     +
Measured Statistics
     +
CloudWatch Metrics
     +
Analysis
     =
Scalability Evidence
```

This directly addresses the scalability requirement.

## Important

Do not start with a conclusion such as:

```text
"Our architecture scales perfectly."
```

Start with measurements.

Then conclude what those measurements actually demonstrate.

### Do NOT

- Fabricate performance numbers
- Use localhost results as final cloud scalability evidence
- Test only `/api/health/`
- Change multiple infrastructure variables between comparison tests
- Compare different backend versions without documenting it
- Disable authentication/authorization for testing
- Commit test credentials
- Expose infrastructure publicly to simplify load testing
- Run uncontrolled load tests
- Generate excessive AWS cost
- Assume adding EC2 instances automatically improves performance
- Hide negative results
- Claim the application is infinitely scalable
- Optimize without identifying a measured bottleneck
- Push test implementation directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Test Environment

- [ ] Load-testing tool is selected
- [ ] Test scripts are stored/documented
- [ ] Tests target the deployed backend through the ALB
- [ ] Representative application endpoints are tested
- [ ] Infrastructure configuration is recorded
- [ ] Test methodology is reproducible

### Metrics

- [ ] Requests per second are recorded
- [ ] Average latency is recorded
- [ ] p95 latency is recorded
- [ ] Error rate is recorded
- [ ] EC2 CPU utilization is recorded
- [ ] Backend instance count is recorded
- [ ] Relevant ALB metrics are recorded
- [ ] Relevant RDS metrics are recorded

### Scalability

- [ ] Multiple load levels are tested
- [ ] Single-instance performance is measured
- [ ] Multi-instance performance is measured where available
- [ ] Equivalent workloads are used for comparison
- [ ] Horizontal-scaling results are analyzed
- [ ] Auto Scaling behavior is evaluated where available
- [ ] Bottlenecks are identified where supported by evidence

### Results

- [ ] Raw or summarized test results are preserved
- [ ] Results table is created
- [ ] At least one useful scalability graph is created
- [ ] Test limitations are documented
- [ ] Results are interpreted rather than merely listed
- [ ] No fabricated statistics are used

### Security

- [ ] Tests do not bypass application authorization
- [ ] Test credentials are not committed
- [ ] Infrastructure security is not weakened for testing
- [ ] Load testing targets only authorized project infrastructure

### Documentation

- [ ] `docs/performance-testing.md` documents the methodology
- [ ] Infrastructure configuration is documented
- [ ] Test scenarios are documented
- [ ] Results are documented
- [ ] Scalability conclusions are supported by measured evidence

## Before Submitting

Verify the load tests can be reproduced.

Run the selected workloads against the deployed environment.

Collect both:

```text
Load Test Results
+
CloudWatch Metrics
```

Create the required tables and graphs.

Review the results with the team before making scalability claims.

Update:

```text
docs/performance-testing.md
docs/system-design.md
```

with measured results and conclusions.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push testing changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`testing/scalability`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure CloudWatch Logging, Metrics, and Monitoring
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure Amazon CloudWatch to provide centralized logging and infrastructure monitoring for the deployed application.

The system should provide visibility into:

- Django backend behavior
- EC2 resource utilization
- Application Load Balancer performance
- Auto Scaling activity
- RDS performance
- application errors

CloudWatch metrics collected here will later support the project's scalability and performance testing.

The goal is to be able to answer questions such as:

```text
How much traffic is the application receiving?

How quickly is the backend responding?

How heavily utilized are the EC2 instances?

Is the database becoming a bottleneck?

Are requests failing?

Did adding backend instances improve performance?
```

Actual scalability experiments and load generation should be handled in a later dedicated issue.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and backend logging configuration.

Potential repository changes include:

- `backend/config/settings.py`
- backend logging configuration
- deployment/startup configuration
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `docs/performance-testing.md` if created

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### CloudWatch Logs

- [ ] Create/configure a CloudWatch log group for the Django backend
- [ ] Send deployed backend logs to CloudWatch
- [ ] Verify application startup logs are available
- [ ] Verify Django application errors are visible
- [ ] Configure an appropriate log retention period
- [ ] Ensure sensitive information is not written to logs
- [ ] Document the logging configuration

### EC2 Monitoring

- [ ] Verify EC2 metrics are available in CloudWatch
- [ ] Monitor CPU utilization
- [ ] Monitor relevant instance health/status metrics
- [ ] Configure additional memory monitoring if required for scalability testing
- [ ] Document which EC2 metrics will be used during performance tests

### Application Load Balancer

- [ ] Monitor ALB request count
- [ ] Monitor target response time
- [ ] Monitor healthy target count
- [ ] Monitor unhealthy target count
- [ ] Monitor backend 4xx/5xx behavior where appropriate
- [ ] Verify ALB metrics are available in CloudWatch

### Auto Scaling

- [ ] Monitor desired instance capacity
- [ ] Monitor in-service instance count
- [ ] Verify scaling events can be observed
- [ ] Verify changes in backend capacity can be correlated with load
- [ ] Document relevant Auto Scaling metrics

### RDS

- [ ] Monitor RDS CPU utilization
- [ ] Monitor database connections
- [ ] Monitor available storage
- [ ] Monitor relevant read/write latency or I/O metrics
- [ ] Verify database metrics are available during load testing
- [ ] Document the RDS metrics selected for scalability analysis

### Dashboard

- [ ] Create a CloudWatch dashboard for the deployed application
- [ ] Include key EC2 metrics
- [ ] Include key ALB metrics
- [ ] Include key RDS metrics
- [ ] Include Auto Scaling capacity where available
- [ ] Organize the dashboard so system behavior can be observed during load testing

### Alarms

- [ ] Configure a small set of useful CloudWatch alarms
- [ ] Configure an EC2 high-utilization alarm
- [ ] Configure an unhealthy backend/target alarm where appropriate
- [ ] Configure a backend/server-error alarm where appropriate
- [ ] Document alarm thresholds and reasoning

## Architecture

CloudWatch should provide visibility across the deployed system.

```text
                        Users
                          │
                          ▼
                         ALB
                          │
                  ┌───────┴───────┐
                  ▼               ▼
                EC2 #1          EC2 #2
                Django          Django
                  │               │
                  └───────┬───────┘
                          ▼
                         RDS


            ───── Monitoring / Logs ─────

                         │
                         ▼
                    CloudWatch
                         │
            ┌────────────┼────────────┐
            ▼            ▼            ▼
           Logs        Metrics     Dashboard
                                      │
                                      ▼
                                    Alarms
```

CloudWatch does not sit in the application request path.

It observes system behavior.

## Backend Logging

Production Django logs should be accessible without requiring developers to manually inspect each EC2 instance.

Avoid:

```text
Developer
   ↓
SSH into EC2 #1
   ↓
Read local log

SSH into EC2 #2
   ↓
Read another log
```

Prefer:

```text
EC2 #1 ──┐
         │
EC2 #2 ──┼──→ CloudWatch Logs
         │
EC2 #N ──┘
```

This becomes especially important when Auto Scaling creates or replaces backend instances.

## Logging Requirements

Logs should contain enough information to diagnose application behavior.

Useful information may include:

```text
Timestamp
Log level
Application/component
Request/error context where appropriate
Exception information
```

Do not intentionally log sensitive information.

Avoid logging:

```text
Authorization headers
Cognito tokens
Passwords
Database credentials
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
AWS credentials
Secrets Manager values
```

## Log Levels

Production logging should use meaningful levels.

For example:

```text
DEBUG
INFO
WARNING
ERROR
CRITICAL
```

Do not enable excessively verbose debug logging in production without a specific reason.

Normal application behavior should not generate large quantities of unnecessary logs.

## Log Retention

CloudWatch logs should have an explicit retention strategy.

Do not leave logs growing indefinitely without considering cost and project requirements.

Choose a reasonable retention period for the class project and document it.

The exact retention period may be adjusted later based on project needs.

## EC2 Metrics

At minimum, monitor:

```text
CPUUtilization
StatusCheckFailed
```

For scalability testing, memory utilization is also useful.

If memory metrics are required, configure the appropriate monitoring mechanism, such as the CloudWatch Agent.

The project should record which metrics are standard AWS metrics and which require additional configuration.

## ALB Metrics

Useful ALB/target metrics include:

```text
RequestCount
TargetResponseTime
HealthyHostCount
UnHealthyHostCount
HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count
HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count
HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
```

These help answer:

```text
How many requests reached the application?

How quickly did targets respond?

Were targets healthy?

Did backend errors increase under load?
```

## Auto Scaling Metrics

When Auto Scaling is available, monitor the capacity of the backend tier.

Useful measurements include:

```text
GroupDesiredCapacity
GroupInServiceInstances
GroupTotalInstances
```

During a scaling test, this allows us to observe:

```text
Load increases
      ↓
CPU/load increases
      ↓
Scaling policy activates
      ↓
Desired capacity increases
      ↓
New instance starts
      ↓
Healthy host count increases
```

## RDS Metrics

Useful RDS measurements include:

```text
CPUUtilization
DatabaseConnections
FreeStorageSpace
ReadLatency
WriteLatency
ReadIOPS
WriteIOPS
```

Not every metric must appear on the main dashboard.

Select metrics that help explain application performance.

For example:

```text
API latency increases
        │
        ├── EC2 CPU low
        │
        └── RDS CPU/latency high

Possible bottleneck:
database tier
```

This is much stronger evidence than simply saying "the application became slow."

## CloudWatch Dashboard

Create a project dashboard that makes the application's behavior easy to observe.

A useful conceptual layout is:

```text
+----------------------------------------+
|           APPLICATION TRAFFIC          |
| Request Count | Target Response Time   |
+----------------------------------------+

+----------------------------------------+
|             BACKEND COMPUTE            |
| EC2 CPU | Instance Count | Health      |
+----------------------------------------+

+----------------------------------------+
|                DATABASE                |
| RDS CPU | Connections | Latency        |
+----------------------------------------+

+----------------------------------------+
|                ERRORS                  |
| 4xx | 5xx | Unhealthy Targets          |
+----------------------------------------+
```

The exact dashboard layout may differ.

The important requirement is that relevant system behavior can be observed together during testing.

## Alarms

Configure a small number of meaningful alarms.

Possible examples:

```text
High EC2 CPU

Unhealthy ALB Target

High Backend 5xx Error Rate
```

Thresholds should be documented.

Do not create dozens of alarms simply to increase the apparent complexity of the architecture.

## Security Requirements

### Sensitive Logs

CloudWatch must not become a repository for application secrets.

Do not log:

- passwords
- AWS access keys
- database credentials
- Django secret keys
- complete authentication tokens
- Secrets Manager payloads

### IAM

EC2 should use its IAM role to send/access the required monitoring resources.

Grant only required CloudWatch/logging permissions.

Avoid:

```text
cloudwatch:*
logs:*
Resource: *
```

where narrower permissions are practical.

### User Information

Avoid logging unnecessary private user information.

Logs should contain operational information needed to diagnose the system rather than copies of entire user requests or profiles.

## Scalability Requirements

Monitoring must allow us to compare different backend configurations.

For example:

```text
Test A
──────
1 EC2

100 concurrent users

Requests/sec:       measured
Average latency:    measured
p95 latency:        measured
Error rate:         measured
EC2 CPU:            measured
RDS CPU:            measured
```

Then:

```text
Test B
──────
2 EC2

100 concurrent users

Requests/sec:       measured
Average latency:    measured
p95 latency:        measured
Error rate:         measured
EC2 CPU:            measured
RDS CPU:            measured
```

CloudWatch provides infrastructure measurements while the later load-testing tool provides client/request measurements.

Together they allow us to explain **why** performance changed.

## Scalability Statistics

The professor specifically requires scalability supported by statistics.

Therefore, later tests should produce data such as:

```text
Users | Instances | Req/s | Avg | p95 | Error % | CPU
-------------------------------------------------------
50    |     1     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...
100   |     1     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...
250   |     1     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...

50    |     2     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...
100   |     2     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...
250   |     2     |  ...  | ... | ... |   ...   | ...
```

Do not fabricate these numbers.

They must come from actual tests.

## Monitoring Auto Scaling

CloudWatch should also allow us to capture a scaling timeline.

Example:

```text
Time    CPU    Instances    p95
--------------------------------
0 min   20%       1         ...
2 min   55%       1         ...
4 min   75%       1         ...
6 min   80%       1         ...
8 min   65%       2         ...
10 min  45%       2         ...
```

This can become excellent evidence for the final report.

Again, all actual values must come from measured results.

## Failure Monitoring

The system should make backend failure observable.

Example:

```text
EC2 #1 healthy
EC2 #2 healthy

       ↓

EC2 #1 fails

       ↓

HealthyHostCount decreases

       ↓

ALB stops routing to EC2 #1

       ↓

ASG replaces instance

       ↓

HealthyHostCount returns
```

CloudWatch metrics/logs should allow this sequence to be demonstrated where practical.

## Performance Baseline

Once monitoring exists, record a simple baseline before full scalability testing.

Document:

```text
Date
Backend Image Version
EC2 Instance Type
Number of EC2 Instances
RDS Instance Class
Test Endpoint
```

This prevents performance results from becoming meaningless because infrastructure configuration changed without being recorded.

## Cost Awareness

CloudWatch can generate additional costs through:

- log ingestion
- log storage
- custom metrics
- dashboards
- alarms

Keep monitoring appropriate for a class project.

Do not enable excessive high-frequency custom metrics or verbose logging without a reason.

Configure log retention rather than keeping unnecessary logs indefinitely.

## Important

Monitoring is different from load testing.

```text
CloudWatch
     ↓
Observes the system

Load Testing Tool
     ↓
Generates controlled traffic
```

We need both.

CloudWatch tells us:

```text
What happened inside AWS?
```

The load-testing tool tells us:

```text
What performance did the client experience?
```

The later scalability-testing issue will combine both.

### Do NOT

- Log passwords
- Log AWS credentials
- Log database credentials
- Log Django secret keys
- Log complete authentication tokens
- Log Secrets Manager contents
- Enable excessive production debug logging
- Keep logs indefinitely without a retention decision
- Give EC2 unnecessary CloudWatch administrative permissions
- Create meaningless alarms simply for complexity
- Treat CloudWatch as the load generator
- Claim scalability based only on CPU graphs
- Invent performance statistics
- Change infrastructure during a comparison test without documenting it
- Modify unrelated application functionality

Title: Infrastructure: Configure AWS Secrets Management and Production Configuration
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Implement secure production configuration management for the Django backend.

Sensitive production values must not be stored in:

- Git
- Docker images
- frontend code
- Launch Templates
- EC2 user-data scripts
- committed `.env` files

AWS-managed secret storage should be used for sensitive configuration, while normal non-sensitive configuration should remain environment-based.

The intended architecture is:

```text
AWS Secrets Manager
        │
        │ IAM-authorized access
        ▼
       EC2
        │
        ▼
 Django Container
        │
        ├── RDS
        ├── S3
        └── Other AWS Services
```

## Where to Work

This task affects AWS infrastructure and backend production configuration.

Potential repository changes include:

- `backend/config/settings.py`
- `.env.example`
- deployment/startup configuration
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `backend/README.md`

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Secrets Management

- [ ] Identify production values that are actually secrets
- [ ] Create appropriate secret(s) in AWS Secrets Manager
- [ ] Store production database credentials securely
- [ ] Store the Django secret key securely
- [ ] Configure EC2 IAM permission to retrieve only required secrets
- [ ] Make required secrets available to the Django runtime
- [ ] Verify Django starts successfully using managed secrets
- [ ] Verify secrets are not required inside the Docker image
- [ ] Verify secrets are not committed to Git
- [ ] Document secret-management architecture without documenting secret values

### Production Configuration

- [ ] Separate sensitive configuration from non-sensitive configuration
- [ ] Configure `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Configure `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
- [ ] Configure production database settings
- [ ] Configure production S3 settings where applicable
- [ ] Configure Cognito settings where applicable
- [ ] Configure production CORS/CSRF settings where applicable
- [ ] Document required configuration variables
- [ ] Keep local development configuration simple and documented

## Secret vs. Configuration

Not every environment variable is a secret.

For example:

```text
Sensitive
─────────
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
DB_PASSWORD
private credentials

Non-sensitive configuration
───────────────────────────
DJANGO_DEBUG
DB_PORT
AWS_REGION
S3 bucket name
Cognito user pool ID
API configuration
```

Treat values according to their sensitivity rather than putting everything into one category.

## Development

Local development may continue using an ignored `.env` file:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
.env
    │
    ▼
Django
```

The `.env` file must remain excluded from Git.

`.env.example` should contain only placeholders:

```env
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=
DJANGO_DEBUG=True

DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_HOST=
DB_PORT=5432
```

Do not place real credentials in `.env.example`.

## Production

Production should not depend on a manually maintained `.env` file committed or copied around by developers.

Conceptually:

```text
              AWS
               │
      ┌────────┴────────┐
      │                 │
      ▼                 ▼
Secrets Manager    Configuration
      │                 │
      └────────┬────────┘
               ▼
              EC2
               │
               ▼
             Django
```

The exact mechanism used to expose configuration to the container should be documented.

## AWS Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager should contain values that require confidential storage.

Examples:

```text
Django Secret Key

Database:
├── username
├── password
├── host where appropriate
├── port where appropriate
└── database name where appropriate
```

Do not create unnecessary separate secrets for every individual environment variable if a logical grouping is easier to manage securely.

## IAM

The backend EC2 role should receive permission to retrieve only the secret resources required by the application.

Conceptually:

```text
EC2 Backend Role
       │
       ▼
GetSecretValue
       │
       ▼
Project Backend Secret
```

Avoid:

```text
secretsmanager:*
Resource: *
```

when narrower permissions are sufficient.

## No Static AWS Credentials

The application should rely on the EC2 IAM role for AWS service authentication.

Correct:

```text
Django
  ↓
EC2 IAM Role
  ↓
AWS Service
```

Avoid:

```text
Django
  ↓
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  ↓
AWS Service
```

Long-lived AWS credentials should not be distributed to backend instances simply so the application can access AWS services.

## Django Production Security

Production Django configuration must use:

```text
DEBUG=False
```

Production errors must not expose:

- stack traces
- environment variables
- database credentials
- secret values
- internal Django configuration

Run:

```bash
python manage.py check --deploy
```

and review applicable Django deployment warnings.

Do not blindly suppress warnings simply to make the command quiet.

## CORS

Production CORS should permit the intended frontend origin.

Conceptually:

```text
CloudFront Frontend
        │
        ▼
       ALB
        │
        ▼
      Django
```

Avoid unrestricted production configuration such as:

```text
Allow every origin
```

when the frontend origin is known.

Development may use different configuration where necessary.

## CSRF

Where Django endpoints rely on CSRF protection, production trusted-origin configuration should reflect the actual application domains.

Do not disable security protections globally simply to fix integration problems.

## Logging

Secrets must not appear in normal logs.

Do not log:

```text
DB_PASSWORD
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
authorization tokens
AWS credentials
complete secret payloads
```

Error handling should provide enough information for debugging without leaking sensitive configuration.

## Secret Rotation

The architecture should allow a secret to be changed without rebuilding the Docker image.

Desired:

```text
Change Secret
     ↓
Update/restart application runtime
     ↓
Application uses new value
```

Not:

```text
Change Secret
     ↓
Edit Dockerfile
     ↓
Rebuild application
```

Full automatic rotation is not required unless the team chooses to implement it.

The important requirement is that application binaries/images do not contain the secret.

## Docker

The same Docker image should work across environments.

```text
                   Same Image
                  /          \
                 ▼            ▼
           Development     Production
                │              │
          Local Config     AWS Config
```

Do not create:

```text
backend-with-dev-password
backend-with-prod-password
```

Configuration belongs outside the image.

## Auto Scaling

This architecture must support new EC2 instances created by the Auto Scaling Group.

A new instance should be capable of obtaining its required configuration through its IAM role.

Conceptually:

```text
Auto Scaling Group
       │
       ▼
    New EC2
       │
       ▼
    IAM Role
       │
       ▼
Secrets Manager
       │
       ▼
Django starts
```

No developer should need to manually SSH into each new instance and paste production passwords.

This is important for horizontal scalability.

## Security Requirements

### Least Privilege

Different AWS components should receive only the permissions they require.

For example:

```text
Backend EC2 Role
├── Pull backend image from ECR
├── Access required media S3 resources
└── Read required application secret

Frontend
└── No backend AWS credentials

RDS
└── Network access restricted to backend
```

### Source Control

Before deployment, verify that Git does not contain:

- production `.env`
- AWS credentials
- database passwords
- Django secret keys
- private keys
- sensitive Cognito credentials

If a real credential was previously committed, simply deleting it from the latest file is not sufficient security remediation.

The credential should be considered exposed and rotated.

## Scalability Requirements

Secret management must not depend on one manually configured EC2 instance.

Incorrect:

```text
EC2 #1
└── manually created secret file

EC2 #2
└── missing configuration
```

Correct:

```text
             Secrets Manager
                /        \
               ▼          ▼
            EC2 #1      EC2 #2
```

Equivalent backend instances should receive equivalent required production configuration.

This supports:

```text
Auto Scaling
     ↓
New Instance
     ↓
Secure Configuration
     ↓
Backend Ready
```

without manual intervention.

## Important

Secrets and configuration are different from application code.

```text
ECR
└── Application image

Secrets Manager
└── Sensitive configuration

Environment/configuration
└── Non-sensitive deployment settings

RDS
└── Persistent relational data

S3
└── Persistent object/media data
```

Keep these responsibilities separate.

### Do NOT

- Commit production `.env` files
- Commit database passwords
- Commit Django secret keys
- Commit AWS access keys
- Put secrets in React
- Put secrets in Docker images
- Put secrets directly in Launch Templates
- Put plaintext secrets in EC2 user-data scripts
- Give EC2 `secretsmanager:*` on all resources unnecessarily
- Give EC2 `AdministratorAccess`
- Log secret values
- Expose secret values through API responses
- Disable Django security features merely to fix deployment problems
- Use unrestricted CORS unnecessarily in production
- Require manual secret setup on every Auto Scaling instance
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Secrets

- [ ] Production Django secret key is externally managed
- [ ] Production database credentials are externally managed
- [ ] Required secrets are available to Django at runtime
- [ ] Docker image contains no production secrets
- [ ] Git contains no production secrets
- [ ] React contains no backend secrets

### IAM

- [ ] Backend EC2 uses an IAM role
- [ ] Backend can retrieve required secret(s)
- [ ] Secret access is restricted to required resources
- [ ] Long-lived AWS credentials are not required on EC2

### Django

- [ ] Production runs with `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is production-configured
- [ ] Production CORS is appropriately restricted
- [ ] CSRF trusted origins are configured where required
- [ ] `python manage.py check --deploy` is reviewed
- [ ] Application logs do not expose sensitive configuration

### Deployment

- [ ] Same Docker image can receive environment-specific configuration
- [ ] Secrets can change without rebuilding the image
- [ ] New backend instances can obtain required configuration
- [ ] Configuration supports the Auto Scaling architecture

### Documentation

- [ ] Required production configuration is documented
- [ ] Sensitive vs. non-sensitive configuration is documented
- [ ] Secrets Manager architecture is documented
- [ ] IAM requirements are documented
- [ ] No actual secret values appear in documentation

## Before Submitting

Verify the production-configured backend can start without secrets embedded in its Docker image.

Run:

```bash
python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy
```

Review the Docker image/configuration and repository for accidentally included secrets.

Verify:

```text
EC2
 ↓
IAM Role
 ↓
Secrets Manager
 ↓
Django
```

Verify a secret can be changed externally without modifying application source code or rebuilding the Docker image.

Update:

```text
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/deployment.md
```

as appropriate.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/secrets-config`

Title: Infrastructure: Deploy React Frontend with Amazon S3 and CloudFront
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Deploy the React frontend using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront.

The production frontend should be built into static assets, stored in S3, and delivered to users through CloudFront.

The frontend should remain independently deployable and scalable from the Django backend.

The intended architecture is:

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
CloudFront
  │
  ▼
S3
  │
  ▼
React Frontend
  │
  │ API Requests
  ▼
ALB
  │
  ▼
Django Backend
```

## Where to Work

Frontend code is located in:

`frontend/`

Potential files/configuration involved:

- `frontend/package.json`
- `frontend/src/`
- `frontend/.env.example`
- frontend build configuration
- shared API client configuration
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`

Relevant documentation:

- frontend README, if present
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Frontend Build

- [ ] Verify the React production build succeeds
- [ ] Verify generated assets are suitable for static hosting
- [ ] Configure the production backend API URL through environment configuration
- [ ] Ensure frontend source code does not contain hardcoded EC2 addresses
- [ ] Ensure no secrets are included in the frontend build

### Amazon S3

- [ ] Create an S3 bucket for the production frontend
- [ ] Upload the production React build to S3
- [ ] Configure bucket permissions appropriately
- [ ] Enable S3 Block Public Access where compatible with the CloudFront architecture
- [ ] Prevent direct public bucket access where practical
- [ ] Document frontend bucket configuration

### Amazon CloudFront

- [ ] Create a CloudFront distribution
- [ ] Configure the frontend S3 bucket as the origin
- [ ] Configure secure CloudFront access to the S3 origin
- [ ] Configure the default root object
- [ ] Configure HTTPS for user-facing frontend traffic
- [ ] Configure appropriate caching behavior
- [ ] Configure SPA routing/error behavior where required
- [ ] Verify the React application loads through CloudFront
- [ ] Verify static assets load correctly
- [ ] Verify browser refresh on frontend routes works correctly

### Backend Integration

- [ ] Configure the frontend to use the deployed backend API endpoint
- [ ] Verify API requests reach the backend through the ALB
- [ ] Configure backend CORS for the deployed frontend origin where required
- [ ] Verify frontend/backend communication works in production

## Architecture

The frontend and backend should be deployed independently.

```text
                    Users
                      │
                      ▼
                  CloudFront
                      │
                      ▼
                     S3
                React Frontend
                      │
                      │ HTTPS API
                      ▼
                     ALB
                      │
                ┌─────┴─────┐
                ▼           ▼
              EC2 #1      EC2 #2
              Django      Django
                │           │
                └─────┬─────┘
                      ▼
                     RDS
```

Application media may use a separate S3 media configuration:

```text
Frontend Assets
      ↓
Frontend S3 + CloudFront

Application Media
      ↓
Media S3
```

Do not mix these responsibilities unnecessarily.

## Why CloudFront

Do not serve the production React application from Django or EC2.

Avoid:

```text
User
 ↓
EC2
 ↓
Django
 ↓
React static files
```

Prefer:

```text
User
 ↓
CloudFront
 ↓
S3
```

This prevents frontend static-file delivery from consuming Django/EC2 application capacity.

It also allows the frontend and backend tiers to scale independently.

## Frontend API Configuration

The backend API location must be environment-configurable.

Conceptually:

```env
VITE_API_BASE_URL=
```

Use the actual environment-variable naming convention established by the frontend.

The production value should point to the stable backend entry point rather than an individual EC2 instance.

Correct:

```text
React
  ↓
ALB / Stable API Endpoint
```

Avoid:

```text
React
  ↓
EC2 #1 Public IP
```

This is required for horizontal backend scaling.

## S3 Origin Security

The frontend bucket should not need to be broadly public if CloudFront is responsible for delivering the application.

Preferred architecture:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Private S3 Origin
```

Configure CloudFront-to-S3 access using the appropriate AWS mechanism.

Direct anonymous S3 access should not be enabled merely to make deployment easier.

## HTTPS

Users should access the production frontend using HTTPS:

```text
Browser
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
CloudFront
```

CloudFront's provided distribution domain can be used initially.

A custom domain and ACM certificate may be configured separately if required.

The frontend should communicate with the production API securely as well.

Avoid a final architecture where:

```text
HTTPS Frontend
      ↓
HTTP Public API
```

## SPA Routing

React applications may contain client-side routes such as:

```text
/
/recipes
/recipes/123
/inventory
/profile
```

Refreshing a client-side route must not result in an unusable S3/CloudFront error page.

Configure CloudFront/S3 behavior as appropriate for the project's React routing strategy.

Do not blindly redirect every backend/API error to `index.html`; this configuration applies to the frontend distribution only.

## Caching

CloudFront should cache static frontend assets appropriately.

Typical build assets such as:

```text
assets/app-<hash>.js
assets/app-<hash>.css
```

can benefit from caching because their filenames change when their content changes.

Be more careful with the main HTML entry point because it determines which asset versions users load.

The exact caching policy should be documented.

## Deployment Updates

Frontend deployment should follow:

```text
Frontend Source
      │
      ▼
npm build
      │
      ▼
Production Assets
      │
      ▼
S3
      │
      ▼
CloudFront
```

When a new frontend version is deployed, ensure users can receive the updated application.

CloudFront invalidation may be used where necessary.

Do not routinely invalidate every cached object unnecessarily if the build already uses content-hashed assets.

## Security Requirements

### Frontend Secrets

Anything shipped in the React bundle must be considered visible to the user.

Therefore, do not place actual secrets in frontend environment variables.

Do not include:

- AWS secret access keys
- database credentials
- Django secret keys
- private Cognito secrets
- server-side credentials

in the React application.

Frontend environment variables are configuration, **not secure secret storage**.

### AWS Access

The browser must not require AWS credentials to retrieve the normal frontend application.

Deployment credentials should remain separate from the application.

### S3

- Keep Block Public Access enabled where compatible with the chosen CloudFront origin design.
- Allow CloudFront to access the required frontend objects.
- Avoid unnecessary public S3 access.

### API Security

CloudFront/S3 security does not replace backend security.

The backend must continue enforcing:

- authentication
- authorization
- ownership
- input validation

React route protection is not authoritative access control.

## CORS

The Django backend may need to explicitly allow requests from the deployed frontend origin.

Conceptually:

```text
https://<frontend-domain>
          │
          ▼
       Django API
```

Do not solve CORS problems by unnecessarily allowing every origin in production.

Avoid:

```text
Allow all origins
```

when the production frontend origin is known.

## Scalability Requirements

Frontend static delivery should not depend on the number of backend EC2 instances.

```text
                    CloudFront
                        │
                        ▼
                       S3
                        │
                        ▼
                     React
                        │
                        ▼
                       ALB
                    /       \
                 EC2 #1    EC2 #2
```

Frontend scaling and backend scaling are therefore separate concerns.

### Frontend Tier

```text
CloudFront + S3
```

handles static application delivery.

### Backend Tier

```text
ALB + Auto Scaling + EC2
```

handles API computation.

### Data Tier

```text
RDS
```

handles relational persistence.

### Media Tier

```text
S3
```

handles application media.

This separation should be documented as part of the system design.

## Performance

CloudFront reduces the need for every user to retrieve static frontend resources directly from the S3 origin.

Useful CloudFront metrics can later include:

```text
Requests
BytesDownloaded
4xxErrorRate
5xxErrorRate
CacheHitRate
```

Frontend delivery metrics should be kept separate from backend API performance metrics when evaluating scalability.

## Scalability Evidence

This issue provides architectural evidence that frontend delivery does not consume backend compute capacity.

Later documentation can show:

```text
Static Request
User → CloudFront → S3

API Request
User → ALB → Django → RDS
```

This separation allows backend load testing to focus on actual API workload instead of static React files.

Do not claim a specific performance improvement without measured results.

## Cost Awareness

S3 and CloudFront usage should remain small for the project, but unnecessary resources should still be avoided.

Do not:

- create multiple unnecessary frontend buckets
- create duplicate distributions without reason
- retain obsolete deployment artifacts indefinitely
- perform unnecessary large invalidations repeatedly

## Important

Frontend S3 and media S3 serve different purposes.

```text
Frontend S3
───────────
index.html
JavaScript
CSS
frontend assets


Media S3
────────
recipe images
uploaded application media
```

Keeping them logically separate makes permissions, caching, and deployment behavior easier to manage.

### Do NOT

- Serve the production React application through Django
- Serve the production React application directly from EC2
- Hardcode an EC2 public IP into React
- Put AWS secret keys in React
- Put database credentials in React
- Put Django secrets in React
- Assume frontend environment variables are secret
- Make S3 broadly public simply to fix CloudFront access
- Disable backend authorization because routes are hidden in React
- Allow all CORS origins unnecessarily in production
- Point production React directly at individual Auto Scaling instances
- Mix frontend deployment files with user-uploaded media unnecessarily
- Claim scalability improvements without measurements
- Modify unrelated frontend functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Frontend Build

- [ ] Production React build succeeds
- [ ] Production API URL is environment-configurable
- [ ] No EC2 address is hardcoded into application source
- [ ] No server-side secrets are included in the frontend bundle

### S3

- [ ] Frontend S3 bucket exists
- [ ] Production build is stored in the bucket
- [ ] Bucket access is configured appropriately
- [ ] Bucket is not unnecessarily publicly exposed
- [ ] Frontend and application media responsibilities are clearly separated

### CloudFront

- [ ] CloudFront distribution exists
- [ ] S3 is configured as the frontend origin
- [ ] CloudFront can securely retrieve frontend assets
- [ ] Frontend is accessible through CloudFront
- [ ] HTTPS works for frontend access
- [ ] Static assets load successfully
- [ ] SPA routes work correctly when refreshed
- [ ] Caching behavior is documented

### Backend Integration

- [ ] Frontend calls the backend through its stable API endpoint
- [ ] Frontend does not depend on a particular EC2 instance
- [ ] Production CORS configuration permits the intended frontend origin
- [ ] Representative API requests work from the deployed frontend

### Security

- [ ] No AWS secret credentials are included in React
- [ ] No database credentials are included in React
- [ ] No Django secret key is included in React
- [ ] S3 is not unnecessarily public
- [ ] HTTPS is used for public frontend access
- [ ] Backend remains responsible for authorization

### Scalability

- [ ] Frontend static delivery does not depend on Django/EC2
- [ ] Frontend deployment can scale independently of backend compute
- [ ] Backend instance count can change without changing the frontend API configuration
- [ ] Architecture is compatible with backend Auto Scaling
- [ ] CloudFront metrics can later be used as supporting performance evidence

### Documentation

- [ ] Frontend deployment procedure is documented
- [ ] S3 frontend configuration is documented
- [ ] CloudFront configuration is documented
- [ ] Production API configuration is documented
- [ ] CORS requirements are documented
- [ ] Architecture diagram includes S3 + CloudFront frontend delivery

## Before Submitting

Build the frontend:

```bash
cd frontend
npm run build
```

Deploy the generated production assets to the configured S3 frontend bucket.

Verify:

```text
Browser
   ↓
HTTPS
   ↓
CloudFront
   ↓
S3
   ↓
React loads
```

Then verify:

```text
React
  ↓
ALB / stable backend endpoint
  ↓
Django
  ↓
API response
```

Test direct navigation/refresh on representative React routes.

Check the browser console/network panel for:

- failed assets
- CORS failures
- mixed-content errors
- incorrect API URLs

Update:

```text
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/deployment.md
```

as appropriate.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/frontend-cloudfront`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure Amazon S3 Media Storage
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure Amazon S3 as the shared object storage service for application media such as recipe images.

Django should store media files in S3 rather than relying on the local filesystem of an EC2 instance or Docker container.

This allows multiple backend instances to access the same media resources and prevents media from being lost when an EC2 instance or container is replaced.

## Where to Work

This task affects AWS infrastructure and Django media configuration.

Potential repository changes include:

- `backend/config/settings.py` — media/storage configuration
- `backend/requirements.txt` — required S3/Django storage dependencies
- `.env.example` — storage configuration variables
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `backend/README.md`

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Amazon S3

- [ ] Create an S3 bucket for application media
- [ ] Choose and document an appropriate bucket name
- [ ] Configure the bucket in the project's AWS region
- [ ] Configure Block Public Access appropriately
- [ ] Configure bucket permissions
- [ ] Configure CORS only if required by the frontend architecture
- [ ] Configure object organization/prefixes where appropriate
- [ ] Document the S3 configuration

### Django

- [ ] Add the required S3 storage integration dependency
- [ ] Configure Django media storage to use S3 in the deployed environment
- [ ] Configure the bucket name through environment-based configuration
- [ ] Configure the AWS region through environment-based configuration
- [ ] Verify media uploads are stored in S3
- [ ] Verify stored media can be retrieved as intended
- [ ] Verify Recipe image fields reference S3-backed media correctly
- [ ] Verify deleting/replacing application instances does not remove media
- [ ] Preserve an appropriate local-development storage option if needed

### AWS / EC2

- [ ] Allow the backend EC2 IAM role to perform only the required S3 operations
- [ ] Verify backend instances can access the media bucket
- [ ] Verify AWS access keys are not required inside the application container
- [ ] Document required IAM permissions

## Architecture

Before S3:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
Django
 │
 ▼
Local Filesystem
 │
 └── recipe-images/
```

This causes problems with horizontal scaling:

```text
EC2 #1
 └── image-a.jpg

EC2 #2
 └── image missing
```

Instead:

```text
             EC2 #1
                │
                │
                ▼
               S3
                ▲
                │
             EC2 #2
```

Both backend instances use the same object storage.

## Target Architecture

```text
                         Users
                           │
                ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                │                     │
                ▼                     ▼
             Frontend             Cognito
                │
                ▼
               ALB
                │
        ┌───────┴───────┐
        ▼               ▼
      EC2 #1          EC2 #2
      Django          Django
        │               │
        └───────┬───────┘
                │
        ┌───────┴────────┐
        ▼                ▼
       RDS               S3
 Relational Data       Media
```

The services have separate responsibilities:

```text
RDS
└── Structured relational data

S3
└── Images / media objects

ECR
└── Docker images

EC2
└── Application compute
```

## Media Storage

Recipe image fields should store/reference media through Django's configured storage system.

Conceptually:

```text
Recipe
├── id
├── name
├── description
└── image
       │
       ▼
    S3 Object
```

Do not store the actual image binary directly inside the Recipe database table.

RDS should contain the information necessary for Django to reference the media object.

## Local vs. Production Storage

The application may use different storage implementations by environment.

Development:

```text
Django
  ↓
Local Media Storage
```

Production:

```text
Django
  ↓
Amazon S3
```

Application feature code should not need to know which storage backend is being used.

Use Django's storage abstraction rather than implementing direct S3 upload logic throughout Recipe components.

## Configuration

Environment-specific values should be configurable.

Conceptually:

```env
AWS_STORAGE_BUCKET_NAME=
AWS_S3_REGION_NAME=
```

Use the actual naming convention established by the project.

Do not put AWS access keys into `.env.example`.

When running on EC2, AWS access should use the EC2 IAM role.

## IAM

Backend instances should access S3 through IAM.

Preferred:

```text
Django Container
      │
      ▼
     EC2
      │
      ▼
  IAM Role
      │
      ▼
      S3
```

Avoid:

```text
Django
  │
  ▼
Hardcoded AWS Access Key
  │
  ▼
 S3
```

The EC2 role should receive only the permissions required for application media operations.

Depending on the final implementation, this may include actions such as:

```text
s3:GetObject
s3:PutObject
s3:DeleteObject
```

only for the required media bucket/prefix.

Do not grant unrestricted S3 administration if the application only needs access to one bucket.

## Bucket Security

Do not automatically make the entire S3 bucket public.

Use:

```text
S3 Block Public Access
```

appropriately.

The exact media-access strategy depends on the application's requirements.

For public recipe images, media may eventually be served through a controlled public delivery mechanism such as CloudFront.

For private user media, access should remain restricted.

The bucket itself should not be broadly exposed simply because some media needs to be viewable.

## Object Naming

Do not rely on raw user-provided filenames as globally unique storage keys.

The storage configuration should prevent accidental collisions.

Conceptually:

```text
recipes/
    <unique-name-or-id>/
        image.jpg
```

or another safe naming strategy supported by the application's storage layer.

Do not use object names to store sensitive user information unnecessarily.

## File Validation

If users are allowed to upload media, backend validation should enforce appropriate restrictions.

Consider:

- supported file types
- maximum upload size
- expected image/media formats

Do not trust a filename extension alone as proof of file type.

Full advanced media-security processing is outside this issue unless required by the project scope.

## Security Requirements

### Credentials

Do not store:

- AWS access keys in Django source
- AWS access keys in Docker images
- AWS access keys in Git
- AWS access keys in frontend code
- secrets in S3 object metadata

EC2 should use its IAM role.

### Least Privilege

The backend should access only the bucket/resources required by the application.

Avoid:

```text
s3:*
Resource: *
```

when narrower permissions are sufficient.

Prefer conceptually:

```text
Required S3 actions
        │
        ▼
Project Media Bucket
```

### Public Access

Do not expose the complete bucket unnecessarily.

Public application media and private user media should not automatically be treated as having identical security requirements.

### Input Validation

Media uploads must be validated by the backend where uploads are supported.

Frontend restrictions alone are not sufficient.

## Scalability Requirements

Media must not depend on an individual EC2 instance.

Incorrect:

```text
             ALB
          /       \
       EC2 #1    EC2 #2
         │
       image
```

Correct:

```text
             ALB
          /       \
       EC2 #1    EC2 #2
          \       /
              S3
```

This allows backend instances to remain interchangeable.

Adding or removing an EC2 instance should not affect previously uploaded media.

## Horizontal Scaling

When Auto Scaling launches a new backend instance:

```text
Auto Scaling
     │
     ▼
New EC2
     │
     ▼
Django
     │
     ▼
S3
```

The new instance should immediately have access to the same application media through its IAM role.

No media synchronization between EC2 instances should be required.

## Performance

Application responses should avoid unnecessarily proxying large media objects through Django when direct/shared object delivery is more appropriate.

Conceptually:

```text
Bad:

Browser
  ↓
Django
  ↓
Download S3 image
  ↓
Django sends image
  ↓
Browser
```

For public/static media, the eventual architecture can use:

```text
Browser
   ↓
CloudFront
   ↓
S3
```

This reduces unnecessary backend workload.

CloudFront configuration can be handled separately.

## Scalability Evidence

S3 itself does not prove that the entire application is scalable.

However, moving media outside EC2 removes an important dependency on individual backend instances.

The final architecture documentation should explain:

```text
Before:
Media tied to EC2 instance

After:
Media stored in shared S3 storage

Result:
Backend instances can be added/replaced without media synchronization.
```

Later load testing will measure application performance independently.

## Durability / Persistence Test

A useful verification test is:

```text
1. Upload Recipe Image
        ↓
2. Image stored in S3
        ↓
3. Stop/recreate Django container
        ↓
4. Retrieve Recipe
        ↓
5. Image still available
```

For stronger validation later:

```text
EC2 #1 uploads image
        ↓
S3
        ↓
EC2 #2 accesses same Recipe
        ↓
Same image available
```

## Cost Awareness

S3 costs depend on:

- stored data
- requests
- data transfer

For the class project, media volume should remain relatively small.

Avoid unnecessarily storing duplicate or very large media files.

## Important

S3 is for object/media storage.

It is not the relational database.

```text
Correct:

Recipe metadata ──→ RDS
Recipe image ─────→ S3
```

Do not:

```text
Recipe relational data ──→ S3 JSON files
```

as a replacement for the application's PostgreSQL data model.

### Do NOT

- Store media only on EC2
- Store media only inside Docker containers
- Store image binaries directly in PostgreSQL
- Commit AWS credentials
- Put AWS access keys in React
- Put AWS access keys in the Docker image
- Give the EC2 role unrestricted S3 administration unnecessarily
- Make the entire bucket public by default
- Trust frontend-only upload validation
- Depend on raw user filenames being unique
- Hardcode bucket configuration throughout application feature code
- Use S3 as a replacement for RDS
- Implement unrelated Recipe functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### S3

- [ ] Application media bucket exists
- [ ] Bucket region/configuration is documented
- [ ] Block Public Access is configured appropriately
- [ ] Bucket permissions follow the intended media-access model
- [ ] CORS is configured only if required

### Django

- [ ] Deployed Django environment can use S3 media storage
- [ ] Recipe images can be stored in S3
- [ ] Recipe image references continue working after backend restart/replacement
- [ ] Storage configuration is environment-based
- [ ] Application feature code uses Django storage abstraction where appropriate

### Security

- [ ] EC2 accesses S3 using an IAM role
- [ ] No AWS access keys are embedded in application code
- [ ] No AWS access keys are embedded in Docker images
- [ ] S3 permissions follow least privilege
- [ ] Bucket is not unnecessarily publicly exposed
- [ ] Backend media validation exists where user uploads are supported

### Scalability

- [ ] Media does not depend on an individual EC2 filesystem
- [ ] Multiple backend instances can reference the same media
- [ ] New/replaced backend instances do not require media synchronization
- [ ] Media architecture is compatible with Auto Scaling
- [ ] Architecture supports future CloudFront delivery

### Documentation

- [ ] S3 setup is documented
- [ ] Required environment configuration is documented
- [ ] IAM requirements are documented
- [ ] Media storage architecture is documented
- [ ] Updated architecture diagram includes S3

## Before Submitting

Verify:

```text
Django
  ↓
Upload Image
  ↓
S3
  ↓
Recipe references image
```

Restart the Django container and verify the image remains available.

Where multiple backend instances are available, verify another backend instance can access the same media.

Review IAM permissions and confirm the backend does not have unnecessarily broad S3 access.

Update:

```text
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/deployment.md
```

as appropriate.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/s3-media`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure EC2 Auto Scaling for Django Backend
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure the Django backend to support horizontal scaling using an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling Group.

Multiple equivalent backend instances should be able to run the same versioned Docker image from Amazon ECR and register with the Application Load Balancer target group.

The system should be able to increase or decrease backend capacity without changing application code.

This issue establishes the scalable backend infrastructure.

Actual scalability claims will later be validated through load testing and measured statistics.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and deployment configuration.

Repository changes may include:

- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- infrastructure/deployment scripts or configuration where appropriate

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

This task builds on:

- Dockerized Django backend
- Amazon ECR
- EC2 backend deployment
- Application Load Balancer

## Tasks

### Launch Template

- [ ] Create an EC2 Launch Template
- [ ] Configure the appropriate AMI
- [ ] Configure the project EC2 instance type
- [ ] Attach the backend EC2 security group
- [ ] Attach the backend IAM instance role
- [ ] Configure storage appropriately
- [ ] Configure backend startup/bootstrap behavior
- [ ] Ensure new instances can pull the backend image from ECR
- [ ] Ensure new instances can start the Django container automatically
- [ ] Ensure runtime configuration is supplied securely

### Auto Scaling Group

- [ ] Create an EC2 Auto Scaling Group
- [ ] Use the Launch Template
- [ ] Configure appropriate VPC/subnets
- [ ] Attach the Auto Scaling Group to the ALB target group
- [ ] Configure minimum capacity
- [ ] Configure desired capacity
- [ ] Configure maximum capacity
- [ ] Configure health checks
- [ ] Verify instances automatically register with the ALB
- [ ] Verify unhealthy/replaced instances are handled correctly

### Scaling Policy

- [ ] Configure an appropriate scaling policy
- [ ] Select a measurable scaling signal
- [ ] Document scaling thresholds/targets
- [ ] Verify the policy can increase capacity
- [ ] Verify capacity can decrease when appropriate
- [ ] Document cooldown/warm-up behavior

## Architecture

Before horizontal scaling:

```text
             Internet
                │
                ▼
               ALB
                │
                ▼
              EC2 #1
                │
                ▼
              Django
```

After this issue:

```text
                         Internet
                            │
                            ▼
                           ALB
                            │
                    ┌───────┴───────┐
                    ▼               ▼
                  EC2 #1          EC2 #2
                  Django          Django
                    │               │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            ▼
                           RDS
```

The backend instances are managed by:

```text
                Auto Scaling Group
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
           EC2 #1              EC2 #2
```

## Launch Template

The Launch Template defines how equivalent backend instances are created.

Conceptually:

```text
Launch Template
├── AMI
├── Instance Type
├── Security Group
├── IAM Role
├── Storage
└── Startup Configuration
```

New backend instances should not require a developer to manually SSH into the machine and configure Django.

The goal is:

```text
Create Instance
      ↓
Startup
      ↓
Pull ECR Image
      ↓
Run Django Container
      ↓
Register with ALB
      ↓
Healthy Backend
```

## Backend Image

All backend instances should run the intended version of the same backend image.

```text
Amazon ECR
     │
     ├──→ EC2 #1
     ├──→ EC2 #2
     └──→ EC2 #N
```

Do not manually maintain different application code on individual EC2 instances.

The deployed image should remain traceable to a Git revision/version.

## Stateless Backend

Horizontal scaling requires backend instances to be interchangeable.

Requests must not depend on always reaching the same server.

Correct:

```text
Request 1
   ↓
EC2 #1

Request 2
   ↓
EC2 #2

Both operate correctly.
```

Persistent state should use shared services.

```text
Application Data
      ↓
     RDS

Media
      ↓
      S3

Authentication
      ↓
   Cognito
```

Do not rely on:

```text
EC2 #1 local filesystem
```

for persistent application data required by other backend instances.

## Auto Scaling Group Capacity

Choose conservative values appropriate for the class project.

Conceptually:

```text
Minimum: 1
Desired: 1
Maximum: 2 or 3
```

The exact values should be documented based on project requirements and AWS cost constraints.

Do not configure unnecessarily large scaling limits.

During the final scalability experiment, desired capacity may be deliberately changed to compare configurations.

## Scaling Policy

Use a measurable infrastructure signal.

A reasonable initial option is CPU utilization.

Conceptually:

```text
Low Load
   ↓
1 EC2

Load Increases
   ↓
CPU / Scaling Metric Reaches Target
   ↓
Auto Scaling Group
   ↓
Launch Additional EC2
   ↓
Register with ALB
   ↓
Traffic Distributed
```

The exact threshold/target must be documented.

Do not claim that a particular threshold is optimal unless supported by testing.

## Health Checks

The Auto Scaling Group should work with the ALB health-check architecture.

```text
ALB
 │
 ├── EC2 #1 → Healthy
 └── EC2 #2 → Healthy
```

If an instance becomes unhealthy:

```text
EC2 #1 → Healthy
EC2 #2 → Unhealthy
```

the system should be capable of replacing the unhealthy backend instance.

New instances must not receive normal traffic until they are ready to serve requests.

## Security Requirements

### IAM

Auto-scaled instances must use the existing backend IAM role or an equivalent least-privilege role.

Do not distribute long-lived AWS credentials through Launch Templates or startup scripts.

Use:

```text
EC2
 ↓
IAM Role
 ↓
Required AWS Services
```

### Secrets

Launch Templates and startup scripts must not expose application secrets unnecessarily.

Do not hardcode:

- database passwords
- Django secret keys
- AWS access keys
- Cognito secrets

The later Secrets Management integration should provide sensitive runtime configuration.

### Network

New EC2 instances must automatically receive the correct backend security group.

The intended path remains:

```text
Internet
   ↓
ALB Security Group
   ↓
EC2 Security Group
   ↓
RDS Security Group
```

New instances should not require public exposure of the Django application port.

## Scalability Requirements

This issue must demonstrate that backend capacity can be changed without redesigning or modifying the Django application.

The architecture should support:

```text
1 Backend
    ↓
2 Backends
    ↓
N Backends
```

within the configured Auto Scaling limits.

Adding another backend should not require:

- changing React
- changing API URLs
- creating another database
- copying application data manually
- modifying Django feature code

## Scalability Experiment Preparation

This infrastructure will later support controlled comparisons.

For example:

```text
Configuration A

ALB
 │
 └── EC2 #1
```

versus:

```text
Configuration B

ALB
 ├── EC2 #1
 └── EC2 #2
```

Run the same workload against both configurations.

Measure:

```text
Concurrent Users
Requests / Second
Average Response Time
p95 Response Time
Error Rate
EC2 CPU
EC2 Memory
RDS Metrics
```

This will provide statistical evidence for the final report.

## Auto Scaling Experiment

We can also demonstrate dynamic scaling:

```text
1 EC2
  │
  ▼
Load Test Begins
  │
  ▼
Scaling Metric Increases
  │
  ▼
Auto Scaling Triggered
  │
  ▼
EC2 #2 Created
  │
  ▼
Health Check Passes
  │
  ▼
ALB Begins Routing Traffic
```

Record:

```text
Time
Active Instance Count
CPU Utilization
Request Rate
Response Time
Scaling Event
```

This gives the final report evidence that the architecture can react to increased demand.

## Scaling Down

The system should also support reducing unnecessary capacity.

Conceptually:

```text
Traffic Decreases
      ↓
Scaling Metric Decreases
      ↓
Auto Scaling Policy
      ↓
Remove Excess Capacity
```

Scale-in behavior should not cause persistent application data loss because application state belongs in shared services rather than individual EC2 instances.

## Failure / Recovery Test

Where practical, test replacement behavior.

For example:

```text
Auto Scaling Group

EC2 #1 ✓
EC2 #2 ✓
```

Terminate one instance during a controlled test.

Expected architecture behavior:

```text
EC2 #1 ✗
EC2 #2 ✓

      ↓

ASG detects capacity below desired

      ↓

EC2 #3 created

      ↓

Health check passes

      ↓

EC2 #2 ✓
EC2 #3 ✓
```

This provides evidence of resilience in addition to scalability.

## Monitoring

Auto Scaling behavior should later be observable through CloudWatch.

Useful information includes:

```text
GroupDesiredCapacity
GroupInServiceInstances
GroupTotalInstances
EC2 CPUUtilization
ALB RequestCount
ALB TargetResponseTime
HealthyHostCount
```

The dedicated monitoring issue will configure final dashboards/alarms.

## Cost Awareness

Auto Scaling can create additional billable resources.

Use conservative limits appropriate for the project.

For example:

```text
Min:     1
Desired: 1
Max:     2
```

may be sufficient during normal development.

Higher capacity can be temporarily configured during controlled scalability testing if necessary.

Do not leave unnecessary test instances running after experiments.

## Important

Auto Scaling provides the **mechanism** for horizontal scaling.

It does not by itself prove that the application performs better.

```text
Auto Scaling
     +
ALB
     +
Stateless Django
     +
Shared RDS
     +
Load Testing
     ↓
Measured Scalability Evidence
```

The final conclusion must come from measured results.

### Do NOT

- Store AWS access keys in Launch Templates
- Store AWS access keys in user-data scripts
- Hardcode database passwords in Launch Templates
- Hardcode Django secrets in startup scripts
- Give Auto Scaling instances AdministratorAccess
- Create separate databases for each EC2 instance
- Store persistent application data on individual EC2 instances
- Require manual SSH configuration for every scaled instance
- Give each EC2 instance different application code
- Hardcode EC2 addresses into React
- Assume requests return to the same backend instance
- Expose backend application ports unnecessarily
- Configure excessive maximum capacity
- Claim performance improvement without measurements
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Launch Template

- [ ] Launch Template exists
- [ ] Backend instance configuration is reproducible
- [ ] Appropriate security group is automatically attached
- [ ] Appropriate IAM role is automatically attached
- [ ] Instance can retrieve the backend image from ECR
- [ ] Django container starts without manual application setup
- [ ] Deployed image version can be identified

### Auto Scaling Group

- [ ] Auto Scaling Group exists
- [ ] Minimum capacity is configured
- [ ] Desired capacity is configured
- [ ] Maximum capacity is configured
- [ ] ASG is connected to the backend target group
- [ ] New instances automatically register with the ALB
- [ ] Healthy instances receive traffic
- [ ] Unhealthy instances can be detected/replaced

### Security

- [ ] No long-lived AWS credentials are included in instance configuration
- [ ] IAM follows least privilege
- [ ] New instances receive the intended security group
- [ ] Application secrets are not embedded in the Docker image
- [ ] Application secrets are not committed to source control
- [ ] Backend ports are not unnecessarily publicly exposed

### Scalability

- [ ] Backend can operate with one instance
- [ ] Backend can operate with multiple equivalent instances
- [ ] Multiple instances use shared persistent storage
- [ ] Client API endpoint does not change when instance count changes
- [ ] Backend behavior does not depend on a specific EC2 instance
- [ ] Scaling policy is documented
- [ ] Architecture is ready for controlled load testing

### Documentation

- [ ] Launch Template configuration is documented
