- [ ] Auto Scaling Group configuration is documented
- [ ] Capacity settings are documented
- [ ] Scaling policy is documented
- [ ] Updated architecture diagram includes ASG
- [ ] Security implications are documented
- [ ] Cost considerations are documented

## Before Submitting

Verify the normal architecture:

```text
Client
  ↓
ALB
  ↓
Auto Scaling Group
  ↓
EC2 Backend(s)
  ↓
Django
  ↓
RDS
```

Verify a newly created instance can automatically:

```text
Launch
  ↓
Pull Image
  ↓
Start Django
  ↓
Pass Health Check
  ↓
Receive ALB Traffic
```

Where practical, test multiple backend instances and verify requests continue working regardless of which healthy target receives them.

Document the actual:

```text
Instance Type
Minimum Capacity
Desired Capacity
Maximum Capacity
Scaling Metric
Scaling Target/Threshold
```

Do not fabricate performance statistics at this stage.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/auto-scaling`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure Application Load Balancer for Django Backend
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the Django backend.

The ALB should provide a single entry point for backend API traffic, route requests to healthy EC2 backend instances, and establish the foundation for horizontal scaling.

This issue configures the load-balancing layer.

A later issue will configure EC2 Auto Scaling and perform scalability/load testing.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and deployment configuration.

Repository changes may include:

- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `backend/README.md`
- Django production configuration where required

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

This task builds on the deployed Django backend.

## Tasks

### Application Load Balancer

- [ ] Create an Application Load Balancer
- [ ] Configure the ALB in the appropriate VPC
- [ ] Configure appropriate subnets
- [ ] Create an ALB security group
- [ ] Create a backend target group
- [ ] Register the EC2 backend as a target
- [ ] Configure the Django health-check endpoint
- [ ] Configure target-group health checks
- [ ] Configure an ALB listener
- [ ] Route incoming API traffic to the backend target group
- [ ] Verify healthy/unhealthy target detection
- [ ] Verify API traffic works through the ALB endpoint
- [ ] Update Django `ALLOWED_HOSTS` where required
- [ ] Document the ALB configuration

### Backend Network Security

- [ ] Update the EC2 security group so backend application traffic can come from the ALB
- [ ] Avoid unnecessary direct public access to the Django application port
- [ ] Verify the ALB can reach the backend
- [ ] Verify unrelated Internet traffic cannot directly access protected backend ports

## Architecture

Before this issue:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
EC2
   │
   ▼
Django
```

After this issue:

```text
                  Internet
                     │
                     ▼
          Application Load Balancer
                     │
                     ▼
                Target Group
                     │
                     ▼
                   EC2
                     │
                     ▼
             Django + Gunicorn
                     │
                     ▼
                   RDS
```

This establishes the routing layer required for future horizontal scaling.

## Target Architecture

Later:

```text
                         Users
                           │
                           ▼
                Application Load Balancer
                           │
                   ┌───────┴───────┐
                   │               │
                   ▼               ▼
                 EC2 #1          EC2 #2
                 Django          Django
                   │               │
                   └───────┬───────┘
                           ▼
                     Amazon RDS
                     PostgreSQL
```

The client should not need to know which backend instance handles a request.

## Target Group

Create a target group for the Django backend.

Conceptually:

```text
ALB
 │
 ▼
Backend Target Group
 │
 ├── EC2 #1
 ├── EC2 #2
 └── future EC2 instances
```

For this issue, one backend target is sufficient to establish the architecture.

The target group must be capable of supporting additional backend instances later.

## Health Checks

Use the backend health endpoint established during EC2 deployment.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /api/health/
```

Expected response:

```json
{
  "status": "ok"
}
```

The target group should periodically request this endpoint.

```text
ALB
 │
 ├── Health Check → EC2 #1 → Healthy
 │
 └── Health Check → EC2 #2 → Healthy
```

If a backend becomes unhealthy:

```text
EC2 #1 → Healthy
EC2 #2 → Unhealthy

          ↓

ALB sends application traffic only to
healthy targets.
```

The health endpoint must remain lightweight.

It must not expose:

- credentials
- environment variables
- database passwords
- AWS configuration
- sensitive application information

## Health Check Behavior

The health check should verify that the Django application process is capable of responding.

Avoid expensive health-check behavior.

For example, do not perform large Recipe queries or Recommendation calculations every time the ALB checks backend health.

A lightweight application-health response is sufficient for this stage.

## Security Groups

Use separate security groups for the ALB and backend.

Conceptually:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
ALB Security Group
   │
   ▼
EC2 Security Group
   │
   ▼
Django
```

### ALB Security Group

Allow required public application traffic.

Conceptually:

```text
Inbound:

HTTP/HTTPS
Source:
Internet
```

The final production architecture should use HTTPS.

### EC2 Security Group

Allow backend application traffic from the **ALB security group**.

Conceptually:

```text
Backend application port
Source:
ALB Security Group
```

Prefer this over:

```text
Backend application port
Source:
0.0.0.0/0
```

This means users communicate with:

```text
User
 ↓
ALB
 ↓
EC2
```

rather than bypassing the load balancer.

## Database Security

The ALB must not communicate directly with RDS.

Correct:

```text
ALB
 ↓
EC2 / Django
 ↓
RDS
```

Not:

```text
ALB
 ↓
RDS
```

RDS should continue accepting PostgreSQL connections only from the appropriate backend infrastructure/security group.

## Django Configuration

Django must accept requests routed through the ALB.

Update environment-based configuration where required.

For example:

```text
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS
```

Do not hardcode the ALB hostname throughout application source code.

The frontend/backend API configuration should eventually use a stable application endpoint rather than a specific EC2 public IP.

## HTTPS

The final deployed application should use HTTPS.

The intended architecture is:

```text
User
 │
 │ HTTPS
 ▼
ALB
 │
 │ Backend traffic
 ▼
EC2
```

HTTPS certificate configuration may be completed in a dedicated domain/HTTPS task if the project does not yet have the required domain/certificate.

Do not treat plain HTTP as the final secure production architecture.

## Security Requirements

### Public Exposure

The ALB should become the public entry point for backend application traffic.

Backend instances should not require unrestricted public access to the application port.

Avoid:

```text
Internet ───────→ EC2:8000
```

Prefer:

```text
Internet
   ↓
ALB
   ↓
EC2:application-port
```

### Security Group Chaining

Use:

```text
ALB Security Group
        ↓
EC2 Security Group
        ↓
RDS Security Group
```

This establishes clear network boundaries.

### Administrative Access

ALB configuration does not require opening SSH access publicly.

Administrative EC2 access should continue following the restricted approach established in the EC2 issue.

### Application Security

The ALB does not replace:

- Cognito authentication
- Django authorization
- API validation
- ownership checks

These remain application responsibilities.

## Scalability Requirements

The ALB is the routing layer that enables horizontal backend scaling.

Without a load balancer:

```text
Client
  ↓
EC2 #1
```

Adding another instance does not automatically distribute traffic.

With the ALB:

```text
             Client
                │
                ▼
               ALB
                │
        ┌───────┴───────┐
        ▼               ▼
      EC2 #1          EC2 #2
```

Clients continue using one backend endpoint while the infrastructure can change the number of backend instances.

## Stateless Backend Requirement

Backend requests must not depend on always reaching the same EC2 instance.

Avoid:

```text
Request 1 → EC2 #1
             ↓
       important local state

Request 2 → EC2 #2
             ↓
       state missing
```

Persistent/shared application state should use appropriate shared services:

```text
Relational Data → RDS
Media           → S3
Authentication  → Cognito
```

This allows the ALB to distribute requests across backend instances.

## Scalability Evidence

This issue establishes the infrastructure required for later quantitative testing.

Later we should compare configurations such as:

```text
Test A
──────
ALB
 ↓
1 EC2


Test B
──────
ALB
 ├── EC2 #1
 └── EC2 #2
```

Under equivalent load, record:

```text
Concurrent Users
Requests / Second
Average Response Time
p95 Response Time
Error Rate
EC2 CPU Utilization
EC2 Memory Utilization
RDS Metrics
```

Example final-report structure:

```text
Concurrent     1 EC2 p95     2 EC2 p95
---------------------------------------
50                ___ ms        ___ ms
100               ___ ms        ___ ms
250               ___ ms        ___ ms
500               ___ ms        ___ ms
```

Actual values must come from load testing.

Do not invent or estimate performance results.

## Failure Demonstration

The ALB also gives us an opportunity to demonstrate resilience.

For example:

```text
ALB
 ├── EC2 #1 ✓
 └── EC2 #2 ✓
```

If later:

```text
EC2 #1 ✗
EC2 #2 ✓
```

the ALB should stop routing normal traffic to the unhealthy target.

This can provide additional system-design evidence during the final demonstration.

## Monitoring

The ALB should be compatible with later CloudWatch monitoring.

Useful metrics include:

```text
RequestCount
TargetResponseTime
HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count
HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count
HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
HealthyHostCount
UnHealthyHostCount
```

The dedicated monitoring issue will configure the final dashboards/alarms.

## Cost Awareness

Use only the infrastructure required for the project.

One healthy backend target is sufficient while initially configuring the ALB.

Additional EC2 instances should be introduced when implementing/testing horizontal scaling rather than kept running unnecessarily throughout development.

## Important

This issue creates the **load-balancing layer**.

It does not yet prove that the application scales.

```text
ALB
 ↓
Scalable Architecture Foundation

ALB
+
Multiple Instances
+
Measured Load Tests
 ↓
Scalability Evidence
```

The professor's scalability requirement will ultimately be supported by actual measurements.

### Do NOT

- Expose the backend application port to `0.0.0.0/0` as the intended final architecture
- Allow ALB direct database access
- Expose RDS publicly
- Put secrets in health-check responses
- Use expensive application operations as health checks
- Hardcode a specific EC2 IP into frontend/application source code
- Assume requests always reach the same EC2 instance
- Store required request/session state only on one EC2 filesystem
- Treat ALB as a replacement for Django authorization
- Claim scalability without measured results
- Implement full Auto Scaling in this issue
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### ALB

- [ ] Application Load Balancer exists
- [ ] Backend target group exists
- [ ] EC2 backend is registered as a target
- [ ] Backend target reports healthy
- [ ] ALB listener routes application traffic to the backend
- [ ] API can be reached through the ALB endpoint
- [ ] Health checks correctly detect backend availability

### Security

- [ ] ALB has a dedicated security group
- [ ] EC2 backend has a dedicated security group
- [ ] Backend application traffic can be restricted to the ALB security group
- [ ] Backend application port is not unnecessarily exposed publicly
- [ ] ALB cannot directly access the database
- [ ] RDS remains protected by its database security group
- [ ] Health endpoint does not expose sensitive information
- [ ] Architecture supports HTTPS as the final public transport

### Django

- [ ] Django accepts traffic routed through the ALB
- [ ] `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is configured appropriately
- [ ] Django continues running with `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Existing API functionality works through the ALB
- [ ] Authentication/authorization behavior remains unchanged

### Scalability

- [ ] Target group supports multiple backend targets
- [ ] Additional equivalent EC2 instances can be registered
- [ ] Application does not require clients to know individual EC2 addresses
- [ ] Backend does not depend on requests reaching one specific EC2 instance
- [ ] Architecture is ready for Auto Scaling
- [ ] ALB metrics can later be used during scalability testing

### Documentation

- [ ] ALB configuration is documented
- [ ] Target-group configuration is documented
- [ ] Health-check configuration is documented
- [ ] Security-group relationship is documented
- [ ] Updated architecture diagram includes the ALB
- [ ] Limitations/current single-instance state are documented accurately

## Before Submitting

Verify:

```text
Client
  ↓
ALB
  ↓
Target Group
  ↓
EC2
  ↓
Django
  ↓
RDS
```

Test the health endpoint through the ALB.

Test representative API endpoints through the ALB rather than through the EC2 public address.

Verify the EC2 application port is not unnecessarily publicly accessible.

Verify the target appears as:

```text
Healthy
```

in the target group.

Update:

```text
docs/aws-architecture.md
docs/deployment.md
```

as appropriate.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/application-load-balancer`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL as the production relational database for the Django backend.

The Django application running on EC2 should connect to RDS using environment-based configuration.

RDS will provide persistent shared relational storage for all backend instances.

The production database must not depend on storage inside an EC2 instance or Docker container.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and Django production configuration.

Repository changes may include:

- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `backend/README.md`
- `.env.example`
- `backend/config/settings.py` if additional environment-based configuration is required

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

This task builds on the PostgreSQL-compatible Django configuration established by the project.

## Tasks

### Amazon RDS

- [ ] Create an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database
- [ ] Select an appropriate PostgreSQL version
- [ ] Select an appropriate project-sized DB instance class
- [ ] Configure database storage
- [ ] Configure database name
- [ ] Configure database credentials securely
- [ ] Place RDS in the appropriate VPC
- [ ] Configure database security groups
- [ ] Disable public database access
- [ ] Configure backups appropriate for the project
- [ ] Document the RDS configuration

### Django / EC2

- [ ] Configure Django to connect to RDS
- [ ] Supply RDS configuration through environment variables
- [ ] Verify EC2 can reach RDS
- [ ] Verify unauthorized/public access to RDS is blocked
- [ ] Run Django migrations against RDS
- [ ] Verify Django Admin works with RDS
- [ ] Verify backend API operations use RDS
- [ ] Verify multiple backend instances could connect to the same database

## Architecture

The intended architecture is:

```text
                    Internet
                       │
                       ▼
                      EC2
                       │
                       │ PostgreSQL
                       ▼
                  Amazon RDS
                  PostgreSQL
```

The database should not be directly exposed to users.

Later:

```text
                         Internet
                            │
                            ▼
                  Application Load Balancer
                            │
                     ┌──────┴──────┐
                     ▼             ▼
                   EC2 #1        EC2 #2
                     │             │
                     └──────┬──────┘
                            ▼
                       Amazon RDS
                       PostgreSQL
```

RDS therefore acts as shared persistent storage for multiple backend instances.

## Network Security

RDS must not be publicly accessible as part of the intended architecture.

Avoid:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
RDS
```

Use:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Application
   │
   ▼
EC2 Security Group
   │
   ▼
RDS Security Group
```

The RDS security group should allow PostgreSQL traffic only from the backend infrastructure that requires database access.

Conceptually:

```text
RDS Security Group

Inbound:

PostgreSQL / TCP 5432
Source:
EC2 Backend Security Group
```

Do not use:

```text
PostgreSQL / TCP 5432
Source:
0.0.0.0/0
```

## Security Group Relationship

Prefer security-group references rather than depending on specific EC2 public IP addresses.

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
Backend Security Group
 │
 │ permitted by
 ▼
Database Security Group
 │
 ▼
RDS
```

This is important for future horizontal scaling because newly created backend instances can receive the same backend security group.

The database does not need a new rule for every individual EC2 instance.

## Database Credentials

Database credentials must not be committed to Git.

Do not store credentials in:

- Django source code
- Dockerfile
- Docker image
- frontend source code
- committed `.env` files
- deployment documentation

For the initial integration, configuration should still be supplied externally.

A later Secrets Management issue will formalize storage/retrieval using AWS-managed secret storage.

Conceptually:

```text
AWS Secret Management
        │
        ▼
       EC2
        │
        ▼
      Django
        │
        ▼
       RDS
```

## Django Configuration

Django should use environment-based configuration.

Conceptually:

```env
DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_HOST=
DB_PORT=5432
```

The RDS endpoint must not be hardcoded into application logic.

The same Django code should support:

```text
Local Development
        │
        ▼
Local PostgreSQL
```

and:

```text
AWS Production
      │
      ▼
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
```

by changing configuration rather than application code.

## Database Migrations

Once RDS is configured, Django migrations must be applied to it.

For example:

```bash
python manage.py migrate
```

Verify:

```bash
python manage.py showmigrations
```

The application must use the same migration history across local PostgreSQL and RDS.

Do not manually create production application tables outside Django migrations.

## Persistent Data

Application data belongs in RDS rather than inside backend containers.

```text
EC2 / Docker
     │
     └── Application Runtime

RDS
     │
     ├── Users
     ├── Ingredients
     ├── Recipes
     ├── RecipeIngredients
     ├── Tags
     ├── Inventory
     ├── Preferences
     └── Other relational application data
```

Restarting or replacing an EC2 instance should not destroy application database data.

## Backup / Recovery

Configure an appropriate backup policy for the project environment.

Document:

- automated backup configuration
- retention period
- whether deletion protection is enabled
- whether final snapshots are expected before production database deletion

The project does not need enterprise-level disaster recovery, but the architecture should demonstrate awareness that persistent production data requires recovery planning.

## Security Requirements

### Database Isolation

RDS should not accept arbitrary connections from the public Internet.

```text
Public User
    │
    X
    ▼
   RDS
```

Backend:

```text
EC2
 │
 ✓
 ▼
RDS
```

### Least Privilege

Database access should be limited to the application infrastructure that requires it.

Do not solve connectivity problems by broadly exposing PostgreSQL to the Internet.

### Credentials

Database credentials must:

- remain outside source control
- remain outside Docker images
- never be sent to React
- never appear in API responses
- not be written into normal application logs

### Django

Django should continue to validate application input and enforce permissions.

RDS network isolation does not replace application-level security.

## Scalability Requirements

RDS provides shared persistent storage so backend instances can remain stateless.

Without shared storage:

```text
EC2 #1 → Local DB #1
EC2 #2 → Local DB #2

✗ Different application state
```

With RDS:

```text
EC2 #1 ──┐
         │
         ▼
        RDS
         ▲
         │
EC2 #2 ──┘

✓ Shared application state
```

This is required for our future horizontal-scaling architecture.

### Database Performance

The application should continue to use:

- appropriate indexes
- foreign keys
- uniqueness constraints
- efficient ORM queries
- pagination
- `select_related()` / `prefetch_related()` where appropriate

RDS does not automatically fix inefficient application queries.

## Scalability Evidence

Record the RDS configuration used during final performance testing.

Examples:

```text
Database Engine:
PostgreSQL

RDS Instance Class:
<actual class>

Allocated Storage:
<actual amount>

Backend Configuration:
1 EC2 / 2 EC2 / etc.
```

Later load testing can correlate application performance with infrastructure metrics.

Useful database-related measurements may include:

- Database connections
- CPU utilization
- Storage activity
- Query latency where measurable
- Application response latency
- Error rate

These measurements will help identify whether scaling the backend moves the bottleneck toward the database.

## Monitoring

RDS should later integrate with CloudWatch monitoring.

Useful metrics include:

```text
CPUUtilization
DatabaseConnections
FreeStorageSpace
ReadLatency
WriteLatency
ReadIOPS
WriteIOPS
```

The dedicated CloudWatch issue will define the final monitoring requirements.

This issue only needs to ensure the RDS deployment is compatible with that monitoring architecture.

## Cost Awareness

Choose an RDS configuration appropriate for a university project.

Do not select unnecessarily large database instances simply to produce better performance numbers.

Performance documentation should record the actual instance configuration so test results remain meaningful.

## Important

RDS is the authoritative persistent relational database for the deployed application.

```text
EC2 / Docker
      ↓
Compute

RDS PostgreSQL
      ↓
Relational Data

S3
      ↓
Images / Objects

ECR
      ↓
Container Images
```

Keep these responsibilities separate.

### Do NOT

- Make RDS publicly accessible as the intended architecture
- Allow PostgreSQL from `0.0.0.0/0`
- Commit database credentials
- Put database credentials in Docker images
- Expose database credentials to React
- Hardcode the RDS endpoint into application logic
- Store production application data in SQLite
- Store the production database inside the Django container
- Give unrelated infrastructure database access
- Manually create Django application tables instead of using migrations
- Assume RDS alone proves scalability
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### RDS

- [ ] Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance/database exists
- [ ] RDS is configured for the project VPC
- [ ] RDS is not publicly accessible
- [ ] Appropriate database security group exists
- [ ] Backup configuration is documented
- [ ] Database configuration is documented

### Connectivity

- [ ] EC2 backend can connect to RDS
- [ ] RDS accepts PostgreSQL traffic from the intended backend security group
- [ ] RDS is not generally reachable from the public Internet
- [ ] Django successfully connects using environment-based configuration

### Django

- [ ] Django migrations apply successfully to RDS
- [ ] `python manage.py check` passes using the RDS configuration
- [ ] Django Admin operates against RDS
- [ ] Backend API reads/writes data through RDS
- [ ] No production SQLite dependency remains

### Security

- [ ] Database credentials are not committed
- [ ] Database credentials are not embedded in Docker images
- [ ] Database credentials are not exposed to the frontend
- [ ] PostgreSQL is not open to `0.0.0.0/0`
- [ ] Database access is restricted using security groups
- [ ] Architecture is compatible with later AWS secret management

### Scalability

- [ ] RDS provides shared storage independent of individual EC2 instances
- [ ] Multiple equivalent backend instances could connect to the database
- [ ] Database architecture supports future ALB/Auto Scaling deployment
- [ ] RDS configuration can be identified during later load testing
- [ ] Application continues to support database indexing/query optimization

## Before Submitting

Verify:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
Django Container
 │
 ▼
RDS PostgreSQL
```

From the backend environment, run:

```bash
python manage.py check
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py showmigrations
```

Perform a basic API write/read test and verify that the data persists in RDS.

Restart/recreate the Django container and verify the previously stored data remains available.

Confirm that RDS is **not publicly accessible** and that the database security group does not allow PostgreSQL from:

```text
0.0.0.0/0
```

Update the relevant architecture and deployment documentation.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/rds-postgresql`

Title: Infrastructure: Deploy Django Backend to Amazon EC2
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Deploy the containerized Django backend to Amazon EC2.

The EC2 instance should pull the versioned backend Docker image from Amazon ECR and run the Django application using production-oriented configuration.

This issue establishes the initial single-instance backend deployment.

Later issues will extend this architecture with:

- Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
- Application Load Balancer
- Multiple EC2 instances / Auto Scaling
- HTTPS
- CloudWatch monitoring
- Secrets management

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and deployment configuration.

Repository changes may include:

- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/deployment.md`
- `backend/README.md`
- deployment scripts/configuration where appropriate

This task builds on:

- Dockerized Django backend
- Amazon ECR backend repository

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### EC2

- [ ] Create/configure an EC2 instance for the Django backend
- [ ] Select an appropriate development/project instance type
- [ ] Configure the EC2 security group
- [ ] Configure an IAM role for the EC2 instance
- [ ] Install/configure Docker on EC2
- [ ] Authenticate EC2 with Amazon ECR through IAM
- [ ] Pull the backend image from ECR
- [ ] Run the Django backend container
- [ ] Supply required runtime environment configuration
- [ ] Verify the backend starts successfully
- [ ] Verify the API can be reached as intended
- [ ] Verify the health endpoint works
- [ ] Document deployment steps

### Django

- [ ] Run with production-oriented settings
- [ ] Ensure `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Configure `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
- [ ] Run through Gunicorn
- [ ] Verify static/API behavior required by the backend
- [ ] Verify Django management commands can be executed on EC2

## Initial Architecture

This issue establishes:

```text
                Internet
                   │
                   ▼
             EC2 Security Group
                   │
                   ▼
              Amazon EC2
                   │
                   ▼
                 Docker
                   │
                   ▼
          Django + Gunicorn
```

The application image comes from:

```text
Git Repository
      │
      ▼
Docker Build
      │
      ▼
Amazon ECR
      │
      ▼
Amazon EC2
      │
      ▼
Django Container
```

This is the **initial deployment architecture**, not the final scalability architecture.

## Target Architecture

Later issues will evolve the deployment toward:

```text
                     Internet
                        │
                        ▼
             Application Load Balancer
                        │
                 ┌──────┴──────┐
                 ▼             ▼
               EC2 #1        EC2 #2
                 │             │
                 ▼             ▼
              Django        Django
                 │             │
                 └──────┬──────┘
                        ▼
                  Amazon RDS
                  PostgreSQL
```

This issue does not need to implement the ALB or multiple EC2 instances.

## EC2 IAM Role

The EC2 instance should use an IAM role rather than long-lived AWS access keys.

Conceptually:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
IAM Instance Role
 │
 ▼
Amazon ECR
```

At this stage, the role should have only the permissions required by the instance.

Initially this may include:

```text
ECR
└── Pull backend container image
```

Additional permissions for services such as S3 or Secrets Manager should be added only when those integrations are implemented.

## Security Group

The EC2 security group must follow least-access principles.

Do not expose unnecessary ports to the Internet.

Conceptually:

```text
Internet
   │
   ├── Application traffic
   │
   ▼
EC2

Administrative access
   │
   └── Restricted separately
```

When the Application Load Balancer is introduced later, the intended architecture becomes:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
ALB Security Group
   │
   ▼
EC2 Security Group
```

At that point, backend application traffic should be accepted from the ALB rather than directly from the entire Internet where practical.

## SSH / Administrative Access

If SSH is used, do not expose it unnecessarily.

Avoid:

```text
SSH / TCP 22
Source: 0.0.0.0/0
```

Prefer restricted administrative access.

Where practical, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager may later be used to reduce reliance on publicly exposed SSH access.

## Runtime Configuration

The Docker image must not contain environment-specific secrets.

EC2 should provide configuration at runtime.

Examples include:

```text
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
DJANGO_DEBUG
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS

DB_NAME
DB_USER
DB_PASSWORD
DB_HOST
DB_PORT
```

Do not commit production values to Git.

Do not bake them into the Docker image.

A later issue will formalize AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store integration.

## Container Deployment

EC2 should pull a versioned backend image from ECR.

Conceptually:

```text
ECR

recipe-backend:<version>
          │
          ▼
        EC2
          │
          ▼
     docker pull
          │
          ▼
     docker run
```

The deployed image should be traceable to its source version.

For example:

```text
Git Commit
81af721

    ↓

ECR Image
recipe-backend:81af721

    ↓

EC2
running recipe-backend:81af721
```

## Health Check

The backend should expose a lightweight health endpoint if one is not already available.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /api/health/
```

Example response:

```json
{
  "status": "ok"
}
```

The health endpoint should be suitable for later use by the Application Load Balancer.

It should not expose:

- credentials
- environment variables
- internal configuration
- sensitive infrastructure details

## Database

This issue does not require Amazon RDS to be completed first.

During initial deployment, use the currently documented database configuration appropriate for the development stage.

However, the deployment must remain configurable so that the database can later be switched to:

```text
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
```

without rebuilding application logic.

Production architecture must not use SQLite as the final persistent database.

## Security Requirements

### AWS Credentials

Do not store AWS access keys on EC2 simply to access ECR.

Use:

```text
EC2
 ↓
IAM Role
 ↓
ECR
```

### Application Secrets

Do not:

- commit production `.env` files
- store secrets in Docker images
- put secrets in deployment documentation
- expose secrets through API responses
- expose secrets through logs

### Django

Production configuration must use:

```text
DEBUG=False
```

Error responses must not expose Django debug pages or sensitive configuration.

### Network

Only required ports should be reachable.

Administrative access should be restricted.

Future ALB deployment should allow the EC2 instance to become less directly exposed.

## Scalability Requirements

The EC2 deployment must not introduce dependencies that prevent additional equivalent backend instances from being created later.

Avoid:

```text
EC2 #1
 └── Important persistent application data
```

Prefer:

```text
                 EC2 #1
                    │
                    │
Shared Services ────┼── RDS
                    ├── S3
                    │
                 EC2 #2
```

The Django application should remain stateless where practical.

The same ECR image should be capable of running on multiple EC2 instances.

## Performance Baseline

Once the EC2 deployment is operational, basic baseline measurements may be collected for later comparison.

Useful measurements include:

```text
Instance Type
Backend Image Version
Average Response Time
p95 Response Time
Requests/sec
CPU Utilization
Memory Utilization
Error Rate
```

Full load testing belongs to the dedicated scalability-testing issue.

Do not claim horizontal scalability based only on successfully deploying one EC2 instance.

## Cost Awareness

Use an appropriately sized EC2 instance for the project rather than unnecessarily large infrastructure.

The purpose of later scalability testing is to demonstrate how architecture behaves as load increases, not to solve performance problems simply by selecting an oversized instance.

Document the EC2 instance type used so performance results can be interpreted correctly.

## Important

This issue establishes a **single working cloud backend instance**.

Do not combine all remaining AWS infrastructure into this issue.

```text
#18
EC2 Backend Deployment

Later:
├── RDS
├── ALB
├── Auto Scaling
├── S3
├── Secrets Management
├── CloudWatch
└── HTTPS
```

Keeping these responsibilities separate makes the architecture easier to implement, test, document, and evaluate.

### Do NOT

- Commit AWS credentials
- Store AWS access keys on EC2 for normal application operation
- Give the EC2 instance AdministratorAccess
- Put application secrets in the Docker image
- Commit production `.env` files
- Run Django with `DEBUG=True` in the production deployment
- Use Django `runserver` as the production server
- Expose unnecessary ports
- Leave unrestricted SSH access as the intended architecture
- Store persistent application data only on the EC2 filesystem
- Hardcode the EC2 public IP in application source code
- Hardcode future RDS information
- Implement ALB/Auto Scaling inside this issue
- Modify unrelated application features
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Deployment

- [ ] EC2 instance is configured
- [ ] Docker runs successfully on EC2
- [ ] EC2 authenticates with ECR
- [ ] Backend image can be pulled from ECR
- [ ] Django container starts successfully
- [ ] Gunicorn serves the Django application
- [ ] Backend API is reachable as intended
- [ ] Health endpoint responds successfully
- [ ] Deployed image version can be identified

### Security

- [ ] EC2 uses an IAM role for AWS service access
- [ ] No long-lived AWS credentials are stored on EC2 for ECR access
- [ ] IAM permissions follow least privilege
- [ ] Security group exposes only required ports
- [ ] Administrative access is restricted
- [ ] Django runs with `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Application secrets are not stored in the Docker image
- [ ] Sensitive configuration is not exposed through the health endpoint

### Scalability

- [ ] Application does not rely on persistent local EC2 state
- [ ] Same ECR image can be deployed to another EC2 instance
- [ ] Deployment architecture remains compatible with a future ALB
- [ ] Deployment architecture remains compatible with future horizontal scaling
- [ ] EC2 instance type is documented for later performance comparison

### Documentation

- [ ] EC2 setup is documented
- [ ] Security-group configuration is documented
- [ ] IAM role requirements are documented
- [ ] ECR pull/deployment process is documented
- [ ] Runtime configuration requirements are documented
- [ ] Backend update/redeployment procedure is documented

## Before Submitting

Verify the backend image exists in ECR.

On the EC2 deployment, verify:

```text
ECR
 ↓
EC2
 ↓
Docker
 ↓
Django + Gunicorn
 ↓
Health Endpoint
```

Run:

```bash
python manage.py check --deploy
```

inside the production-configured backend environment where practical.

Verify:

```text
DEBUG=False
```

and confirm that sensitive Django debug information is not publicly exposed.

Update the relevant AWS/deployment documentation.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

Title: Infrastructure: Configure Amazon ECR for Backend Images
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) as the container image registry for the Django backend.

The Docker image created for the backend should be buildable locally or through CI/CD, pushed to ECR, and later pulled by EC2 instances for deployment.

This creates a consistent deployment pipeline:

```text
Backend Source Code
        │
        ▼
   Docker Build
        │
        ▼
    Docker Image
        │
        ▼
    Amazon ECR
        │
        ▼
   EC2 Instance(s)
        │
        ▼
 Django Backend
```

ECR should store application images only. Application configuration, credentials, and persistent data must remain outside the image.

## Where to Work

This task primarily involves AWS infrastructure and deployment documentation.

Repository changes may include:

- `docs/aws-architecture.md` — ECR architecture and deployment flow
- `docs/deployment.md` — deployment instructions, if present
- `backend/README.md` — backend image build/push instructions where appropriate
- GitHub Actions configuration later if CI/CD is implemented

This task uses the Docker image established by:

- Issue #15 — Dockerize Django Backend

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

- [ ] Create an Amazon ECR repository for the Django backend
- [ ] Choose and document a consistent repository name
- [ ] Configure appropriate repository settings
- [ ] Authenticate Docker with ECR
- [ ] Build the backend Docker image
- [ ] Tag the image for ECR
- [ ] Push the image to ECR
- [ ] Verify the image exists in ECR
- [ ] Verify the image can be pulled from ECR
- [ ] Establish an image-tagging convention
- [ ] Configure an ECR image lifecycle policy if appropriate
- [ ] Document the build/tag/push workflow
- [ ] Document required AWS permissions
- [ ] Ensure no AWS credentials or application secrets are stored in the image or repository

## Architecture

ECR acts as the container image registry between development/CI and deployment.

```text
Developer / GitHub Actions
           │
           ▼
      Docker Build
           │
           ▼
       Amazon ECR
           │
           ▼
      EC2 Instance
           │
           ▼
      Docker Pull
           │
           ▼
     Django Container
```

Later, when horizontal scaling is introduced:

```text
                       Amazon ECR
                           │
                 ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                 ▼                   ▼
               EC2 #1              EC2 #2
                 │                   │
                 ▼                   ▼
          Django Container     Django Container
```

Each backend instance should be capable of running the same application image.

## Repository

Create a dedicated ECR repository for the backend.

Conceptually:

```text
recipe-backend
```

or another project-specific name agreed upon by the team.

Do not create separate container repositories for individual Django features such as:

```text
ingredients
recipes
inventory
recommendations
```

The Django backend is currently deployed as one application and should therefore have one backend application image.

## Image Tagging

Do not rely only on `latest`.

Use identifiable image tags so deployments can be traced to a specific application version.

Examples:

```text
recipe-backend:latest
recipe-backend:dev
recipe-backend:v1.0.0
recipe-backend:<git-commit-sha>
```

For automated deployment later, a Git commit SHA is particularly useful:

```text
ECR

recipe-backend:a82c91f
recipe-backend:34de920
recipe-backend:81af721
```

This allows a deployed image to be traced back to the source revision that produced it.

`latest` may exist for convenience, but deployments should not depend exclusively on an ambiguous mutable tag.

## Build and Push Flow

Conceptually:

```bash
cd backend

docker build -t recipe-backend .
```

Authenticate Docker with ECR using the AWS CLI.

Then tag the image:

```bash
docker tag recipe-backend:<tag> <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repository>:<tag>
```

Push:

```bash
docker push <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repository>:<tag>
```

The exact AWS account, region, repository, and tag values should come from the team's AWS environment.

Do not hardcode sensitive AWS credentials into scripts or documentation.

## Image Pull

Later, EC2 will retrieve the backend image:

```text
EC2
 │
 │ authenticated AWS request
 ▼
ECR
 │
 ▼
Docker Image
 │
 ▼
Django
```

EC2 should eventually use an IAM role with the required ECR pull permissions rather than storing long-lived AWS access keys on the instance.

## Security Requirements

### AWS Authentication

Do not store:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

inside:

- Docker images
- Dockerfiles
- Git
- application source code
- committed `.env` files

AWS access should use appropriate IAM identities and roles.

### EC2 Access to ECR

The intended production architecture is:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
IAM Role
 │
 ▼
ECR Pull Permission
```

rather than:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
Hardcoded AWS Access Keys
 │
 ▼
ECR
```

### Least Privilege

IAM permissions should grant only the actions necessary for the role.

For example:

```text
Deployment/CI Identity
    │
    ├── Authenticate to ECR
    └── Push required backend images

EC2 Instance Role
    │
    ├── Authenticate to ECR
    └── Pull required backend images
```

The EC2 role should not receive broad administrative AWS permissions simply to pull an application image.

## Image Security

The image pushed to ECR must not contain:

- Django secret keys
- database passwords
- Cognito secrets
- AWS credentials
- real `.env` files
- production configuration secrets
- local development databases

Application secrets will be provided separately at runtime.

```text
ECR Image
├── Application Code
├── Python Runtime
└── Dependencies

NOT:

├── Database Password
├── AWS Credentials
└── Django Secret Key
```

## Scalability Requirements

ECR supports the backend's horizontal deployment architecture by providing a common application artifact.

```text
                    ECR Image
                       │
          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
          ▼            ▼            ▼
       EC2 #1       EC2 #2       EC2 #3
```

Every backend instance should be capable of retrieving and running an equivalent application image.

This helps ensure that scaling backend capacity does not require manually rebuilding the application separately on every EC2 instance.

ECR itself does not prove application scalability.

Actual scalability will later be demonstrated through:

- Application Load Balancer
- Multiple backend instances
- Load testing
- CloudWatch metrics
- Performance statistics

## Image Lifecycle

Container images can accumulate over time.

Configure or document an ECR lifecycle strategy where appropriate.

For example:

```text
Keep:
- Current production images
- Recent development images
- Required rollback versions

Expire:
- Old untagged images
- Unneeded historical development builds
```

Do not create a lifecycle policy that could automatically delete an image currently required for production or rollback.

## Deployment Traceability

The deployed application version should eventually be traceable:

```text
Git Commit
    │
    ▼
Docker Build
    │
    ▼
ECR Image Tag
    │
    ▼
EC2 Deployment
```

Example:

```text
Git commit:
81af721

        ↓

ECR:
recipe-backend:81af721

        ↓

EC2:
running recipe-backend:81af721
```

This will also make debugging and rollback easier.

## Important

ECR stores **application images**, not application data.

```text
ECR
 ↓
Docker Images

RDS
 ↓
Application Database

S3
 ↓
Application Media

Secrets Manager / Parameter Store
 ↓
Sensitive Configuration
```

Keep these responsibilities separate.

### Do NOT

- Store AWS credentials in Docker images
- Store application secrets in ECR images
- Commit AWS access keys
- Store database passwords in Docker images
- Put real `.env` files into images
- Give EC2 AdministratorAccess just to pull ECR images
- Give CI/CD unrestricted AWS permissions unnecessarily
- Use ECR as persistent application storage
- Create separate ECR repositories for every Django app
- Depend exclusively on the `latest` image tag
- Manually maintain different backend images on different EC2 instances
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push infrastructure changes directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### ECR

- [ ] Backend ECR repository exists
- [ ] Repository naming convention is documented
- [ ] Docker can authenticate with ECR
- [ ] Backend image can be tagged for ECR
- [ ] Backend image can be pushed successfully
- [ ] Backend image can be pulled successfully
- [ ] Image-tagging convention is documented
- [ ] Image lifecycle strategy is documented/configured where appropriate

### Security

- [ ] No AWS credentials are stored in the image
- [ ] No application secrets are stored in the image
- [ ] No real `.env` file is included in the image
- [ ] Required ECR IAM permissions are documented
- [ ] EC2 pull access is designed to use an IAM role
- [ ] IAM permissions follow least privilege

### Scalability

- [ ] The same backend image can be used by multiple backend instances
- [ ] Deployment does not require rebuilding application code separately on each EC2 instance
- [ ] Image version can be identified from its tag
- [ ] Architecture supports future horizontal EC2 scaling

### Documentation

- [ ] Image build process is documented
- [ ] ECR authentication process is documented
- [ ] Image tagging process is documented
- [ ] Image push process is documented
- [ ] Image pull process is documented

## Before Submitting

Verify the backend Docker image still builds:

```bash
cd backend

docker build -t recipe-backend .
```

Push a test/versioned image to ECR.

Verify the image appears in the ECR repository.

Then verify that the image can be pulled again.

Do not include AWS credentials, account secrets, or sensitive configuration in screenshots/documentation committed to the repository.

Update the relevant deployment/AWS documentation.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/ecr`

Title: Infrastructure: Configure PostgreSQL Development Environment
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Configure PostgreSQL as the primary relational database for backend development.

The application will eventually use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in production. Local development should therefore use the same database engine where practical to reduce differences between development and production behavior.

The database configuration must remain environment-based so the same Django application can connect to:

```text
Local PostgreSQL
        or
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
```

without changing application source code.

## Where to Work

Backend code is located in:

`backend/`

Primary files for this task may include:

- `backend/config/settings.py` — Django database configuration
- `backend/requirements.txt` — PostgreSQL driver dependency
- `.env.example` — database environment variable documentation
- `backend/README.md` — local PostgreSQL setup instructions

If Docker-based PostgreSQL development is used, appropriate Docker configuration may also be added.

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

- [ ] Add the required PostgreSQL Python database driver
- [ ] Configure Django to connect to PostgreSQL
- [ ] Read database configuration from environment variables
- [ ] Configure local PostgreSQL development
- [ ] Document required database environment variables
- [ ] Verify Django migrations work with PostgreSQL
- [ ] Verify Django tests work with PostgreSQL
- [ ] Verify Django Admin works with PostgreSQL
- [ ] Verify the Dockerized backend can connect to PostgreSQL
- [ ] Document local database setup in `backend/README.md`
- [ ] Ensure database credentials are not committed

## Architecture

Development:

```text
Django
   │
   ▼
PostgreSQL
```

Later in AWS:

```text
Django / EC2
      │
      ▼
Amazon RDS
PostgreSQL
```

The Django application should not need different database code for these environments.

Instead:

```text
                Django
                  │
                  ▼
          Environment Config
             /          \
            ▼            ▼
Local PostgreSQL     Amazon RDS
```

## Environment Configuration

Database configuration should be supplied through environment variables.

Conceptually:

```env
DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_HOST=
DB_PORT=5432
```

The exact variable names should follow the project's established configuration convention.

Django should read these values rather than hardcoding database configuration.

For example, do not use:

```python
"HOST": "my-production-db.xxxxx.rds.amazonaws.com",
"PASSWORD": "mypassword",
```

inside `settings.py`.

`.env.example` should document required variables without containing real credentials.

## Local Development

Developers should have a documented way to run PostgreSQL locally.

Two reasonable approaches are acceptable:

### Option A — Local PostgreSQL Installation

```text
Developer Computer
├── Django
└── PostgreSQL
```

### Option B — PostgreSQL Container

```text
Developer Computer
│
├── Django
│
└── Docker
     └── PostgreSQL
```

If Docker is used for PostgreSQL, database data should use persistent storage rather than disappearing whenever the container is recreated.

The team should document the chosen standard approach so developers do not each invent a different database setup.

## Docker Integration

The Dockerized Django backend from Issue #15 must be able to connect to PostgreSQL.

Conceptually:

```text
Django Container
       │
       ▼
PostgreSQL
```

Do not assume:

```text
localhost
```

always refers to the database server when Django itself is running inside a container.

Database host configuration must remain environment-dependent.

## Django Migrations

Existing and future Django migrations must work against PostgreSQL.

Verify:

```bash
python manage.py migrate
```

and:

```bash
python manage.py showmigrations
```

The project should not maintain separate migration histories for SQLite and PostgreSQL.

## Security Requirements

Database credentials are secrets.

They must not be:

- committed to Git
- hardcoded in Django settings
- stored in the Dockerfile
- exposed to the frontend
- placed in documentation using real credentials

Local credentials may be supplied through an ignored `.env` file.

Production credentials will later use the project's AWS secret-management approach.

Conceptually:

```text
Development
.env (ignored)
     │
     ▼
Django

Production
AWS Secret Management
     │
     ▼
Django
     │
     ▼
RDS
```

The production RDS database will later be protected using AWS networking/security groups rather than being openly accessible from the Internet.

## Scalability / Performance Requirements

PostgreSQL should support the application's future scalability requirements.

When implementing models and queries:

- Frequently queried fields should be considered for indexing.
- Foreign-key relationships should be used appropriately.
- Uniqueness should be enforced at the database level where appropriate.
- Query behavior should be measurable during later performance testing.
- Database access should avoid unnecessary repeated queries.
- Application features should not rely on SQLite-specific behavior.

Examples of likely frequently queried relationships include:

```text
Ingredient.name

Recipe
   ↓
RecipeIngredient
   ↓
Ingredient

Recipe
   ↓
Tag

User
   ↓
InventoryItem

User
   ↓
SavedRecipe
```

Do not add arbitrary indexes to every field.

Indexes should correspond to actual lookup, filtering, relationship, or uniqueness requirements.

## PostgreSQL and Scalability

Using PostgreSQL alone does **not** prove that the system is scalable.

Later testing will measure the behavior of the application and database under increasing load.

Examples:

```text
50 concurrent users
100 concurrent users
250 concurrent users
500 concurrent users
```

Measurements may include:

- Request throughput
- Average API latency
- p95 API latency
- Error rate
- Database query performance
- EC2 CPU utilization
- Database utilization

The purpose of this issue is to establish the database environment required for that later testing.

## SQLite

SQLite may remain useful for isolated experimentation if needed, but PostgreSQL should become the standard development database for application integration.

The team should avoid developing features that only work correctly with SQLite.

Production must not use SQLite.

## Important

Application code should depend on Django's database abstraction rather than environment-specific database assumptions.

```text
Application Code
       │
       ▼
Django ORM
       │
       ▼
PostgreSQL
```

This makes the later transition:

```text
Local PostgreSQL
       ↓
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL
```

primarily a configuration/infrastructure change.

### Do NOT

- Commit database passwords
- Hardcode database credentials
- Hardcode the future RDS hostname
- Expose database credentials to React
- Put database passwords in the Dockerfile
- Use SQLite as the production database
- Create separate application logic for local PostgreSQL and RDS
- Create separate Django migrations for development and production
- Make the production RDS database publicly accessible as the intended architecture
- Add unnecessary indexes without understanding their purpose
- Modify unrelated application functionality
- Push implementation directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Database

- [ ] Django successfully connects to PostgreSQL
- [ ] PostgreSQL is the documented standard development database
- [ ] Existing Django migrations apply successfully
- [ ] New migrations work correctly
- [ ] Django Admin works with PostgreSQL
- [ ] Django tests pass using PostgreSQL

### Configuration

- [ ] Database configuration comes from environment variables
- [ ] Database hostname is configurable
- [ ] Database port is configurable
- [ ] Database name is configurable
- [ ] Database username is configurable
- [ ] Database password is configurable
- [ ] `.env.example` documents required variables

### Docker

- [ ] Dockerized Django backend can connect to PostgreSQL
- [ ] Container configuration does not assume the database is inside the Django container
- [ ] Database data is persistent if PostgreSQL is containerized locally

### Security

- [ ] No real database credentials are committed
- [ ] Database credentials are not present in frontend code
- [ ] Database credentials are not embedded in the Docker image
- [ ] Configuration is compatible with later AWS secret management

### Scalability

- [ ] Application does not depend on SQLite-specific behavior
- [ ] Database design supports appropriate indexing
- [ ] Database relationships use appropriate constraints
- [ ] Database configuration is compatible with future Amazon RDS deployment
- [ ] Database behavior can later be measured through load/performance testing

## Before Submitting

Start PostgreSQL using the team's documented development method.

Run:

```bash
cd backend

python manage.py check
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py showmigrations
python manage.py test
```

Verify Django is actually connected to PostgreSQL rather than silently using SQLite.

If Issue #15 has been completed, also verify the Dockerized backend can connect to the PostgreSQL development database.

Update `backend/README.md` with the required setup instructions.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push infrastructure changes directly to `main`.**

## Suggested Branch

`infrastructure/postgresql`

Title: Infrastructure: Dockerize Django Backend
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Containerize the Django backend so the application can run consistently across development, testing, and AWS deployment environments.

The Docker image will later be used to deploy the backend to Amazon EC2.

The container should provide a reproducible backend runtime without storing application state or secrets inside the image.

## Where to Work

Backend code is located in:

`backend/`

Primary files for this task:

- `backend/Dockerfile` — backend container definition
- `backend/.dockerignore` — files excluded from the Docker build context
- `backend/requirements.txt` — Python dependencies
- `backend/config/` — Django configuration
- `.env.example` — required environment variable documentation, where applicable

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

Create files if they do not already exist.

## Tasks

- [ ] Create a Dockerfile for the Django backend
- [ ] Create `.dockerignore`
- [ ] Install backend dependencies inside the image
- [ ] Configure the container to run Django
- [ ] Configure the production container to use an appropriate WSGI application server such as Gunicorn
- [ ] Expose the backend application port
- [ ] Ensure Django configuration is supplied through environment variables where appropriate
- [ ] Ensure database configuration is not hardcoded into the image
- [ ] Ensure secrets are not copied into the image
- [ ] Verify Django migrations can be executed from the container
- [ ] Verify Django management commands can be executed from the container
- [ ] Verify the container can connect to the configured database
- [ ] Document local Docker build/run commands
- [ ] Verify existing Django tests can run from the container

## Expected Architecture

Development currently runs approximately as:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Django Development Server
    │
    ▼
Local Database
```

Docker introduces a reproducible backend runtime:

```text
Developer / CI / EC2
         │
         ▼
    Docker Image
         │
         ▼
 Django + Gunicorn
         │
         ▼
Configured Database
```

Later, the same application container can participate in the AWS architecture:

```text
                  Application Load Balancer
                           │
                 ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                 ▼                   ▼
               EC2                 EC2
                 │                   │
                 ▼                   ▼
          Django Container     Django Container
                 │                   │
                 └─────────┬─────────┘
                           ▼
                      Amazon RDS
                      PostgreSQL
```

The application should therefore avoid depending on local container state.

## Dockerfile

The Dockerfile should:

1. Use an appropriate Python base image
2. Set an application working directory
3. Install Python dependencies
4. Copy the backend application
5. Configure the application runtime
6. Start the production Django application using Gunicorn

Conceptually:

```dockerfile
FROM python:<supported-version>-slim

WORKDIR /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

COPY . .

EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["gunicorn", "config.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
```

This is an architectural example only.

Use the Python/Django versions and dependency setup defined by the project.

## `.dockerignore`

Create:

```text
backend/.dockerignore
```

It should exclude unnecessary or sensitive files from the Docker build context.

Examples include:

```text
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]

.venv/
venv/

.env
.env.*

db.sqlite3

.git/
.gitignore

.pytest_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/

*.log

.DS_Store
```

Do not blindly copy this list if a file is required for the build.

## Environment Configuration

Configuration that differs between environments must not be baked into the Docker image.

For example:

```text
Development
    ↓
Local environment variables

Production
    ↓
AWS-managed environment/secrets
```

The application should be configurable using environment variables for values such as:

```text
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY
DJANGO_DEBUG
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS

DB_NAME
DB_USER
DB_PASSWORD
DB_HOST
DB_PORT
```

The exact variable names should follow the project's configuration documentation.

`.env.example` may document required variables but must not contain actual secrets.

## Database

The Docker image should not depend on SQLite for production deployment.

Development may temporarily continue to support SQLite if the project currently uses it, but the backend must be configurable to connect to PostgreSQL.

Later:

```text
Django Container
       │
       ▼
PostgreSQL / Amazon RDS
```

Database data must not be stored inside the application container.

## Migrations

The container must support normal Django management commands.

For example:

```bash
docker run ... python manage.py check
```

```bash
docker run ... python manage.py migrate
```

```bash
docker run ... python manage.py test
```

Migration execution should remain an explicit deployment/management operation.

Do not automatically run migrations independently from every backend replica in a way that could cause multiple instances to race during deployment.

## Security Requirements

The container must follow secure deployment practices.

### Secrets

Do not:

```dockerfile
ENV DJANGO_SECRET_KEY="actual-secret"
ENV DB_PASSWORD="actual-password"
```

Do not copy `.env` files containing secrets into the image.

Secrets should be injected at runtime.

### Container Contents

The final image should not unnecessarily contain:

- `.git`
- local virtual environments
- development databases
- environment files containing secrets
- test coverage output
- unrelated local files

### Django Production Configuration

The production deployment must not rely on Django's development server:

```bash
python manage.py runserver
```

Use an appropriate WSGI server such as Gunicorn.

Production configuration must also support:

```text
DEBUG = False
```

### Dependency Security

Python dependencies should be explicitly tracked in the project's dependency file so container builds are reproducible.

Do not install arbitrary undeclared packages manually on the EC2 instance as part of the normal deployment process.

## Scalability Requirements

The container must support running multiple independent instances of the Django backend.

This means application correctness must not depend on files or mutable state stored inside one application container.

Avoid architecture such as:

```text
EC2 #1
└── Container
     └── Important Application State
```

because another backend instance would not have access to that state.

Instead:

```text
              Django #1
                 │
                 │
Shared Services ─┼── RDS
                 ├── S3
                 └── Other external shared state
                 │
              Django #2
```

The Django application should remain stateless where practical.

This allows:

```text
1 Backend Instance
        ↓
2 Backend Instances
        ↓
N Backend Instances
```

without redesigning application functionality.

## Docker Image and AWS

The initial deployment may run the container directly on one EC2 instance.

Conceptually:

```text
EC2
 │
 ▼
Docker
 │
 ▼
Django
```

Later, the image can be stored in Amazon ECR:

```text
Developer / CI
      │
      ▼
Docker Image
      │
      ▼
Amazon ECR
      │
      ▼
EC2 Instance(s)
```

ECR configuration and EC2 deployment may be handled in separate infrastructure issues.

## Local Verification

A developer should be able to build the backend image:

```bash
cd backend

docker build -t recipe-backend .
```

and run it with the required environment configuration.

Conceptually:

```bash
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env recipe-backend
```

Then:

```text
http://localhost:8000/
```

or the documented API health endpoint should be reachable.

Exact commands may vary according to the final project configuration.

## Performance / Scalability Evidence

This issue does not need to prove production scalability by itself.

However, the resulting Docker deployment must be compatible with later load testing.

The same backend application should be deployable as multiple instances so later testing can compare configurations such as:

```text
Configuration A
1 EC2 / backend instance

vs.

Configuration B
Multiple backend instances behind ALB
```

Later scalability testing will collect measurements such as:

- Concurrent users
- Requests per second
- Average response time
- p95 response time
- Error rate
- CPU utilization
- Memory utilization

Do not make unsupported scalability claims based solely on the use of Docker.

## Important

Docker is the application's **deployment unit**, not the source of application state.

```text
Docker
   ↓
Application Runtime

RDS
   ↓
Persistent Relational Data

S3
   ↓
Persistent Media/Object Data
```

This separation is important for horizontal scalability.

### Do NOT

- Commit `.env` files containing secrets
- Put database passwords in the Dockerfile
- Put `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` in the Dockerfile
- Copy unnecessary secrets into the Docker image
- Use Django `runserver` as the production application server
- Store production database data inside the application container
- Store important application state only on the EC2/container filesystem
- Hardcode an RDS hostname into application source code
- Hardcode AWS credentials
- Install undeclared dependencies manually on EC2 as the normal deployment strategy
- Make Docker-specific changes to unrelated Django features
- Push feature implementation directly to `main`

## Acceptance Criteria

### Functionality

- [ ] Backend Dockerfile exists
- [ ] `.dockerignore` exists
- [ ] Docker image builds successfully
- [ ] Django starts successfully inside the container
- [ ] Gunicorn is used for the production container runtime
- [ ] Backend API is reachable from the host
- [ ] Django management commands can run inside the container
- [ ] Django tests can run successfully using the container environment

### Configuration

- [ ] Environment-specific configuration is supplied externally
- [ ] Database configuration is not hardcoded
- [ ] Production PostgreSQL configuration is supported
- [ ] `.env.example` documents required configuration where appropriate

### Security

- [ ] No secrets are stored in the Dockerfile
- [ ] No real `.env` file is copied into the image
- [ ] No AWS credentials are stored in the image
- [ ] Production configuration supports `DEBUG=False`
- [ ] Unnecessary local/development files are excluded from the image

### Scalability

- [ ] Application data is not stored inside the backend container
- [ ] Backend does not depend on a specific container instance for application state
- [ ] Multiple equivalent backend containers could use the same external database
- [ ] Container design is compatible with future ALB/horizontal scaling
- [ ] Deployment can later be included in automated load testing

## Before Submitting

Verify the existing backend outside Docker:

```bash
cd backend

python manage.py check
python manage.py test
```

Build the image:

```bash
docker build -t recipe-backend .
```

Run the container and verify the backend API.

Also verify Django from inside the container:

```bash
docker run --rm ... recipe-backend python manage.py check
```

```bash
docker run --rm ... recipe-backend python manage.py test
```

Document any required environment variables or setup steps in `backend/README.md`.

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push feature implementation directly to `main`.**
