`infrastructure/docker-backend`

Title: Full Stack: Saved Recipes
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Allow Registered Users to save recipes to their account and access their saved recipes later.

Saved Recipes are a Registered User feature.

Guests can browse and view recipes but cannot persist saved recipes unless they create/sign into an account.

## Where to Work

This task affects both backend and frontend.

### Backend

Primary locations:

- `backend/apps/users/` and/or `backend/apps/recipes/`, following the ownership defined in `docs/database-design.md`
- relevant serializers, views, URLs, models, migrations, and tests

### Frontend

Primary locations:

- `frontend/src/features/recipes/`
- `frontend/src/pages/`
- `frontend/src/services/api/recipeService.js`

Use the existing shared API client:

`frontend/src/services/api/apiClient.js`

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `frontend/README.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `docs/api-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Data Relationship

Saved Recipes represent a relationship between a Registered User and a Recipe.

Conceptually:

```text
User
  │
  │ M:N
  ▼
Recipe
```

This may be implemented using an explicit relationship model if required by `docs/database-design.md`.

For example:

```text
SavedRecipe
├── id
├── user
├── recipe
└── created_at
```

The same Recipe must not be saved multiple times by the same user.

The `(user, recipe)` relationship must be unique at the database level.

The original Recipe remains the authoritative Recipe record. Saving a Recipe must create only the relationship between the User and Recipe rather than duplicating Recipe data.

## Tasks

### Backend

- [ ] Implement the Saved Recipe relationship
- [ ] Associate Saved Recipes with the authenticated user
- [ ] Enforce database-level uniqueness for `(user, recipe)`
- [ ] Prevent duplicate saves
- [ ] Implement endpoint for retrieving Saved Recipes
- [ ] Implement endpoint for saving a Recipe
- [ ] Implement endpoint for removing a Saved Recipe
- [ ] Ensure users can only manage their own Saved Recipes
- [ ] Add appropriate validation
- [ ] Support efficient retrieval of related Recipe data
- [ ] Avoid N+1 database queries when retrieving Saved Recipes
- [ ] Add pagination if required by the project's API design
- [ ] Add tests for authentication, ownership, duplicate prevention, and CRUD behavior

### Frontend

- [ ] Add save/unsave functionality to appropriate Recipe interfaces
- [ ] Display whether a Recipe is currently saved
- [ ] Implement Saved Recipes page or dashboard section
- [ ] Retrieve the user's Saved Recipes
- [ ] Allow users to remove Saved Recipes
- [ ] Handle loading state
- [ ] Handle empty Saved Recipes state
- [ ] Handle API errors
- [ ] Handle authentication-required behavior for Guests
- [ ] Use the existing Recipe/domain API service structure
- [ ] Use the existing shared API client

## Security & Scalability Requirements

### Security

- Saved Recipe operations require authentication.
- User identity must come from the authenticated request context.
- The frontend must not determine ownership by sending a `user_id`.
- Users can only retrieve their own Saved Recipes.
- Users can only create Saved Recipes for themselves.
- Users can only remove their own Saved Recipes.
- Cross-user access or modification must be rejected.
- Recipe IDs supplied by the client must be validated before creating a Saved Recipe relationship.
- Authorization must be enforced by the backend and must not rely only on frontend restrictions.

### Scalability / Performance

- Enforce uniqueness of the `(user, recipe)` relationship at the database level.
- User/Recipe relationship fields must support efficient lookup.
- Saved Recipe retrieval should efficiently query by authenticated user.
- The `(user, recipe)` relationship must support efficient existence checks for determining whether a Recipe is already saved.
- Avoid N+1 database queries when retrieving Recipe information for Saved Recipes.
- Use appropriate Django ORM relationship loading such as `select_related()` or equivalent where applicable.
- Saved Recipe lists should support pagination if the result set can grow significantly.
- Do not duplicate Recipe data inside Saved Recipe records.
- The retrieval endpoint should return sufficient Recipe information for the frontend to display the Saved Recipes list without requiring one additional API request per Recipe.

Conceptually, retrieving a Saved Recipes page should avoid behavior such as:

```text
1 query   → SavedRecipe relationships
100 queries → 100 individual Recipe records
```

Instead, related Recipe information should be retrieved efficiently with the Saved Recipe query.

## Additional Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Saved Recipe endpoints require authentication
- [ ] Cross-user access is rejected
- [ ] Duplicate `(user, recipe)` relationships are prevented
- [ ] Database-level uniqueness protects against duplicate relationships
- [ ] Concurrent or repeated save requests cannot create duplicate `(user, recipe)` relationships
- [ ] Saved Recipe retrieval uses efficient relationship queries
- [ ] Saved Recipe retrieval does not introduce an N+1 database query pattern
- [ ] Saved Recipe lists can be paginated according to project API conventions
- [ ] Recipe data is not duplicated when a Recipe is saved

## API

Expected endpoints should follow `docs/api-design.md`.

Conceptually:

```text
GET    /api/users/me/saved-recipes/
POST   /api/users/me/saved-recipes/
DELETE /api/users/me/saved-recipes/{recipe_id}/
```

### Retrieve Saved Recipes

```text
GET /api/users/me/saved-recipes/
```

Returns Saved Recipes belonging to the authenticated user.

The response should contain sufficient Recipe information for the frontend to render the Saved Recipes interface without making an additional request for every individual Recipe.

The exact response structure and pagination format should follow `docs/api-design.md`.

### Save a Recipe

```text
POST /api/users/me/saved-recipes/
```

Example request:

```json
{
  "recipe_id": 15
}
```

The frontend should **not** send an arbitrary `user_id`.

The backend must determine the user from the authenticated request.

If the Recipe does not exist, the backend should return the appropriate API error according to project conventions.

If the Recipe is already saved, the API must not create a duplicate relationship.

### Remove a Saved Recipe

```text
DELETE /api/users/me/saved-recipes/{recipe_id}/
```

Example:

```text
DELETE /api/users/me/saved-recipes/15/
```

Here, `15` represents the Recipe ID.

The backend should remove the Saved Recipe relationship belonging to the authenticated user and that Recipe.

The frontend should not need to know the internal `SavedRecipe.id` in order to unsave a Recipe.

A user must not be able to remove another user's Saved Recipe relationship.

## Expected User Flow

```text
Recipe Detail
     │
     ▼
[ Save Recipe ]
     │
     ▼
Saved to User Account
     │
     ▼
Dashboard / Saved Recipes
```

Later:

```text
Saved Recipes

Chicken Fried Rice
Kimchi Stew
Vietnamese Spring Rolls
```

A user should also be able to remove a Saved Recipe.

For example:

```text
Saved Recipes
      │
      ▼
Chicken Fried Rice
      │
      ▼
[ Remove ]
      │
      ▼
Removed from Saved Recipes
```

## Guest Behavior

Guests may view Recipes normally.

If a Guest attempts to use a save action, the interface may direct them to sign in.

```text
Guest
  ↓
Recipe
  ↓
Save
  ↓
Sign In Required
```

Do not create permanent anonymous Saved Recipe records.

Do not rely on `localStorage` as a replacement for authenticated Saved Recipes.

## Registered User Behavior

```text
Registered User
      │
      ├── Browse Recipes
      ├── View Recipe
      ├── Save Recipe
      ├── View Saved Recipes
      └── Remove Saved Recipe
```

The backend remains responsible for determining which user owns each Saved Recipe relationship.

## Dependencies

**Blocked by:**

- Backend: Implement Recipe Models & API
- Frontend: Implement Application Foundation
- Authentication: Integrate Amazon Cognito

Frontend Recipe Detail integration additionally benefits from:

- Frontend: Implement Recipe Detail Page

```text
Recipe Models & API ──────────┐
                              │
Amazon Cognito Integration ───┼──→ Saved Recipes
                              │
Application Foundation ───────┘

Recipe Detail Page ─────────────→ Full Recipe Detail UI Integration
                                  (soft dependency)
```

The Recipe Detail Page is not required for implementing the Saved Recipe backend or Saved Recipes page, but it is required for integrating the save/unsave control into the final Recipe Detail interface.

## Important

Saved Recipes represent a User-to-Recipe relationship.

Do not copy an entire Recipe into the user's account when they save it.

```text
Correct:

User ──→ SavedRecipe ──→ Recipe
```

Not:

```text
User
 └── CopiedRecipe
      ├── copied name
      ├── copied ingredients
      └── copied instructions
```

The original Recipe remains the authoritative Recipe record.

The Saved Recipe relationship should only store information specific to the relationship, such as:

```text
SavedRecipe
├── id
├── user
├── recipe
└── created_at
```

## Do NOT

- Duplicate Recipe records when saving
- Copy Recipe ingredients or instructions into Saved Recipe records
- Allow users to retrieve another user's Saved Recipes
- Allow users to modify another user's Saved Recipes
- Accept arbitrary `user_id` values from the frontend
- Trust frontend ownership checks as authorization
- Store Saved Recipes only in `localStorage`
- Create permanent Saved Recipe data for Guests
- Create another API client
- Call `fetch()` directly from React components
- Introduce one API request per Recipe when displaying Saved Recipes
- Introduce avoidable N+1 database queries
- Implement Reviews as part of this task
- Implement Shopping Lists as part of this task
- Implement recommendation logic as part of this task
- Modify unrelated functionality
- Change shared API contracts without discussing it with the team

## Acceptance Criteria

### Functional

- [ ] Registered User can save a Recipe
- [ ] Registered User can retrieve Saved Recipes
- [ ] Registered User can remove a Saved Recipe
- [ ] Saved state can be shown on applicable Recipe interfaces
- [ ] Saved Recipes can be displayed in the frontend
- [ ] Empty Saved Recipes state is handled
- [ ] Loading states are handled
- [ ] API errors are handled
- [ ] Guests cannot create persistent Saved Recipes

### Data Integrity

- [ ] Duplicate saves are prevented
- [ ] `(user, recipe)` uniqueness is enforced at the database level
- [ ] Repeated/concurrent save attempts cannot create duplicate relationships
- [ ] Saved Recipe belongs to the authenticated user
- [ ] Recipe data is not duplicated when saved
- [ ] Removing a Saved Recipe removes the relationship, not the Recipe itself

### Security

- [ ] Saved Recipe endpoints require authentication
- [ ] Backend determines user identity from authenticated request context
- [ ] Frontend does not send arbitrary `user_id` values
- [ ] Users cannot retrieve another user's Saved Recipe relationships
- [ ] Users cannot modify/remove another user's Saved Recipe relationships
- [ ] Invalid Recipe IDs are handled safely

### Performance / Scalability

- [ ] Saved Recipe lookup by user is efficient
- [ ] Saved-state existence checks are efficient
- [ ] Related Recipe data is retrieved efficiently
- [ ] Saved Recipe retrieval does not introduce an N+1 query pattern
- [ ] Saved Recipe retrieval does not require one frontend API request per Recipe
- [ ] Pagination follows project API conventions where applicable

### Quality

- [ ] Backend tests pass
- [ ] `python manage.py check` passes
- [ ] `npm run lint` passes
- [ ] `npm run build` passes
- [ ] Existing functionality still works

## Before Submitting

### Backend

```bash
cd backend
python manage.py check
python manage.py test
```

### Frontend

```bash
cd frontend
npm run lint
npm run build
```

Manually test the primary Registered User flow:

```text
Sign In
→ Open Recipe
→ Save Recipe
→ Confirm Saved State
→ View Saved Recipes
→ Remove Recipe
→ Confirm Recipe Is No Longer Saved
```

Also manually test:

```text
Guest
→ Open Recipe
→ Attempt Save
→ Sign In Required
```

And:

```text
Registered User
→ Save Recipe
→ Attempt to Save Same Recipe Again
→ No Duplicate Relationship Created
```

Then open a Pull Request into `main`.

**Do not push feature implementation directly to `main`.**

`feature/saved-recipes`

Title: Backend: Recipe Search & Filtering
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Implement recipe lookup, search, and filtering.

Users should be able to browse/search Recipes and narrow results using supported criteria such as cuisine, dietary requirements, and allergies.

This functionality should work for both Guests and Registered Users.

Registered Users' saved preferences and allergies may be applied as default filters when user-profile integration is available.

Recipe search/filtering must remain separate from ingredient-based recommendation matching.

## Where to Work

Backend code is located in:

`backend/`

Primary locations for this task:

- `backend/apps/recipes/` — Recipe search/filter functionality
- `backend/apps/recipes/views.py` — Recipe API views
- `backend/apps/recipes/serializers.py` — request/response serialization
- `backend/apps/recipes/urls.py` — Recipe API routes
- `backend/apps/recipes/tests/` — Recipe search/filter tests

This task may also use existing data from:

- `backend/apps/users/` — saved preferences and allergies
- `backend/apps/ingredients/` — canonical Ingredient and Allergen data

Do not duplicate models or relationships owned by these apps.

Relevant documentation:

- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/requirements.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `docs/api-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### Core Search

- [ ] Implement Recipe search by supported name/title fields
- [ ] Define search behavior according to `docs/api-design.md`
- [ ] Return matching Recipe data through the existing Recipe API
- [ ] Ensure search works without authentication

### Filtering

- [ ] Implement cuisine filtering
- [ ] Implement dietary filtering supported by the Recipe/Tag data model
- [ ] Implement allergy filtering using structured Ingredient/Allergen relationships
- [ ] Support multiple compatible filters in the same request
- [ ] Support multiple values for a filter where allowed by `docs/api-design.md`
- [ ] Define AND/OR semantics for multi-value filters according to the documented API contract
- [ ] Prevent duplicate Recipe results when filtering across many-to-many relationships
- [ ] Handle invalid or unsupported filter values

### Guest Behavior

- [ ] Ensure Guests can browse Recipes
- [ ] Ensure Guests can search Recipes
- [ ] Ensure Guests can explicitly select supported filters
- [ ] Do not require authentication for normal Recipe lookup

### Registered User Behavior

- [ ] Support Registered User saved preferences as default filters where applicable
- [ ] Support saved allergy exclusions where applicable
- [ ] Allow explicitly supplied filters to override or extend defaults according to the documented API behavior
- [ ] Ensure user-specific defaults are derived only from the authenticated user's profile

### Performance / Quality

- [ ] Implement pagination
- [ ] Ensure filtering occurs through database queries where practical
- [ ] Optimize related-object retrieval for serialized Recipe data
- [ ] Avoid N+1 queries
- [ ] Add appropriate indexes for frequently searched/filtered fields or relationships
- [ ] Add tests covering search, filtering, authentication-independent behavior, invalid input, and major filter combinations

## Security & Scalability Requirements

### Security

- Validate all search/filter parameters.
- Reject or safely handle unsupported filter values.
- Do not construct unsafe raw SQL from user-supplied search/filter values.
- Use Django ORM parameterization and structured queries.
- Allergy filtering must remain authoritative on the backend.
- Do not rely on frontend filtering to enforce allergy exclusions.
- User-specific default filters must only come from the authenticated user's profile.
- Guests must not be able to supply another user's identity to obtain that user's saved preferences.
- Search/filter input must not allow clients to bypass Recipe visibility rules established elsewhere in the Recipe API.

### Scalability / Performance

- Recipe search results must support pagination.
- Filtering should occur in the database where practical rather than loading all Recipes into Python memory.
- Frequently searched/filterable fields and relationships should be appropriately indexed according to actual query patterns.
- Tag filtering should use the structured Recipe ↔ Tag relationship.
- Allergy filtering should use the structured Recipe → Ingredient → Allergen relationships.
- Related Tags, Ingredients, and other serialized relationships should be loaded efficiently using appropriate Django ORM techniques such as `select_related()` and/or `prefetch_related()` where applicable.
- Avoid N+1 queries when filtering and serializing Recipes, Tags, Ingredients, and Allergens.
- Queries across many-to-many relationships must not return duplicate Recipe rows.
- Search/filter performance should scale with the requested page/result set rather than requiring the entire Recipe table to be loaded into application memory.
- Do not issue additional database queries for every Recipe in a result page when the related data can be retrieved efficiently.

This endpoint will later be included in system load/performance testing.

Conceptually, avoid behavior such as:

```text
1 query  → Recipe search
50 queries → Tags for 50 Recipes
50 queries → Ingredients for 50 Recipes
50 queries → Allergens for 50 Recipes
```

Instead, related data required by the API response should be retrieved using efficient relationship queries.

## Additional Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Search/filter parameters are validated
- [ ] Unsupported filter values are handled consistently
- [ ] Recipe results are paginated
- [ ] Filtering is performed efficiently through database queries
- [ ] Appropriate searchable/filterable fields or relationships are indexed
- [ ] Tag filtering does not require loading all Recipes into application memory
- [ ] Allergy filtering does not require loading all Recipes into application memory
- [ ] Allergy filtering remains backend-controlled
- [ ] Implementation avoids obvious N+1 query behavior
- [ ] Many-to-many filtering does not produce duplicate Recipe results
- [ ] Search/filter behavior works for Guests without authentication
- [ ] User-specific defaults cannot expose or use another user's profile data

## Expected API

Recipe lookup should use the existing Recipe API.

Conceptually:

```text
GET /api/recipes/
GET /api/recipes/?search=chicken
GET /api/recipes/?cuisine=korean
GET /api/recipes/?diet=vegan
GET /api/recipes/?allergy=peanut
```

Filters should also be combinable where supported:

```text
GET /api/recipes/?search=rice&cuisine=korean&diet=vegetarian
```

Multiple values may be supported where defined by `docs/api-design.md`.

For example, depending on the documented API convention:

```text
GET /api/recipes/?cuisine=korean&cuisine=vietnamese
```

or:

```text
GET /api/recipes/?cuisine=korean,vietnamese
```

Do not introduce a new parameter format independently.

Follow `docs/api-design.md` as the authoritative API contract.

## Filter Semantics

Filter behavior must be deterministic and documented.

When multiple different filter categories are supplied, they should be combined according to the API contract.

Conceptually:

```text
Search: chicken
Cuisine: Korean
Diet: Halal

        ↓

Recipes matching the applicable
search AND filter constraints
```

For multiple values within the same category, the implementation must follow the semantics defined by `docs/api-design.md`.

For example, cuisine values might conceptually mean:

```text
Korean OR Vietnamese
```

while some dietary combinations may require different semantics depending on the data model.

Do not guess these semantics inside the implementation.

If the current API documentation does not define multi-value behavior, establish the contract with the team before implementing it.

## Search Behavior

Recipe search should support normal Recipe lookup.

Example:

```text
Search: "fried rice"

        ↓

Chicken Fried Rice
Kimchi Fried Rice
Vegetable Fried Rice
```

Search should operate on the supported searchable Recipe fields defined by the API/data model.

Search should not depend on the user's Ingredient Inventory.

Ingredient-based matching belongs to the Recommendation system.

For example:

```text
Search:
"chicken"

        ↓

Recipes matching "chicken"
according to Recipe search rules
```

Not:

```text
User Inventory
├── Chicken
├── Rice
└── Onion

        ↓

Recipes user can make
```

The second behavior belongs to the Recommendation system.

## Filtering Behavior

Examples of supported filter categories may include:

```text
Cuisine
├── Vietnamese
├── Korean
├── Japanese
├── Italian
└── Mexican

Diet
├── Vegan
├── Vegetarian
└── Halal

Allergies
├── Peanut
├── Shellfish
├── Dairy
└── Other supported allergens
```

The exact supported values must follow the Recipe/database design.

Do not invent unsupported classifications independently of the documented data model.

Filtering must use structured data.

For example:

```text
Recipe
  │
  ├── Tag: Korean
  ├── Tag: Vegetarian
  └── Ingredients
```

rather than searching Recipe descriptions for classification keywords.

## Registered User Defaults

Registered Users may have saved:

```text
Profile
├── Dietary Preferences
├── Cuisine Preferences
└── Allergies
```

These may be used as default filtering information when User Profile integration is available.

Conceptually:

```text
Authenticated User
       │
       ▼
Saved Preferences
       │
       ▼
Default Recipe Filters
       │
       ▼
Recipe Search
```

Example:

```text
User preference:
Halal

User searches:
"chicken"

        ↓

Halal-compatible chicken Recipes
```

Users should still be able to adjust supported filters from the interface.

### Explicit Filters vs. Defaults

Explicit query parameters must interact with saved defaults according to `docs/api-design.md`.

The behavior must be deterministic.

For example, the API contract should define whether an explicitly supplied cuisine filter:

```text
?cuisine=korean
```

replaces:

```text
Saved cuisine preference:
Vietnamese
```

or extends it.

Do not silently invent merge/override behavior in the implementation.

### Allergy Defaults

Saved allergies should be treated more carefully than ordinary preferences.

Cuisine and dietary preferences represent user preferences.

Allergy exclusions represent safety-related filtering criteria.

If saved allergies are automatically applied, explicit Recipe search parameters must not silently disable those exclusions unless the documented product/API behavior explicitly supports that action.

The backend remains authoritative for applying active allergy exclusions.

## Guest Behavior

Guests have no saved profile preferences.

They can still explicitly provide supported filters:

```text
Guest
  │
  ├── Browse Recipes
  ├── Search
  ├── Cuisine Filter
  ├── Dietary Filter
  └── Allergy Filter
```

Authentication should not be required for normal Recipe search.

Guest search/filter requests must not attempt to load user-profile defaults.

## Allergy Filtering

Allergy filtering should be treated separately from ordinary cuisine preferences.

If a Recipe contains an Ingredient associated with an active excluded Allergen, that Recipe should not be returned.

Conceptually:

```text
Recipe
  │
  ├── Ingredient
  ├── Ingredient
  └── Ingredient
         │
         ▼
      Allergen
         │
         ▼
Active Allergy Exclusion
         │
         ▼
Recipe Excluded
```

Allergy checks must use the canonical structured Ingredient/Allergen relationships established by the data model.

Do not infer allergens from Recipe names, Ingredient display strings, descriptions, or frontend logic when structured Allergen data exists.

### Example

Suppose:

```text
Recipe: Peanut Noodles

Ingredients:
├── Noodles
├── Soy Sauce
└── Peanut Butter
       │
       ▼
Allergen: Peanut
```

With:

```text
?allergy=peanut
```

the Recipe should be excluded from the returned results.

The backend remains authoritative for this behavior.

## Duplicate Result Prevention

Filtering through Tags, Ingredients, and Allergens may introduce joins across many-to-many or one-to-many relationships.

A Recipe must appear only once in the API result set even if multiple related records satisfy the query.

Conceptually, avoid:

```text
Recipe A
Recipe A
Recipe A
Recipe B
```

The API should return:

```text
Recipe A
Recipe B
```

Use appropriate ORM query construction and deduplication such as `distinct()` where required by the final relationship/query design.

## Search vs. Recommendation

Keep these responsibilities separate.

### Recipe Search

Answers:

> What Recipes match the filters/search criteria I selected?

```text
Search + Filters
       │
       ▼
Recipe Query
       │
       ▼
Matching Recipes
```

Search operates on Recipe properties and classifications.

### Recommendation Engine

Answers:

> What Recipes can I make, or almost make, with the Ingredients I have?

```text
Available Ingredients
       │
       ▼
RecommendationService
       │
       ▼
Recipe Matches
```

Recommendation logic may consider:

```text
Inventory
Missing Ingredients
Ingredient Coverage
Match Scores
```

These responsibilities do not belong in Recipe search/filtering.

Search/filter functionality must not duplicate `RecommendationService`.

## Dependencies

**Blocked by:**

- Backend: Implement Ingredient Foundation
- Backend: Implement Recipe Models & API

User-specific default filtering additionally depends on:

- Backend: Implement User Profile & Preferences

Basic Guest search/filtering can be implemented before authentication integration is complete.

Conceptually:

```text
Ingredient Foundation ────────┐
                              │
Recipe Models & API ──────────┼──→ Recipe Search & Filtering
                              │
User Profile & Preferences ───┘
           │
           └──→ User-specific defaults
                (additional dependency)
```

The core Recipe search/filter functionality should not be blocked by authentication if Guest filtering can already be implemented.

## Important

Filtering should use structured application data rather than trying to infer Recipe properties from Recipe names or descriptions.

For example, avoid logic such as:

```python
if "vegan" in recipe.description.lower():
    ...
```

Recipe filtering should use the fields and relationships established by the application's data model.

### Recipe Classification

Recipe classifications should use the shared `Tag` system defined in `docs/database-design.md`.

Examples:

```text
DIET     → Vegan, Vegetarian, Halal
CUISINE  → Korean, Vietnamese, Italian
COST     → Cheap, Moderate, Expensive
OTHER    → Quick, High Protein, Easy
```

Conceptually:

```text
Recipe
  │
  └── RecipeTag
          │
          ▼
         Tag
          │
          ├── type/category
          └── value
```

Search/filter logic should reuse this shared classification system rather than creating separate cuisine/diet classification systems.

## Do NOT

- Implement ingredient recommendation matching here
- Duplicate `RecommendationService`
- Use user Inventory as part of normal Recipe search
- Implement filtering primarily in React
- Trust frontend filtering as authoritative
- Load the entire Recipe table into Python memory for normal filtering
- Perform allergy filtering only on the frontend
- Infer dietary status from Recipe names or descriptions
- Infer allergy status from Recipe names or descriptions
- Infer cuisine from Recipe names or descriptions
- Create duplicate Ingredient models
- Create a separate classification system when the shared Tag system already supports it
- Return duplicate Recipes because of relationship joins
- Require authentication for normal Recipe search
- Allow Guests to access Registered User preference data
- Construct raw SQL directly from untrusted query parameters
- Implement AI-based Recipe classification
- Implement Shopping Lists
- Implement Reviews
- Modify unrelated Django apps
- Change shared models or API contracts without discussing it with the team

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Recipes can be browsed without authentication
- [ ] Recipes can be searched by supported name/title fields

Title: Infrastructure: Amazon Cognito Authentication Integration
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Integrate Amazon Cognito as the application's authentication provider.

Users should be able to:

- Create an account
- Verify their account
- Sign in
- Sign out
- Maintain authenticated application state
- Access authenticated application functionality

The React frontend will authenticate users through Amazon Cognito and send the resulting authentication token with protected API requests to the Django backend.

Django remains responsible for:

- Application authorization
- Application-specific user data
- Resource ownership
- Permissions
- Mapping Cognito identities to application users

Authentication and authorization must remain separate responsibilities.

## Where to Work

This task affects multiple parts of the project.

### Frontend

`frontend/`

Primary locations:

- `frontend/src/features/auth/` — authentication UI and frontend authentication logic
- `frontend/src/services/api/apiClient.js` — attaching authentication tokens to API requests
- `frontend/src/pages/` — login/signup/verification/onboarding pages
- `frontend/.env.example` — public Cognito configuration

Use the existing shared API client:

`frontend/src/services/api/apiClient.js`

Do not create a separate API client specifically for authentication.

### Backend

`backend/`

Primary locations may include:

- `backend/apps/users/` — application User/Profile integration
- Django REST Framework authentication/permission configuration
- `backend/config/settings.py` — authentication configuration
- relevant authentication utilities/middleware
- authentication and authorization tests

### AWS

Configure the required Amazon Cognito resources for the application.

Relevant documentation:

- `frontend/README.md`
- `backend/README.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `docs/api-design.md`
- `docs/aws-architecture.md`
- `docs/database-design.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Authentication Architecture

The intended authentication flow is:

```text id="ckf5ba"
User
 │
 ▼
React
 │
 │ Sign Up / Sign In
 ▼
Amazon Cognito
 │
 │ Authentication
 ▼
JWT Token
 │
 ▼
React
 │
 │ Authorization: Bearer <token>
 ▼
Shared apiClient
 │
 ▼
Django REST API
 │
 │ Validate Token
 ▼
Authenticated Cognito Identity
 │
 ▼
Application User
 │
 ▼
Authorization / Ownership Check
 │
 ▼
Protected Resource
```

Amazon Cognito is responsible for authentication.

Django is responsible for application data and authorization.

```text id="ydwz2m"
Amazon Cognito
├── Identity
├── Signup
├── Login
├── Password handling
├── Account verification
└── Authentication tokens

Django
├── User/Profile
├── Preferences
├── Allergies
├── Inventory
├── Saved Recipes
├── Reviews
├── Resource ownership
└── Permissions
```

Cognito authentication does **not** replace Django authorization.

A valid Cognito token proves identity. Django must still determine what that identity is allowed to access.

## Identity Mapping

Each authenticated Cognito identity must map to the appropriate application User.

The mapping must use a stable Cognito identity identifier according to the documented authentication/database design.

Conceptually:

```text id="ax9azl"
Cognito User
     │
     │ stable identity
     ▼
Application User
     │
     ├── Profile
     ├── Preferences
     ├── Allergies
     ├── Inventory
     └── Saved Recipes
```

Do not rely on mutable display information such as a username or email address as the only application ownership identifier if the selected Cognito flow provides a stable identity identifier.

Repeated authenticated requests from the same Cognito identity must resolve to the same application User.

Concurrent or repeated first-time requests must not create duplicate application User records.

The exact mapping strategy must follow `docs/database-design.md` and `docs/system-design.md`.

## Tasks

### AWS / Cognito

- [ ] Create/configure a Cognito User Pool
- [ ] Create/configure the application client
- [ ] Configure signup/sign-in behavior
- [ ] Configure account verification

- [ ] Configure appropriate development URLs/settings
- [ ] Configure production-compatible settings where applicable

- [ ] Ensure the selected app client configuration is appropriate for a browser-based React application

### Frontend

- [ ] Implement Sign Up interface
- [ ] Implement account verification interface
- [ ] Implement Sign In interface
- [ ] Implement Sign Out
- [ ] Track authenticated user state
- [ ] Restore authenticated state appropriately after application reload
- [ ] Display logged-in user state in the application UI
- [ ] Protect Registered User routes where appropriate
- [ ] Attach authentication token to protected backend requests through `apiClient`
- [ ] Handle expired authentication state
- [ ] Handle invalid authentication state
- [ ] Handle unauthorized API responses appropriately
- [ ] Clear authenticated state appropriately on Sign Out
- [ ] Allow users to continue to optional onboarding after registration
- [ ] Avoid duplicating authentication-token logic across components/services

### Backend

- [ ] Validate Cognito-issued authentication tokens
- [ ] Validate token signature
- [ ] Validate token issuer
- [ ] Validate token expiration
- [ ] Validate audience/client/token-use claims as required by the selected Cognito token flow
- [ ] Reject malformed tokens
- [ ] Reject expired tokens
- [ ] Reject tokens issued by an unexpected User Pool
- [ ] Reject tokens that do not satisfy the expected application/token-use requirements
- [ ] Associate authenticated Cognito identities with application Users
- [ ] Prevent duplicate application Users for the same Cognito identity
- [ ] Expose authenticated User information through `/api/users/me/`

- [ ] Protect Admin endpoints appropriately
- [ ] Enforce ownership after authentication
- [ ] Ensure Guest/public endpoints remain accessible without authentication
- [ ] Add authentication/permission tests

## JWT Validation

Django must independently validate authentication tokens received from the frontend.

Conceptually:

```text id="h4c01b"
Incoming JWT
     │
     ▼
Parse Token
     │
     ▼
Verify Signature
     │
     ▼
Verify Issuer
     │
     ▼
Verify Expiration
     │
     ▼
Verify Expected Client/Audience
     │
     ▼
Verify Expected Token Use
     │
     ▼
Extract Stable Cognito Identity
     │
     ▼
Resolve Application User
```

Do not consider a token valid merely because it can be decoded.

Token claims must be cryptographically verified according to the selected Cognito flow.

## Cognito Public Keys / JWKS

Cognito JWT signature verification requires trusted public signing keys.

The backend should retrieve and use the appropriate Cognito public key set according to the selected AWS/Cognito architecture.

Public signing keys should be cached appropriately rather than unnecessarily retrieving them from Cognito for every authenticated API request.

Conceptually, avoid:

```text id="px8olx"
API Request
    ↓
Download Cognito Keys
    ↓
Validate Token

API Request
    ↓
Download Cognito Keys
    ↓
Validate Token

API Request
    ↓
Download Cognito Keys
```

Prefer:

```text id="7t1ch7"
Cognito Public Keys
        │
        ▼
Validated / Cached Key Set
        │
        ├── Request 1
        ├── Request 2
        ├── Request 3
        └── ...
```

The implementation must still support safe key refresh/rotation when Cognito signing keys change.

Do not permanently hardcode signing keys into the application.

## Security Design Requirements

### Authentication

- Use Cognito-issued tokens for authentication.
- Django must independently validate received tokens.
- Token signature must be verified.
- Token issuer must be verified.
- Token expiration must be verified.
- Audience/client and token-use claims must be validated as appropriate to the selected Cognito flow.
- Expired tokens must be rejected.
- Invalid tokens must be rejected.
- Malformed tokens must be rejected.
- Tokens from an unexpected Cognito configuration must be rejected.

### Authorization

- Authorization must still be enforced by Django after authentication.
- A valid token does not automatically authorize access to arbitrary resources.
- User-specific resources must verify ownership.
- Admin functionality must require appropriate backend permissions.
- Frontend route protection is a UX feature and must not be treated as backend security.

### Credentials / Secrets

- AWS credentials must never be shipped to the browser.
- Cognito configuration that is public by design must be distinguished from actual secrets.
- Secrets must not be committed to source control.
- Tokens must not be hardcoded.
- Production authentication traffic must use HTTPS.
- IAM permissions must follow least privilege.

### Logging

Authentication events/errors should be observable through appropriate logging.

Do not log:

- Full JWTs
- Authentication credentials
- Passwords
- Sensitive token contents
- Secrets

Logs may include safe operational information needed for debugging and monitoring.

## Authentication Performance / Scalability

Authentication is performed on protected API requests and must not introduce an unnecessary external network request for every API call.

Requirements:

- Cache Cognito public signing keys appropriately.
- Support safe signing-key refresh/rotation.
- Avoid querying Cognito directly for every protected API request when local JWT verification is sufficient.
- Application User lookup should use an indexed stable Cognito identity field.
- Cognito identity → application User lookup should be efficient.
- The Cognito identity mapping must enforce uniqueness where appropriate.
- Repeated requests from the same identity must not create duplicate User records.
- Authentication processing should remain stateless at the Django API layer where practical.
- Authentication failures should fail safely without exposing internal security details.

Conceptually:

```text id="lvhw61"
Request
   │
   ▼
JWT Validation
   │
   ▼
Indexed Identity Lookup
   │
   ▼
Application User
   │
   ▼
Authorization
```

Avoid:

```text id="z8ucpu"
Request
   │
   ▼
External Cognito Request
   │
   ▼
Multiple User Lookups
   │
   ▼
Protected Resource
```

for every normal authenticated API request when the token can be validated locally using cached trusted signing keys.

Authentication endpoints/protected API behavior should be included in later system load/performance testing.

- [ ] Missing authentication is rejected for protected endpoints

## Account Creation Flow

Conceptually:

```text id="4bfmqv"
Sign Up
   │
   ▼
Cognito
   │
   ▼
Verification
   │
   ▼
Account Verified
   │
   ▼
Sign In / Authenticated Session
   │
   ▼
Application User
   │
   ▼
Optional Onboarding
   │
   ├── Allergies
   ├── Dietary Preferences
   └── Cuisine Preferences
   │
   ├── Save
   └── Skip
   │
   ▼
Dashboard
```

Preference onboarding is optional.

Users must not be prevented from using their account because they skipped preference setup.

Application-specific preferences should be stored in the application's database rather than treating Cognito as the primary application-data store.

## Guest Access

Authentication must **not** be required for functionality intended for Guests.

Guests should continue to be able to:

- Search/select Ingredients
- Submit temporary Ingredient selections
- Request Recipe recommendations
- Search Recipes
- Filter Recipes
- View Recipe details

Registered Users receive additional functionality such as:

- Persistent Inventory
- Profile/preferences
- Saved Recipes
- Reviews when implemented
- Other account-specific features

Conceptually:

```text id="0k9nhp"
Guest
  │
  └── Public Features

Registered User
  │
  ├── All Guest Features
  └── Account Features

Admin
  │
  ├── All Registered User Features
  └── Administrative Features
```

Authentication integration must not accidentally convert public Recipe or Recommendation endpoints into protected endpoints.

## API Authentication

Protected requests should conceptually use:

```http id="j4fr9e"
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The shared frontend API client should be responsible for attaching authentication information.

```text id="nmtmvf"
Component
    │
    ▼
Domain Service
    │
    ▼
apiClient
    │
    ├── Base URL
    ├── Common Headers
    └── Authentication Token
    │
    ▼
Django REST API
```

Individual components should not manually attach authentication tokens.

Individual domain services should not independently reimplement token-handling logic.

## Authentication Failure Behavior

Authentication failures should return the appropriate API response according to `docs/api-design.md`.

Conceptually:

```text id="o10k97"
Missing / Invalid / Expired Authentication
              │
              ▼
Appropriate Authentication Error
              │
              ▼
Frontend Handles Authentication State
```

The frontend should handle authentication failures consistently.

For example, depending on the documented application behavior, it may:

- Clear invalid authenticated state
- Prompt the user to sign in again
- Redirect from protected pages
- Preserve public Guest functionality

Do not expose sensitive validation details to clients unnecessarily.

## Frontend Token Handling

Authentication state and token handling should be centralized through the selected Cognito authentication integration.

Do not:

```text id="uy9i08"
Component A → stores its own token
Component B → stores its own token
Component C → stores its own token
```

Prefer:

```text id="pgfzvo"
Authentication Layer
        │
        ▼
Authenticated State
        │
        ▼
Shared apiClient
        │
        ▼
Protected API Requests
```

The exact token/session storage mechanism should follow the selected Cognito frontend library and the documented project security architecture.

Do not introduce a custom token-storage approach independently.

## Google Sign-In

Google authentication is a desired authentication option, but it may be integrated separately if necessary.

The authentication architecture should not prevent adding Google as a Cognito federated identity provider later.

Conceptually:

```text id="jz7t2o"
Email/Password ──┐
                 │
Google ──────────┼──→ Cognito ──→ Application
                 │
Future Provider ─┘
```

Do not implement a separate Google-specific application authentication system outside Cognito.

Google authentication should eventually federate through the agreed Cognito authentication architecture.

## Email / Phone Verification

Account verification should use capabilities provided by Cognito.

Initial implementation may use email verification for simplicity.

Phone verification can be added if required by the project scope.

Do not build a custom verification-code system in Django.

## Environment Configuration

Do not hardcode Cognito configuration throughout the application.

Frontend configuration that is safe to expose to the browser should use Vite environment variables where appropriate.

For example:

```env id="4nlg5n"
VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID=
VITE_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID=
VITE_COGNITO_REGION=
```

Update `.env.example` with required variable names but **do not commit secrets**.

Values intentionally exposed to a browser application must still be distinguished from AWS credentials or other sensitive secrets.

Backend/AWS-sensitive configuration should use the project's documented environment/secret-management approach.

Production and development configuration should be separable without requiring source-code changes.

## Dependencies

**Blocked by:**

- Backend: Implement User Profile & Preferences
- Frontend: Implement Application Foundation

The task can be developed independently of Recipes and Recommendations.

Conceptually:

```text id="mq7z3u"
Frontend Foundation ──────┐
                          │
Amazon Cognito ───────────┼──→ Authentication Integration
                          │
User/Profile Backend ─────┘
```

Authentication Integration then enables account-specific features such as:

```text id="jclngd"
Authentication Integration
          │
          ├──→ Persistent Inventory
          ├──→ Saved Recipes
          ├──→ User Preferences
          └──→ Reviews
```

Public Guest functionality should not depend on authentication integration.

## Important

Authentication and authorization are different responsibilities.

```text id="kbq4ta"
Authentication
"Who are you?"
       │
       ▼
Amazon Cognito

Authorization
"What are you allowed to do?"
       │
       ▼
Django
```

A request can therefore be:

```text id="it0as5"
Authenticated
     ✓

Authorized
     ✗
```

For example:

```text id="rb9ff5"
User A
  │
  │ Valid Cognito Token
  ▼
Django
  │
  │ Attempts User B Resource
  ▼
403 / Access Rejected
```

Django must still enforce ownership and permissions even if the frontend hides protected functionality.

## Do NOT

- Build a separate username/password authentication database
- Store user passwords in Django
- Implement custom password hashing/authentication
- Build a custom email verification-code system
- Treat decoding a JWT as sufficient validation
- Accept tokens without verifying their signature
- Trust frontend authorization checks as security
- Treat a valid Cognito token as permission to access arbitrary resources
- Allow users to select another application's User identity through request parameters
- Create duplicate application Users for the same Cognito identity
- Put application preferences/inventory primarily in Cognito
- Hardcode Cognito signing keys
- Hardcode tokens
- Hardcode AWS credentials
- Commit secrets
- Log complete authentication tokens
- Store authentication tokens independently in arbitrary components
- Manually attach tokens in every feature service
- Create another API client for authenticated requests
- Call `fetch()` directly from React components for protected API calls
- Contact Cognito unnecessarily for every normal protected API request when local token verification is sufficient
- Require authentication for Guest functionality
- Implement Google authentication outside the agreed Cognito architecture
- Modify unrelated application features
- Change the authentication architecture without discussing it with the team

Title: Frontend: Implement Profile, Preferences & Allergies UI
Author: sophia-dao
Description:
## Goal

Implement the frontend interface that allows Registered Users to view and manage their profile, dietary preferences, cuisine preferences, and allergies.

Preferences and allergies are optional during onboarding but should be saved to the user's account when provided.

These settings will later be used automatically as default filters when generating Recipe recommendations and may also be used by other Recipe filtering functionality.

This task is responsible for the frontend interface and API integration only.

The backend remains authoritative for:

- User identity
- Profile data validation
- Supported preference/allergy values
- Authorization
- Recommendation/filtering behavior

## Where to Work

Frontend code is located in:

`frontend/`

Primary locations for this task:

- `frontend/src/features/profile/` — Profile and preference components/logic
- `frontend/src/pages/` — Profile page
- `frontend/src/services/api/userService.js` — User/Profile API calls
- `frontend/src/components/common/` — reusable components where appropriate

Use the existing shared API client:

`frontend/src/services/api/apiClient.js`

Do not create another API client.

Relevant documentation:

- `frontend/README.md`
- `docs/requirements.md`
- `docs/api-design.md`
- `docs/system-design.md`
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`

## Tasks

### API Service

- [ ] Create `frontend/src/services/api/userService.js`
- [ ] Use the existing shared `apiClient`
- [ ] Implement Profile API methods according to `docs/api-design.md`
- [ ] Implement Preferences API methods according to `docs/api-design.md`
- [ ] Implement Allergies API methods according to `docs/api-design.md`
- [ ] Do not expose arbitrary User IDs through Profile service methods

### Profile

- [ ] Implement the Profile page
- [ ] Retrieve the authenticated User's Profile
- [ ] Display basic User information
- [ ] Allow supported Profile information to be updated
- [ ] Distinguish editable and non-editable Profile fields
- [ ] Initialize form state from API data
- [ ] Handle Profile validation errors

### Dietary Preferences

- [ ] Display current dietary preferences
- [ ] Allow dietary preferences to be selected
- [ ] Allow dietary preferences to be removed
- [ ] Use supported values from the backend/API where available
- [ ] Avoid duplicating preference values in frontend state

### Cuisine Preferences

- [ ] Display current cuisine preferences
- [ ] Allow cuisine preferences to be selected
- [ ] Allow cuisine preferences to be removed
- [ ] Use supported values from the backend/API where available
- [ ] Avoid duplicating preference values in frontend state

### Allergies

- [ ] Display current allergies
- [ ] Allow allergies to be added
- [ ] Allow allergies to be removed
- [ ] Clearly distinguish allergies from ordinary preferences
- [ ] Use supported Allergen values from the backend/API where available
- [ ] Avoid duplicating Allergy values in frontend state

### Save / Update Behavior

- [ ] Implement appropriate save/update behavior
- [ ] Prevent accidental duplicate submissions while a save is in progress
- [ ] Disable or otherwise handle Save appropriately while submitting
- [ ] Update displayed state after a successful save
- [ ] Preserve appropriate form state when validation fails
- [ ] Provide success feedback after saving
- [ ] Display backend validation errors appropriately
- [ ] Handle API/network errors
- [ ] Avoid falsely showing success before the backend confirms the update

### UI State

- [ ] Handle initial loading state
- [ ] Handle saving/updating state
- [ ] Handle API error state
- [ ] Handle validation error state
- [ ] Handle empty optional-preference state
- [ ] Avoid rendering stale Profile data after successful updates
- [ ] Handle navigation/reload without depending on local-only Profile state

### Onboarding

- [ ] Support reuse of the same preference interface/components during optional onboarding where practical
- [ ] Allow onboarding preference setup to be skipped
- [ ] Ensure skipped preferences can be configured later from the Profile page

### Accessibility / Usability

- [ ] Use accessible labels for Profile controls
- [ ] Ensure preference/allergy controls are keyboard accessible
- [ ] Make selected/unselected states visually understandable
- [ ] Make validation and API errors understandable to the user
- [ ] Do not rely only on color to communicate selection/error state

## Security & Scalability Requirements

### Security

- User identity must come from authenticated context.
- Frontend Profile operations must target the current authenticated User.
- Frontend must not be capable of selecting another User ID for Profile updates.
- `userService` methods for `/api/users/me/...` must not accept arbitrary User IDs.
- Backend validation remains authoritative.
- Backend authorization remains authoritative.
- Frontend route protection must not be treated as the security boundary.
- Avoid storing private Profile data unnecessarily in browser storage.
- Do not persist Profile, Allergy, or preference data in `localStorage` as the authoritative data source.
- Do not expose sensitive authentication information through Profile components.
- Do not log private Profile information unnecessarily.
- API error handling should not expose sensitive backend/internal information unnecessarily.

Conceptually:

```text id="5hkdkt"
Authenticated User
       │
       ▼
Profile Page
       │
       ▼
userService
       │
       ▼
apiClient
       │
       │ Authentication Token
       ▼
/api/users/me/...
       │
       ▼
Backend Determines User
```

Not:

```text id="s6s7t3"
Profile Page
     │
     ▼
Select user_id = 123
     │
     ▼
Update User 123
```

### Scalability / Performance

- Avoid unnecessary duplicate Profile/Preferences/Allergies API requests.
- Do not request the same data independently from multiple child components when it can be managed by the Profile feature/page.
- Do not issue an API request for every individual preference or Allergy item when the API supports bulk retrieval/update.
- Use the existing User/Profile endpoints rather than creating feature-specific duplicate endpoints.
- Supported preference/allergy options should come from shared application data/API contracts where available rather than requiring repeated frontend hardcoding.
- Profile updates should send only the data required by the documented API contract.
- Avoid unnecessary application-wide state for data used only by the Profile feature.
- Reusable Profile/preference components should be usable by both the Profile page and optional onboarding where practical.

Conceptually, avoid:

```text id="a9ryjn"
Profile Page
   │
   ├── Request Profile
   ├── Request Preference 1
   ├── Request Preference 2
   ├── Request Preference 3
   ├── Request Allergy 1
   ├── Request Allergy 2
   └── ...
```

Prefer the documented API structure:

```text id="g85wfj"
Profile Page
   │
   ├── Profile Request
   ├── Preferences Request
   └── Allergies Request
```

or another efficient structure defined by `docs/api-design.md`.

Do not introduce additional requests solely because the frontend component structure is split into smaller components.

## Additional Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Profile operations target the authenticated User
- [ ] No arbitrary User ID is accepted from the UI
- [ ] No arbitrary User ID is accepted by `userService` Profile methods
- [ ] Backend validation errors are handled correctly
- [ ] Private Profile information is not unnecessarily persisted locally
- [ ] Duplicate save requests are prevented while an update is in progress
- [ ] Successful state is shown only after backend confirmation
- [ ] Frontend state reflects the successfully persisted backend state
- [ ] Preference/Allergy controls do not create duplicate selections
- [ ] Profile components do not introduce unnecessary duplicate API requests

## Expected Interface

The exact design is flexible.

Conceptually:

```text id="y5iqgr"
------------------------------------------
Profile
------------------------------------------

Alex
user@example.com

[ Avatar / Placeholder ]

Dietary Preferences

☑ Halal
☐ Vegan
☐ Vegetarian

Cuisine Preferences

[ Vietnamese × ]
[ Korean × ]

Allergies

[ Peanut × ]
[ Shellfish × ]

[ Save Changes ]
------------------------------------------
```

Do not hardcode the exact available values if the backend/API provides them dynamically.

Allergies should be visually and conceptually distinguishable from ordinary cuisine/dietary preferences.

For example:

```text id="rwnkyi"
Preferences
├── Dietary
│   ├── Halal
│   ├── Vegan
│   └── Vegetarian
│
└── Cuisine
    ├── Vietnamese
    └── Korean

Allergies
├── Peanut
└── Shellfish
```

## API

Use the User/Profile APIs documented in:

`docs/api-design.md`

Expected endpoints include:

```text id="ngn76e"
GET   /api/users/me/
PATCH /api/users/me/

GET   /api/users/me/preferences/
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences/

GET /api/users/me/allergies/
PUT /api/users/me/allergies/
```

Create:

`frontend/src/services/api/userService.js`

Conceptually:

```javascript id="nq50zr"
import { apiClient } from "./apiClient";

export const userService = {
  getProfile() {
    return apiClient.get("/api/users/me/");
  },

  updateProfile(data) {
    return apiClient.patch("/api/users/me/", data);
  },

  getPreferences() {
    return apiClient.get("/api/users/me/preferences/");
  },

  updatePreferences(data) {
    return apiClient.patch("/api/users/me/preferences/", data);
  },

  getAllergies() {
    return apiClient.get("/api/users/me/allergies/");
  },

  updateAllergies(data) {
    return apiClient.put("/api/users/me/allergies/", data);
  },
};
```

The exact request/response structures must follow `docs/api-design.md`.

Do not modify the shared API contract independently.

### User Identity

Notice that these service methods do **not** accept:

```javascript id="8tj31f"
getProfile(userId)
updateProfile(userId, data)
```

Instead:

```javascript id="j5c6g8"
getProfile()
updateProfile(data)
```

because:

```text id="2ylx3v"
Authenticated Session
       │
       ▼
apiClient
       │
       ▼
Django
       │
       ▼
Authenticated User
```

determines ownership.

The frontend should never need to send an arbitrary `user_id` to update the current User's Profile.

## Data Loading

When the Profile page loads:

```text id="t99a2b"
Profile Page
     │
     ▼
Loading
     │
     ├── Profile
     ├── Preferences
     └── Allergies
     │
     ▼
Initialize Form State
     │
     ▼
Display Profile
```

Do not display stale/default form values as though they were confirmed User settings while API data is still loading.

If one request fails, the UI should handle the failure according to the application's documented error-handling behavior rather than silently treating missing data as confirmed empty preferences.

## Save Behavior

Conceptually:

```text id="75v8uw"
User Changes Settings
        │
        ▼
[ Save Changes ]
        │
        ▼
Saving...
        │
        ▼
Backend Validation
        │
        ├── Success
        │      │
        │      ▼
        │  Update UI State
        │      │
        │      ▼
        │  Success Feedback
        │
        └── Error
               │
               ▼
        Preserve Form State
               │
               ▼
        Display Error
```

Do not optimistically treat Profile data as permanently saved if the backend request fails unless the project deliberately implements an optimistic-update strategy with appropriate rollback behavior.

While a save request is in progress, the interface should prevent accidental repeated submissions.

## Validation

Frontend validation may improve usability, but backend validation remains authoritative.

Conceptually:

```text id="kx8tqg"
Frontend Validation
        │
        │ UX / Early Feedback
        ▼
Backend Validation
        │
        │ Authoritative
        ▼
Persisted Data
```

If the backend rejects an update:

```text id="8gl82b"
Save
 │
 ▼
Backend Validation Error
 │
 ▼
Display Appropriate Error
 │
 ▼
User Corrects Input
```

Do not silently discard backend validation errors.

## Optional Onboarding

Preference setup should **not** be required to create or use an account.

Conceptually:

```text id="l01q8h"
Account Created
      │
      ▼
Optional Preference Setup
      │
      ├── Dietary Preferences
      ├── Cuisine Preferences
      └── Allergies
      │
      ├── Save → Continue
      │
      └── Skip → Continue
```

A User who skips onboarding should be able to configure these settings later from the Profile page.

Skipping onboarding should conceptually result in:

```text id="1hdm7f"
Account
   │
   ├── Dietary Preferences: none
   ├── Cuisine Preferences: none
   └── Allergies: none
```

rather than preventing access to the application.

Where practical, reuse Profile preference components:

```text id="v58u6d"
Preference Components
        │
        ├──→ Optional Onboarding
        │
        └──→ Profile Page
```

Do not build two unrelated implementations of the same preference-selection interface unless their requirements genuinely differ.

## Recommendation Integration

This task stores and manages User preferences.

It does **not** implement Recipe recommendation/filtering logic itself.

Later:

```text id="39e7oh"
User Preferences
       │
       ▼
Django Backend
       │
       ▼
RecommendationService
       │
       ▼
Filtered Recommendations
```

For example:

```text id="4o6zjo"
Profile:
Diet = Halal
Allergy = Peanut

        ↓

Saved to Backend

        ↓

Future Recommendation Request

        ↓

RecommendationService applies
supported defaults/exclusions
```

The frontend should not independently decide which Recipes satisfy the User's saved dietary preferences or allergies.

The backend Recommendation Service remains responsible for applying saved preferences and allergies.

## Allergy Handling

Allergies must remain conceptually separate from ordinary preferences.

```text id="b07ag3"
Cuisine Preference
"I prefer Korean food"

Dietary Preference
"I follow a Halal diet"

Allergy
"I must avoid Peanut"
```

The Profile frontend is responsible for allowing the User to manage these values.

It is **not** responsible for determining whether a Recipe contains an Allergen.

That behavior belongs to backend Recipe filtering/recommendation logic using structured Recipe/Ingredient/Allergen data.

## Authentication Integration

Full authenticated behavior depends on Amazon Cognito integration.

Conceptually:

```text id="54u6a4"
Amazon Cognito
      │
      ▼
Authenticated User
      │
      ▼
apiClient
      │
      ▼
User/Profile API
      │
      ▼
Profile Page
```

The Profile feature should use authentication state provided by the application's authentication architecture.

Do not build authentication logic directly into Profile components.

The Profile page may be developed against the backend API before Cognito integration is complete, but the final implementation must use the application's shared authentication flow.

## Dependencies

**Blocked by:**

- Frontend: Implement Application Foundation
- Backend: Implement User Profile & Preferences

Full authenticated behavior additionally depends on:

- Authentication: Integrate Amazon Cognito

Conceptually:

```text id="fgl5sz"
Frontend Foundation ───────────┐
                               │
User Profile Backend ──────────┼──→ Frontend Profile
                               │
Cognito Authentication ────────┘
        │
        └──→ Full authenticated integration
```

Basic interface/component and service development may proceed before Cognito integration is complete if the User/Profile API contract is already established.

## Important

Preferences should remain optional.

The frontend should not prevent Users from accessing normal application functionality simply because they have not configured dietary or cuisine preferences.

Allergies should be clearly distinguishable from general preferences.

The backend remains the authoritative source for persisted Profile/preference/Allergy data.

Conceptually:

```text id="49dxbp"
Frontend State
     │
     │ edits
     ▼
Backend API
     │
     │ validation + persistence
     ▼
Application Database
```

The frontend should not become an independent source of truth for Profile data.

## Do NOT

- Create another API client
- Call `fetch()` directly from components
- Hardcode backend URLs
- Hardcode User identity
- Accept arbitrary User IDs through Profile service methods
- Build a separate authentication system
- Implement Cognito authentication directly inside Profile components
- Require preference onboarding
- Block normal application access because optional preferences are empty
- Implement recommendation matching in React
- Implement Recipe filtering in this feature
- Implement Allergy filtering in React as the authoritative filter
- Determine Recipe allergen safety in the Profile frontend
- Store User preferences only in `localStorage`
- Treat browser storage as the authoritative Profile data source
- Store private Profile information unnecessarily in browser storage
- Hardcode preference/Allergy values when the backend/API provides them dynamically
- Send one API request for every individual preference/Allergy when bulk update endpoints exist
- Allow duplicate preference/Allergy selections
- Show a successful save before the backend confirms the update
- Implement Inventory functionality in this feature
- Implement AI preference detection
- Modify unrelated frontend features
- Change shared API contracts without discussing it with the team

## Matching Mode 1: `AVAILABLE_ONLY`

Return Recipes whose **required Ingredients are all available** to the User.

Example:

```text
User has:

Egg
Cabbage
Soy Sauce
Kimchi
```

Recipe requires:

```text
Egg
```

Result:

```text
✓ MATCH
```

Recipe requires:

```text
Egg
Cabbage
```

Result:

```text
✓ MATCH
```

Recipe requires:

```text
Egg
Soy Sauce
Kimchi
```

Result:

```text
✓ MATCH
```

Recipe requires:

```text
Egg
Chicken Breast
```

Result:

```text
✗ NO MATCH
```

A Recipe does **not** need to use every Ingredient the User has.

The rule is:

```text
Required Recipe Ingredients ⊆ Available User Ingredients
```

For example:

```text
User Ingredients:

A, B, C, D, E

Recipe requires:

A, C

Result:

MATCH
```

Unused User Ingredients do not affect eligibility.

### Optional Ingredients

Optional Recipe Ingredients must not cause an otherwise valid Recipe to fail `AVAILABLE_ONLY`.

For example:

```text
User has:

Egg
Rice

Recipe:

Required:
- Egg
- Rice

Optional:
- Green Onion
```

The User does not have Green Onion.

Result:

```text
✓ MATCH
```

because all **required** Ingredients are available.

Optional Ingredients may be included in presentation metadata if the API contract requires them, but they must not be treated as missing required Ingredients.

## Matching Mode 2: `PARTIAL_MATCH`

Return Recipes that use at least some of the Ingredients available to the User, even if additional required Ingredients are missing.

Example:

```text
User has:

Egg
Cabbage
Soy Sauce
Kimchi
```

Recipe requires:

```text
Egg             ✓ Available
Chicken Breast  ✗ Missing
Soy Sauce       ✓ Available
Rice            ✗ Missing
```

The Recipe may still appear.

The result should identify:

```text
Matched Required Ingredients
Missing Required Ingredients
Match Score
```

Conceptually:

```text
Available Ingredients
        │
        ▼
Required Recipe Ingredients
        │
        ├── Intersection → Matched
        │
        └── Difference   → Missing
```

Recipes with stronger required-Ingredient overlap should generally appear before weaker matches.

The exact ordering must remain deterministic.

## Match Score

For the initial implementation, use the deterministic score defined by the project:

```text
match_score =
matched_required_ingredients / total_required_ingredients
```

Example:

```text
Recipe requires 5 Ingredients.

User has 4 of them.

match_score = 4 / 5 = 0.80
```

The API may represent this according to `docs/api-design.md`, for example:

```text
0.80
```

or:

```text
80%
```

Follow `docs/api-design.md` for the authoritative representation.

Do not independently introduce a different score format or algorithm.

### Required vs. Optional Ingredients

Only required Ingredients participate in the initial match-score denominator unless `docs/api-design.md` or another authoritative design document explicitly specifies otherwise.

For example:

```text
Required:
A
B
C

Optional:
D
E

User has:
A
B
D
```

Initial score:

```text
Matched required = 2
Total required   = 3

match_score = 2 / 3
```

The presence of optional Ingredient `D` does not change the required-Ingredient score.

### Zero Required Ingredients

The implementation must explicitly handle a Recipe with zero required Ingredients rather than performing division by zero.

Behavior for such Recipes should follow the Recipe data constraints and `docs/api-design.md`.

If the Recipe model guarantees at least one required Ingredient, validate/enforce that invariant in the appropriate owning layer rather than relying on Recommendation code to fail unexpectedly.

Do not silently invent a score formula for this edge case.

## Partial Match Eligibility

`PARTIAL_MATCH` should only return Recipes satisfying the overlap behavior established by the API/design.

Conceptually, for the initial behavior:

```text
Matched Required Ingredients > 0
```

Example:

```text
User:
A, B

Recipe:
A, C, D

Matched:
A

Missing:
C, D

Score:
1 / 3
```

Result:

```text
PARTIAL MATCH
```

Whereas:

```text
User:
A, B

Recipe:
C, D

Matched:
None
```

should not be treated as an Ingredient-based partial match unless the documented API contract explicitly defines zero-overlap results.

## Deterministic Ranking

`PARTIAL_MATCH` results should rank stronger matches ahead of weaker matches according to the documented matching rules.

Primary ordering:

```text

        ↓
Earlier result
```

```text

Recipe B: 0.75
Recipe C: 0.50
```

```text

2. Recipe B

```

### Tie-Breaking

Equal match scores must not produce unstable/unpredictable ordering.

Use a deterministic secondary ordering consistent with the application's API/database design.

For example, if no other product requirement exists, an existing stable Recipe field such as Recipe ID may be used as a final tie-breaker.

The important requirement is:

```text
Same Data + Same Request
        │
        ▼
Stable Result Ordering
```

This is particularly important for:

- Pagination
- Automated tests
- Load testing
- Consistent frontend behavior

Do not introduce random ranking.

```text

      │
      ▼
For each Recipe
      │
      ▼

      ▼
```

```text
        │

        │

        │
```

```text

prefetch_related()

annotate()
Count()
Q()
Exists()
Subquery()
```

The requirement is efficient query behavior, not use of a particular Django method.

### Avoid N+1 During Serialization

Query efficiency must include result serialization.

An implementation such as:

```text

      +
100 Result Recipes
      ×
Ingredient Query Per Recipe
```

still has an N+1 problem even if the initial Recipe query is efficient.

Required related data should be fetched efficiently before serialization.

Do not return an unbounded Recipe dataset if the application Recipe collection can grow significantly.

Stable ordering must be used with pagination.

### Database Indexing

Use the indexes and relationships defined by `docs/database-design.md`.

Frequently queried Recipe/Ingredient relationship fields should support efficient lookups.

Do not create redundant indexes without checking the existing model/database design.

Saved Inventory does not need to block implementation/testing of the core matching algorithm.

For example:

```text
Core RecommendationService
        │
        ├── Guest Ingredient IDs ✓
        │
        └── Inventory IDs        later integration
```

Do not create temporary replacement Ingredient, Recipe, Inventory, or User models while waiting for dependencies.

## Important

The Recommendation module owns Recipe matching logic.

It should answer:

> Given these available Ingredients, which Recipes match, which required Ingredients are present/missing, and what is the deterministic match score?

It should **not** own:

- User Inventory
- Recipe definitions
- Canonical Ingredient definitions
- User authentication
- User Profile data

Conceptually:

```text
Inventory
    │
    ▼
Available Ingredients
    │
    ▼
RecommendationService
    ▲
    │
Recipe Requirements
    ▲
    │
Recipes
```

Ownership remains:

```text
Ingredient App
    └── Canonical Ingredients

Recipe App
    └── Recipes + RecipeIngredient relationships

Inventory App
    └── User's saved Ingredients

Users App
    └── Profile / Preferences / Allergies

Recommendations App
    └── Matching + Recommendation result generation
```

This separation should be preserved.

- Create separate Recommendation Engines for Guests and Registered Users
- Create another Ingredient model
- Create another Recipe model
- Create another Inventory model
- Duplicate User/Profile models
- Store Guest Ingredients as persistent User Inventory
- Allow Guest requests to retrieve private Inventory
- Accept arbitrary `user_id` values for private Inventory Recommendation requests
- Count duplicate submitted Ingredient IDs multiple times
- Count optional Ingredients as required for `AVAILABLE_ONLY`
- Count optional Ingredients in the required-Ingredient match-score denominator unless explicitly required by the API contract
- Require a Recipe to use every Ingredient the User entered
- Perform division by zero for Recipes with no required Ingredients
- Implement Recommendation calculations in React
- Implement Recommendation calculations inside the Inventory app
- Implement Recommendation calculations inside the Recipe app
- Put all Recommendation business logic directly in the API view
- Execute one Ingredient query per Recipe
- Reintroduce N+1 queries during serialization
- Use random/non-deterministic ranking
- Implement AI/ML Recommendations
- Implement AI-generated Recipes
- Implement Shopping Lists as part of this task
- Implement Reviews as part of this task
- Modify unrelated Django apps
- Change shared models or API contracts without discussing it with the team

## Database Uniqueness

The same canonical Ingredient should not appear more than once in the same User's Inventory.

Conceptually:

```text
User A + Egg
      │
      ▼
InventoryItem #1

User A + Egg again
      │
      ▼
Rejected / Existing Relationship
```

But:

```text
User A + Egg
User B + Egg
```

is valid because each User maintains an independent Inventory.

The database should enforce uniqueness of:

```text
(user, ingredient)
```

using the constraint mechanism defined by the project's Django/database conventions.

Do not rely only on frontend duplicate prevention.

Do not rely only on a serializer check.

Conceptually:

```text
Frontend Prevention
        +
Serializer Validation
        +
Database Constraint
```

The database constraint is the final protection against duplicate relationships, including concurrent requests.

```json
}
```

```json

  "id": 42,
  "ingredient": {
    "id": 10,
    "name": "Egg"
  }
}
```

Do not confuse these identifiers when implementing retrieval, update, or deletion.

Inventory queries should remain efficient as the number of Users and Inventory Items grows.

- Inventory lookup should be scoped by authenticated User at the database level.
- User ownership fields should support efficient lookup.
- `(user, ingredient)` uniqueness should be enforced by the database.
- Related Ingredient information should be retrieved efficiently.
- Inventory serialization should avoid N+1 queries.

```text

```

must remain the final source of truth.

The API should handle a duplicate creation attempt according to the documented API behavior rather than creating two Inventory rows.

Conceptually:

```text
Application Validation
        │
        ▼
Database Constraint
        │
        ▼

(User, Ingredient)
```
